explanation.summary: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia prophylaxis in HIV is indicated when CD4 falls below 200 cells/microlitre, when the CD4 percentage falls below 14, or with a previous PJP episode. First-line is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (cotrimoxazole) 160/800 mg orally daily, with weekly thrice-daily dosing as an alternative. This dose also covers toxoplasmosis prophylaxis (indicated below CD4 100 with positive IgG). Prophylaxis can be stopped once CD4 sustains above 200 for at least 3 to 6 months on antiretroviral therapy. Mycobacterium avium complex prophylaxis with azithromycin is indicated below CD4 50.
key_points: PJP prophylaxis: cotrimoxazole when CD4 below 200 or below 14 percent.
Toxoplasma prophylaxis (cotrimoxazole) when CD4 below 100 plus IgG positive.
MAC prophylaxis (azithromycin) when CD4 below 50.
explanation.pearls: In sulfa allergy, alternatives include dapsone 100 mg daily after checking G6PD status, or atovaquone 1500 mg daily with food; pentamidine is reserved for cases when oral agents fail.

options.rationale: MAC prophylaxis is recommended when CD4 falls below 50 cells/microlitre, not at 250. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

Cryptococcal prophylaxis is not routinely recommended in Australia; cryptococcal antigen screening is used to drive pre-emptive therapy at lower CD4 thresholds. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)
Routine toxoplasmosis prophylaxis is initiated when CD4 falls below 100 with positive IgG; cotrimoxazole covers both at 250. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)
ASHM recommends Pneumocystis prophylaxis with cotrimoxazole when CD4 falls below 200 cells/microlitre or below 14 percent, and at 200 to 250 borderline cases. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)
Latent TB therapy depends on a positive QuantiFERON or tuberculin test, not on HIV status alone. (Source: ASHM HIV management guideline)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle for septic shock comprises: measure lactate (and remeasure if at or above 2 mmol/L), obtain blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad-spectrum antibiotics, begin rapid fluid resuscitation with 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate at or above 4 mmol/L, and start vasopressors if hypotension persists during or after fluid resuscitation to maintain mean arterial pressure at or above 65 mmHg. Source control is added as soon as feasible.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, fluid 30 mL/kg, vasopressors if needed.
Lactate above 4 mmol/L mandates fluid resuscitation regardless of blood pressure.
Target MAP 65 mmHg; start noradrenaline first-line if hypotension persists after fluids.
explanation.pearls: If lactate has not fallen by at least 10 percent after the initial 30 mL/kg, reassess for source control failure, occult bleeding, or evolving cardiogenic shock from sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy.

options.rationale: Septic shock with lactate at 4.2 mmol/L requires 30 mL/kg early fluid, not a 250 mL challenge approach. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Resuscitation runs in parallel with source identification; imaging must not delay fluids in shock. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Vasopressors are started for ongoing hypotension despite adequate fluid resuscitation, not as the first action. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Hydrocortisone is reserved for septic shock requiring ongoing noradrenaline at 0.25 mcg/kg/min or more, not first-line. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle for septic shock with lactate above 4 mmol/L includes 30 mL/kg fluid, broad-spectrum antibiotics, and lactate clearance reassessment. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Active pulmonary tuberculosis is diagnosed in any patient with consistent symptoms (cough at least 3 weeks, weight loss, night sweats), abnormal chest radiograph (especially upper lobe airspace disease with cavitation), and positive sputum acid-fast smear or culture. A positive QuantiFERON shows TB infection but cannot distinguish latent from active disease; the clinical and radiological picture does that. Standard induction is rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol (RIPE) for 2 months, then rifampicin and isoniazid for a further 4 months, with directly observed therapy ideally and public health notification mandatory.
key_points: Cavitating CXR plus smear-positive sputum equals active TB regardless of QFT.
RIPE for 2 months then RH for 4 months is standard sensitive-strain therapy.
Notify public health and isolate from the moment active TB is suspected.
explanation.pearls: Add pyridoxine 25 mg daily to any isoniazid-containing regimen to prevent peripheral neuropathy, particularly in malnourished, pregnant, or HIV-positive patients.

options.rationale: Cavitating CXR and smear-positive sputum indicate active TB, not latent, and require four-drug therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)
Empirical four-drug therapy should start immediately for smear-positive active TB; cultures and susceptibility refine the regimen later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

Active pulmonary TB with smear-positive disease mandates respiratory isolation, public health notification, and the standard RIPE regimen for 2 months induction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)
Rifampicin plus isoniazid for 3 months is a latent TB regimen and is inadequate for confirmed active disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

Fluoroquinolone monotherapy is contraindicated; it risks rapid resistance and is reserved for multidrug-resistant TB regimens under specialist supervision. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Antiviral therapy for laboratory-confirmed influenza is recommended for high-risk patients (chronic lung disease, chronic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, diabetes, immunocompromise, pregnancy or postpartum, age 65 or above, severe obesity, Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander adults, residents of aged care) and for any patient with severe illness. Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line; treatment within 48 hours is most effective but later treatment still reduces complications in high-risk groups. Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in chronic airway disease.
key_points: High-risk groups benefit from oseltamivir even after 48 hours.
Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days is first-line.
Avoid inhaled zanamivir in COPD or asthma due to bronchospasm risk.
explanation.pearls: Reduce oseltamivir to 30 mg twice daily for an eGFR of 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73m2, and to 30 mg daily for an eGFR of 10 to 30 mL/min/1.73m2; standard dosing risks accumulation toxicity in renal impairment.

options.rationale: The 48 hour rule applies to low-risk healthy outpatients; high-risk patients benefit even when treatment starts later. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)
Inhaled zanamivir is contraindicated in patients with underlying airway disease such as COPD because it can precipitate bronchospasm. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)
Amantadine is no longer recommended for seasonal influenza because of widespread resistance and a poor side effect profile. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)
Oseltamivir is recommended for high-risk groups including COPD even when symptoms have lasted beyond 48 hours, because of mortality benefit. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)
Supportive care alone misses the morbidity and mortality benefit of antiviral therapy in high-risk patients. (Source: CDNA influenza guidelines)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency in any patient with known adrenal insufficiency who is unwell, vomiting, or shocked. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat followed by 50 mg every 6 hours (or a continuous infusion of 200 mg per 24 hours), rapid 0.9% saline resuscitation 1 L over the first hour, glucose correction with 50 mL of 50% dextrose if hypoglycaemic, and treatment of any precipitant such as infection. High-dose hydrocortisone exerts sufficient mineralocorticoid effect that fludrocortisone is not needed during the acute phase. Sick-day rules: double oral hydrocortisone dose for intercurrent illness; switch to IM hydrocortisone for vomiting.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is the first parenteral dose in adrenal crisis.
Use 0.9 percent saline and glucose correction alongside steroid replacement.
Sick day rule: double oral steroid for intercurrent illness; IM hydrocortisone if vomiting.
explanation.pearls: Every Addison's patient should carry an emergency IM hydrocortisone kit (100 mg) and have a documented sick day plan; failure of community administration is a recurrent driver of preventable crisis admissions.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis requires parenteral therapy because oral absorption is unreliable in vomiting and shock. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)
Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and giving steroid alone without fluids fails to treat the hypovolaemia and hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)
Hyponatraemia in adrenal crisis is corrected by cortisol replacement and 0.9 percent saline; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

Fludrocortisone has no role in the acute resuscitation of adrenal crisis; hydrocortisone IV provides both glucocorticoid and partial mineralocorticoid effect. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)
Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, rapid saline resuscitation, and glucose correction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is a time-critical emergency. Where altered consciousness, focal neurology, seizure, immunocompromise, or papilloedema is present, CT must precede LP to exclude a mass lesion; however, antibiotics and adjunctive dexamethasone must not wait. Adjuvant dexamethasone 10 mg IV every 6 hours for 4 days, given before or with the first antibiotic, reduces mortality and neurological sequelae from pneumococcal meningitis. Australian Therapeutic Guidelines empirical therapy is ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours when age above 50 or immunocompromise to cover Listeria, with vancomycin added if resistant pneumococcus is suspected.
key_points: Empirical adults: ceftriaxone 2 g IV; add benzylpenicillin if age above 50 or immunocompromised.
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV must be given before or with the first antibiotic dose.
CT before LP if focal neurology, GCS below 13, seizures, or papilloedema; antibiotics first.
explanation.pearls: Targeted dexamethasone benefit is greatest in pneumococcal meningitis and uncertain in meningococcal disease; once CSF gram stain shows meningococci, dexamethasone can be withdrawn.

options.rationale: Focal neurology, altered consciousness, or seizure mandates CT before LP; dexamethasone and antibiotics must not wait for imaging, with benzylpenicillin added for Listeria cover above age 50. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)
Focal neurological signs and reduced GCS contraindicate immediate LP because of coning risk; CT must precede LP here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)
Dexamethasone benefit in pneumococcal meningitis requires administration before or with the first antibiotic, not later. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

Vancomycin is added when penicillin-resistant pneumococcus is suspected (overseas travel, prior antibiotics) and aciclovir if encephalitis is the leading diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)
Antibiotic timing drives mortality in meningitis; intracranial pressure management must run alongside, not delay, antimicrobial therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Suspected native-valve infective endocarditis without prosthetic material and without severe penicillin allergy is treated empirically in Australia with benzylpenicillin (viridans streptococci, enterococci) plus flucloxacillin (staphylococci) plus low-dose gentamicin (synergy), pending culture. Severe penicillin allergy or MRSA risk substitutes vancomycin for benzylpenicillin and flucloxacillin. Empirical therapy starts immediately after three sets of blood cultures are drawn.
key_points: AU empirical native valve IE: benzylpenicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin
MRSA or severe penicillin allergy: vancomycin substitutes
Antibiotics start immediately after three sets of cultures
explanation.pearls: Synergistic low-dose gentamicin is given for the first 2 weeks then reviewed - renal toxicity is the limiting factor.

options.rationale: Empirical vancomycin alone (or with gentamicin) is reserved for severe penicillin allergy or MRSA risk; benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin is the AU first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Ceftriaxone monotherapy lacks reliable staphylococcal cover; not first-line empirical. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

AU empirical regimen for native-valve infective endocarditis without prosthesis and without severe penicillin allergy covers viridans streptococci, staphylococci, and enterococci pending culture data. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Daptomycin plus rifampicin is a salvage regimen for prosthetic valve MRSA endocarditis; not empirical native valve cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Delaying antimicrobials in confirmed endocarditis with embolic stroke risk is unsafe; empirical therapy begins immediately after cultures are drawn. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Subacute breathlessness with a dry cough, marked exertional desaturation, diffuse interstitial infiltrates and a raised LDH in advanced HIV is Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia until proven otherwise. Treatment is high dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days. Adjunctive corticosteroid is the other essential decision: in moderate to severe disease, defined by a room air PaO2 below 70 mmHg or a large alveolar-arterial gradient, prednisolone started with or just before the antimicrobial reduces respiratory deterioration and mortality. Antiretroviral therapy follows within about two weeks. In context, an opportunistic infection at a CD4 count below 200 is often the first presentation of HIV in Australia, and every such diagnosis also requires prophylaxis planning, notification and partner notification.
key_points: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole for 21 days is first line treatment.
Add corticosteroid when the room air PaO2 is below 70 mmHg.
Start the corticosteroid with or before the first antimicrobial dose.
Begin antiretroviral therapy within about two weeks, watching for immune reconstitution.
explanation.pearls: A normal resting saturation does not exclude Pneumocystis pneumonia; walk the patient and repeat the saturation, and take an arterial blood gas before deciding about corticosteroid.

options.rationale: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is first line, and adjunctive corticosteroid is added when the PaO2 on room air is below 70 mmHg because it reduces the deterioration that follows organism lysis and lowers mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antimicrobial therapy alone is correct for mild disease, where the room air PaO2 is 70 mmHg or above and oxygen saturation is preserved; this man sits below that threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

This is the regimen for moderate to severe community-acquired pneumonia with a lobar or focal infiltrate, and it has no useful activity against Pneumocystis jirovecii. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antiretroviral therapy is started within about two weeks of beginning treatment for most opportunistic infections, but it does not treat the pneumonia and starting it alone leaves the infection untreated. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Pentamidine is a second line agent reserved for severe sulfonamide hypersensitivity or treatment failure, and it carries hypoglycaemia, nephrotoxicity and pancreatitis risks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH)

explanation.summary: A positive interferon gamma release assay is not by itself an indication to treat. Preventive therapy is offered when the estimated benefit from reducing reactivation exceeds the risk of hepatotoxicity, which rises steeply with age and alcohol use.
key_points: Prioritise recent contacts, HIV, dialysis, transplantation, silicosis and planned biologic therapy.
Isoniazid hepatitis risk rises markedly after the age of 35 and with hazardous alcohol use.
When therapy is not offered, give clear symptom education and a route back to care.
explanation.context: Most people with latent tuberculosis never reactivate, and the roughly 5 to 10% lifetime risk is concentrated in the first two years after infection and in those who become immunosuppressed. That is what makes latent tuberculosis a risk stratification problem rather than an infection to be eradicated wherever it is found. The same arithmetic explains why screening is offered selectively: testing a population in whom treatment would not follow generates harm without benefit. Where treatment is declined or not indicated, the safety net is knowing which symptoms, chiefly cough of more than two or three weeks, fever, night sweats and weight loss, should prompt urgent review.

options.rationale: Preventive therapy is targeted at those with a meaningful reactivation risk, such as recent contacts, HIV, dialysis, transplantation or planned tumour necrosis factor inhibitors. At 74 with daily alcohol use, remote exposure and no risk factor, drug induced hepatitis risk outweighs the benefit. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee (NTAC) guidelines)

Isoniazid preventive therapy suits a person with latent infection who does have a reactivation risk factor and an acceptable hepatic risk, typically younger and without hazardous alcohol use. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Rifampicin is the choice where preventive therapy is indicated but isoniazid is unsuitable, such as isoniazid resistant source cases or intolerance, and where the many rifampicin drug interactions can be managed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Serial chest radiography is used as part of follow up for a person with fibrotic changes of untreated old disease who declines or cannot take preventive therapy. Serial imaging of a normal film detects nothing. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee (NTAC) guidelines)

Sputum culture is indicated where symptoms, an abnormal radiograph or immunosuppression raise a real suspicion of active disease. Culture on an asymptomatic patient with a normal film is unwarranted. (Source: NSW Health: Tuberculosis)

explanation.summary: Surviving Sepsis 2021 defines hour-1 bundle elements as measuring lactate, taking blood cultures, giving broad-spectrum antibiotics, starting 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L, and starting vasopressors if MAP remains under 65 mmHg or lactate stays elevated after initial fluid. Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor. Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement persists beyond modest doses. Transfusion targets a haemoglobin of about 70 g/L unless ischaemia is present.
key_points: Vasopressor trigger: MAP under 65 mmHg or lactate above 4 mmol/L after 30 mL/kg crystalloid
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor
Hydrocortisone added for ongoing high vasopressor requirement
explanation.pearls: Start vasopressors via peripheral large-bore access if a central line is delayed - do not wait for central access while the patient remains hypoperfused.

options.rationale: Persistent hypoperfusion (MAP under 65 mmHg or persistently elevated lactate above 4 mmol/L) after 30 mL/kg crystalloid is the trigger for vasopressors. Noradrenaline is first-line. Surviving Sepsis 2021 supports this within the first hour. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Beyond 30 mL/kg, further fluid is guided by dynamic assessment; ongoing hypoperfusion needs noradrenaline, not more fluid by default. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Vancomycin is added when MRSA risk is present (recent hospitalisation, prior MRSA, healthcare exposure); not all septic shock patients need it. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Hydrocortisone is added when vasopressor requirement persists (often greater than 0.25 mcg/kg/min noradrenaline); not before vasopressors. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)
Transfusion threshold in septic shock is haemoglobin under 70 g/L in most patients; not 100 g/L. (Source: Surviving Sepsis Campaign 2021)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection presents with pain disproportionate to examination, sensory loss, crepitus, dusky skin, and rapid systemic deterioration. The LRINEC score (>=6 intermediate, >=8 high) is supportive but should not be used to rule out NF in the presence of clinical hard signs. Urgent surgical exploration and debridement is both diagnostic and therapeutic. Empirical antibiotics are broad-spectrum (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for exotoxin suppression. Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive after source control.
key_points: Hard clinical signs override an intermediate LRINEC
Theatre is diagnosis plus treatment in NF
Empirical cover: broad-spectrum beta-lactam plus clindamycin
explanation.pearls: Pain out of proportion plus crepitus plus mottled skin = call theatre before completing imaging; you can debride a clean thigh and apologise, but cannot un-die the patient.

options.rationale: Imaging may help selected stable cases but should NOT delay theatre when bedside hard signs are present; surgical exploration is the gold standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pain disproportionate to examination, sensory loss, crepitus, and rapid progression are clinical hard markers of necrotising soft tissue infection that override an intermediate LRINEC score. Theatre exploration is the diagnosis and treatment combined; empirical IV broad-spectrum cover plus clindamycin (toxin suppression) precedes culture data. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Delay of even hours significantly increases mortality; bedside hard signs alone justify theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Cellulitis does not produce crepitus, sensory loss, or pain disproportionate; treating as cellulitis misses NF. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive after surgical source control, never a substitute. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Pregnancy is a Category C risk factor for severe influenza and complications. Oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily for 5 days should be started as soon as influenza is suspected or confirmed, with no gestational restriction. Treatment within 48 hours of symptom onset gives the greatest benefit, but late initiation still reduces complications. Influenza vaccine is also recommended at any gestation. Bacterial co-infection is treated only when clinical or imaging evidence supports it.
key_points: Oseltamivir is preferred antiviral in pregnancy at any gestation
Start as soon as influenza suspected, ideally within 48 hours
Influenza vaccine offered at any stage of pregnancy
explanation.pearls: Don't withhold oseltamivir past 48 hours - moderate-to-severe disease in pregnancy still benefits from later start.

options.rationale: Oseltamivir is preferred in pregnancy because of systemic absorption needed for severe disease; zanamivir is reserved for resistance. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)
Pregnant women with influenza are at high risk of severe disease and need antiviral therapy promptly. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

Pregnancy is an independent risk factor for severe influenza. Oseltamivir is recommended at any gestation as soon as influenza is suspected or confirmed, ideally within 48 hours of symptom onset, but late presentations also benefit. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)
Peramivir is reserved for inpatients unable to tolerate oral therapy; oseltamivir is first-line outpatient. (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

Empirical antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of bacterial co-infection (e.g. pneumonia on imaging, raised inflammatory markers, second deterioration). (Source: ATAGI/CDNA influenza in pregnancy 2023)

explanation.summary: Preoperative blockade for phaeochromocytoma starts with alpha antagonism (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD escalated, or doxazosin 2-4 mg BD as alternative) for 10-14 days before surgery. Beta blockade is added only after alpha blockade for tachycardia or arrhythmia, never before. Liberal salt and fluid intake corrects volume contraction. Operating without this preparation produces severe intraoperative hypertensive crisis and postoperative hypotension. Calcium channel blockers are adjuncts.
key_points: Alpha blockade always before beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phenoxybenzamine 10-14 days preoperative is traditional first-line
Salt loading and fluid expansion mitigate postoperative hypotension
explanation.pearls: If catecholamine surge is severe perioperatively, IV phentolamine (alpha) and magnesium sulfate are the rescue agents - never beta-block first.

options.rationale: Calcium channel blockers are second-line or adjunctive; alpha blockade is the first step. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)
Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade can precipitate unopposed alpha-mediated hypertensive crisis and is contraindicated. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)
Operating without preoperative blockade carries significant haemodynamic instability and mortality risk. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

Alpha blockade is started first (10-14 days preoperatively) to prevent intraoperative hypertensive crisis. Phenoxybenzamine is the traditional choice. A beta-blocker is added only after alpha blockade is established. Liberal salt and fluid intake support volume expansion. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)
Labetalol has a beta:alpha ratio of about 7:1 oral and 3:1 IV, providing inadequate alpha cover for preoperative phaeochromocytoma preparation. (Source: Endocrine Society phaeochromocytoma 2014)

explanation.summary: A markedly elevated aldosterone-renin ratio is a screening result, not a diagnosis. Confirmation of primary aldosteronism requires non-suppression of aldosterone after a salt load (intravenous saline 2 L over 4 hours, fludrocortisone suppression, or oral sodium loading with 24-hour urinary aldosterone). Once confirmed, CT adrenal looks for adenoma versus hyperplasia, and adrenal vein sampling lateralises in surgical candidates. Empirical mineralocorticoid antagonism is reserved for non-surgical candidates.
key_points: ARR is screen only; suppression test confirms primary aldosteronism
CT and AVS follow confirmation
Beta-blockers and MRAs interfere with ARR; ACEi and CCB are acceptable
explanation.pearls: Hypokalaemia is present in only about a third of primary aldosteronism cases - normokalaemia does not exclude it.

options.rationale: ARR has been performed correctly off interfering agents (excluding indapamide is impractical when BP is uncontrolled); confirmation should now proceed. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)
CT before confirmation risks chasing an incidentaloma in a patient who has essential hypertension and a false-positive ARR. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)
AVS is reserved for confirmed primary aldosteronism in surgical candidates after CT; not the next step. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)
Empirical mineralocorticoid antagonism misses surgically curable adenomas in confirmed primary aldosteronism. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

A positive ARR is a screening test only; confirmation of primary aldosteronism requires a suppression test (saline infusion, fludrocortisone suppression, or oral sodium loading). Confirmation precedes subtype imaging and adrenal vein sampling. (Source: Endocrine Society primary aldosteronism 2016)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection should be suspected with tearing chest or back pain, hypertension, pulse or BP differential between limbs, or a new aortic regurgitation murmur. CT angiography is first-line in stable patients because it confirms diagnosis, classifies type (Stanford A involves ascending; type B does not), and maps branch vessel involvement for surgical or endovascular planning. TOE is the alternative in unstable patients. Immediate management is heart rate control (IV esmolol or labetalol) targeting HR <60 then SBP <120 mmHg.
key_points: Stable patients: CT angiogram first
Unstable: bedside TOE alternative
Heart rate control before blood pressure
explanation.pearls: Stanford type A involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency; type B is initially medically managed unless complicated by ischaemia, rupture, or refractory pain.

options.rationale: CT angiography is first-line in stable patients with suspected aortic dissection; it confirms diagnosis, identifies type, and maps branch involvement. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)
TTE has limited sensitivity for type B dissection and does not map branch involvement; it is adjunctive. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)
TOE is reserved for haemodynamically unstable patients who cannot be transported for CT; CT is preferred when stable. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)
MRA is excellent but slower and less available; CT is first-line in the acute setting. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)
D-dimer has high sensitivity but is not used to rule out dissection in high pre-test probability; proceed directly to CT. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases 2024)

explanation.summary: Suspected bacterial meningitis requires empiric IV antibiotics within 30 minutes. Australian eTG empiric therapy is ceftriaxone 2 g IV plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV if age >50, pregnant, or immunocompromised (Listeria cover). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given with or before the first antibiotic dose; it reduces neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. CT brain is required before lumbar puncture only in patients with focal neurology, seizure, immunocompromise, GCS <12, or papilloedema; LP should not delay antibiotics.
key_points: Empiric ceftriaxone +/- benzylpenicillin within 30 minutes
Dexamethasone with or before first antibiotic dose
Listeria cover in age >50, pregnant, immunocompromised
explanation.pearls: Notify public health within 24 hours of suspected meningococcal disease and offer ciprofloxacin 500 mg single dose to close household contacts within the previous 7 days.

options.rationale: AU eTG specifies empiric ceftriaxone plus benzylpenicillin (for Listeria cover in age >50, immunocompromised, or pregnant) with dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)
Dexamethasone given before or with first antibiotic dose reduces neurological sequelae in S. pneumoniae meningitis; omission is non-standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)
Vancomycin monotherapy does not cover Gram-negative or Listeria; ceftriaxone is the empiric backbone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

CSF neutrophil-predominant with low glucose indicates bacterial meningitis; aciclovir is added if HSV encephalitis suspected, not as monotherapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)
Empiric antibiotics must be given within 30 minutes of suspicion in bacterial meningitis; Gram stain delay risks death. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic - Meningitis)

explanation.summary: The Glasgow-Blatchford score uses urea, haemoglobin, blood pressure, pulse, and clinical features to risk-stratify upper GI bleeds. A score of 0 corresponds to a less than 1% rebleeding risk and these patients can be safely discharged with outpatient endoscopy. Higher scores warrant admission and earlier endoscopy. Mallory-Weiss tear is a typical low-risk diagnosis. PPI infusion is reserved for high-risk ulcers identified at endoscopy.
key_points: GBS 0: outpatient gastroscopy is safe
Higher GBS: admit for inpatient endoscopy
IV PPI infusion after endoscopy, not empirically
explanation.pearls: A urea-to-creatinine ratio above 100 (using urea mmol/L and creatinine micromol/L) suggests an upper rather than lower source of GI bleeding due to absorption of digested blood.

options.rationale: Glasgow-Blatchford score of 0 identifies a very low risk group safely managed as outpatient; AU and BSG guidelines support discharge with outpatient endoscopy. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)
Urgent gastroscopy is for haemodynamic instability or ongoing bleeding; this patient is stable with GBS 0. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)
GBS 0 has very low risk of rebleeding; routine admission is not required. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)
IV PPI infusion is for confirmed high-risk ulcer post-endoscopy; not indicated empirically in low-risk GBS 0. (Source: BSG Upper GI Bleeding 2022)
Haemoglobin is normal and there is no active bleeding; transfusion has no indication. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

explanation.summary: TTP is a thrombotic microangiopathy driven by ADAMTS13 deficiency causing microvascular platelet thrombi, leading to microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurological signs, renal impairment, and fever. The PLASMIC score (platelet count, haemolysis markers, malignancy absence, transplant absence, MCV, INR, creatinine) identifies high-risk cases. Treatment is plasma exchange (PEX) with corticosteroid started before ADAMTS13 confirmation; caplacizumab and rituximab are AU-funded adjuncts. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated unless life-threatening bleeding.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis triggers PEX before ADAMTS13
Platelet transfusion contraindicated in TTP
Adjuncts: caplacizumab, rituximab
explanation.pearls: PLASMIC score 6-7 has a positive predictive value >90% for ADAMTS13 <10%; this threshold supports immediate plasma exchange while awaiting confirmatory testing.

options.rationale: TTP is a haematological emergency with high untreated mortality; plasma exchange must be started on clinical grounds (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, neurology) before ADAMTS13. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)
Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless life-threatening bleeding; it may worsen thrombosis. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)
Cyclophosphamide is not part of TTP induction; the AU pathway is plasma exchange + steroid +/- rituximab/caplacizumab. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)
Eculizumab is for atypical HUS not TTP; relatively low creatinine and severe neurology with PLASMIC favours TTP. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)
ADAMTS13 results take days; waiting risks death. Clinical PLASMIC score guides immediate exchange. (Source: HSANZ TTP Position Statement)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and altered mental state. Triggers include intercurrent illness, vomiting of replacement therapy, and surgery. IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg/24 hours is the AU standard, with isotonic crystalloid for hypotension. At hydrocortisone doses >=40 mg/day, no separate fludrocortisone is needed. Underlying trigger (gastroenteritis here) must be treated. Patient education and sick-day rules with parenteral hydrocortisone kit at home prevent recurrence.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV + 0.9% NaCl is the AU regimen
No fludrocortisone needed at stress doses
Treat trigger and educate sick-day rules
explanation.pearls: Patients with Addison should carry a Medic-Alert bracelet and a parenteral hydrocortisone 100 mg IM kit; instruct partners and family to administer in vomiting or unconsciousness.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg plus isotonic crystalloid resuscitation; fludrocortisone is not needed acutely as hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid activity at stress dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for diagnostic settings where Synacthen testing is planned; hydrocortisone is preferred in crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Oral therapy is contraindicated in vomiting and shock; parenteral is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis corrects with cortisol replacement and fluid; insulin-dextrose risks hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Hyponatraemia in adrenal crisis is corrected by hydrocortisone plus isotonic fluid; hypertonic saline risks osmotic demyelination given chronic hyponatraemia of unknown duration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) commonly presents with upper airway, lower airway, and renal disease; PR3-ANCA is the typical serology. Severe organ-threatening disease is induced with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus pulse and oral corticosteroids. Rituximab is preferred for PR3-ANCA, women of childbearing age, and to avoid cyclophosphamide toxicity. Plasma exchange is adjunctive in alveolar haemorrhage or severe AKI requiring dialysis. Maintenance is rituximab or azathioprine with low-dose steroid.
key_points: Severe AAV: rituximab or cyclophosphamide + steroid
Rituximab preferred for PR3-ANCA
Plasma exchange adjunctive in haemorrhage or dialysis
explanation.pearls: PEXIVAS trial showed plasma exchange did not improve death or ESRD outcomes overall but a 2024 KDIGO update retains it as an option for diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with hypoxia.

options.rationale: ANCA-associated vasculitis with severe organ-threatening disease is induced with rituximab or cyclophosphamide plus high-dose steroids; rituximab is preferred in PR3-ANCA and avoids cyclophosphamide gonadotoxicity. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)
Methotrexate is reserved for non-organ-threatening disease; severe renal involvement requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)
Plasma exchange is adjunctive in pulmonary haemorrhage or dialysis-dependent renal involvement; monotherapy does not address autoantibody production. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)
MMF can be used for milder disease or maintenance; severe organ-threatening disease requires rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)
Hydroxychloroquine has no role in ANCA-associated vasculitis induction; it is used in lupus. (Source: KDIGO ANCA Vasculitis 2024)

explanation.summary: Myeloma cast nephropathy is the most common cause of AKI in multiple myeloma. Free kappa light chains co-precipitate with Tamm-Horsfall protein causing tubular casts; hypercalcaemia, dehydration, NSAIDs, and contrast worsen injury. AU management combines aggressive isotonic hydration to lower urinary light chain delivery, treatment of hypercalcaemia (initially with hydration; bisphosphonates after renal recovery), and prompt anti-myeloma therapy (typically bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, dexamethasone) to reduce light chain production. Avoid nephrotoxins.
key_points: Hydration + anti-myeloma therapy together preserve renal function
Bisphosphonates held until renal recovery
Plasma exchange not routine in cast nephropathy
explanation.pearls: A serum free light chain reduction of >=50% within 21 days of bortezomib-based induction predicts renal recovery in approximately 80% of cast nephropathy cases.

options.rationale: Cast nephropathy AKI in myeloma improves with hydration to reduce light chain delivery and prompt anti-myeloma therapy (typically bortezomib-based); both are needed to preserve renal function. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)
Bisphosphonates require renal function correction first; zoledronic acid is held until creatinine improves and hydration is established. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)
Pamidronate has lower renal toxicity than zoledronate but still requires fluid resuscitation first; hypovolaemia is the immediate threat. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)
Plasma exchange does not consistently improve renal outcomes in cast nephropathy and is not a substitute for hydration plus anti-myeloma therapy. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)
High cut-off dialysis without anti-myeloma therapy does not stop new light chain production; combined treatment is the AU standard. (Source: HSANZ Multiple Myeloma Position Statement)

explanation.summary: The 0/1-hour high-sensitivity troponin algorithm streamlines acute chest pain triage in Australian EDs. Rule-out requires 0-hour hs-cTnT <5 ng/L if symptom onset >3 hours, or 0-hour <12 ng/L with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L. Rule-in requires 0-hour ≥52 ng/L OR 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L (men) or ≥3 ng/L (women) above an above-URL baseline. The 'observation zone' between rule-out and rule-in triggers further serial troponin, imaging, or risk stratification. NSTEMI rule-in mandates DAPT, parenteral anticoagulation (heparin or enoxaparin or fondaparinux), and angiography timing by risk class.
key_points: 0/1-hour rule-in: 0-hour above URL plus 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L.
0/1-hour rule-out: very low 0-hour OR very low + delta <3 ng/L.
NSTEMI: DAPT, parenteral anticoagulant, early invasive within 24 hours for high-risk.
Thrombolysis is for STEMI without timely PCI access, not NSTEMI.
explanation.pearls: hs-cTnT 0/1-hour: delta ≥5 ng/L above an above-URL baseline rules in NSTEMI and triggers early invasive angiography.

options.rationale: Thrombolysis is for ST elevation MI when timely PCI is not available; NSTEMI is managed by antithrombotic therapy and invasive angiography, not thrombolysis. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

The 0/1-hour algorithm rules out only when 0-hour hs-cTnT is below the URL AND 1-hour delta is below threshold; this patient meets neither criterion. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

The conventional 0/3 or 0/6 hour algorithm is superseded by the 0/1 hour high-sensitivity protocol in AU EDs when hs-cTn is available, which already provides the diagnosis. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

CT coronary angiography is for low-risk chest pain after troponin rule-out; once NSTEMI is ruled in, invasive coronary angiography is the procedure of choice. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

ESC/CSANZ 0/1-hour algorithm rules in NSTEMI when the 0-hour hs-cTnT is above the URL with a 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L; early invasive angiography within 24 hours plus DAPT and parenteral anticoagulation is the AU approach. (Source: CSANZ 2025 Acute Coronary Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated by ASCIA: IM adrenaline 0.5 mg of 1:1000 (500 mcg) into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if symptoms persist. Lay the patient flat with legs raised, give high-flow oxygen, and obtain IV access. IV adrenaline infusion (titrated to response, typically starting at 1 mcg/min) is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis. Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts, not primary treatment, and do not reverse cardiorespiratory compromise. Biphasic reactions occur in approximately 5-20 percent within 4-6 hours; observe for 4 hours minimum.
key_points: Adult ASCIA dose: 0.5 mg (500 mcg) IM 1:1000 into mid-anterolateral thigh.
Repeat every 5 minutes if persistent; lie flat with legs raised.
IV adrenaline infusion only after IM failure in a monitored setting.
Observe minimum 4 hours for biphasic reaction (5-20%).
explanation.pearls: Adult anaphylaxis: 0.5 mg IM adrenaline 1:1000 every 5 minutes if persistent; IV bolus is for arrest, not anaphylaxis.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.rationale: 0.3 mg is the paediatric EpiPen dose for 20 kg or above; the adult standard ASCIA dose is 0.5 mg of 1:1000 IM. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.rationale: ASCIA adult anaphylaxis dose is 0.5 mg (500 mcg) IM 1:1000 into the mid-anterolateral thigh, repeated every 5 minutes if symptoms persist, before considering IV adrenaline infusion. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.rationale: Intravenous bolus adrenaline 1 mg is for cardiac arrest, not anaphylaxis; IV adrenaline in anaphylaxis is given by titrated infusion in a monitored setting, after IM has failed. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.rationale: Steroids and antihistamines do not treat acute anaphylaxis cardiorespiratory compromise; adrenaline must be given first and is never delayed by adjuncts. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol is an adjunct for persistent bronchospasm AFTER adrenaline; it does not address hypotension or airway oedema and does not replace adrenaline. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis 2023

explanation.summary: Paracetamol overdose management in Australia uses the 150 mg/L Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 to 16 hours post-ingestion; any level above the line triggers N-acetylcysteine. The 21-hour two-bag protocol gives 200 mg/kg over 4 hours, then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours. Earlier NAC (within 8 hours) prevents the majority of hepatotoxicity; later treatment still benefits established disease. Massive ingestion (>30 g or >500 mg/kg) may justify a 3-bag higher-dose protocol. Repeat levels and LFTs at end of NAC determine completion or extension.
key_points: AU nomogram: 150 mg/L 4-hour line; treat any level above.
21-hour 2-bag protocol: 200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours.
NAC most effective within 8 hours of ingestion.
Massive ingestion (>500 mg/kg) may use 3-bag higher-dose regimen.
explanation.pearls: AU paracetamol nomogram 150 mg/L line at 4 hours = NAC; at 6 hours threshold is approximately 125 mg/L.

sources.label: NSW Poisons Information Centre Paracetamol Guideline

options.rationale: The 200 mg/L line is the 4-hour value of the higher-risk North American nomogram; AU uses the 150 mg/L 4-hour line and at 6 hours the threshold is around 125 mg/L. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

On the Australian Rumack-Matthew 150 mg/L line, the 6-hour threshold is approximately 125 mg/L; this patient's level of 200 mg/L is above the line and requires NAC. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)
Activated charcoal is considered within 1-2 hours of ingestion; at 6 hours post-ingestion it adds no benefit and delays NAC which is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

NAC efficacy is greatest within 8-10 hours of ingestion; delaying for a further level wastes the protective window when the current level is already above the AU threshold. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Haemodialysis for paracetamol is reserved for massive ingestion (>500 mg/kg) with very high levels (>1000 mg/L) or established acidosis with coma; this patient has a single moderate ingestion and is alert. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

explanation.summary: Isoniazid is ceased when the alanine aminotransferase exceeds five times the upper limit of normal without symptoms, or three times with symptoms or jaundice. Preventive therapy treats a probability, so the tolerance for harm is low.
key_points: Check liver function at baseline and at intervals, and instruct the patient to report nausea, anorexia or dark urine.
Hepatitis risk rises with age, hazardous alcohol use, chronic viral hepatitis and pregnancy.
After recovery, a rifampicin based regimen may be considered with specialist input.
explanation.context: The threshold for stopping a drug depends on what the drug is buying. In active tuberculosis, where the disease is lethal and the regimen is curative, hepatotoxicity is managed by staged withdrawal and sequential reintroduction so that treatment can continue. In latent infection the patient is well, the benefit is a modest reduction in a lifetime probability, and the same laboratory result warrants simply stopping. Monthly clinical review, asking directly about anorexia, nausea and dark urine, catches more injury than testing alone, since symptoms often precede the most dangerous rises.

options.rationale: Preventive therapy is stopped when transaminases exceed five times the upper limit without symptoms, or three times with symptoms or a rising bilirubin. The risk of continuing outweighs the benefit of preventing a disease she does not yet have. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee (NTAC) guidelines)

Continuing with weekly liver tests suits a modest asymptomatic rise below three times the upper limit, which is common early and often settles with closer monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Dose reduction has no role: isoniazid hepatotoxicity is idiosyncratic rather than dose dependent at therapeutic doses, and a halved dose is both unsafe and inadequate. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Ursodeoxycholic acid is used for cholestatic conditions such as primary biliary cholangitis, indicated by a raised alkaline phosphatase. This is a hepatocellular pattern and no agent protects against it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Rifampicin comes as a later step once transaminases have normalised and preventive therapy is still wanted, under specialist advice. Switching immediately risks compounding injury with another hepatotoxic drug. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed steroid doses, vomiting, or trauma in patients with primary or secondary adrenal insufficiency. Classic features are hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and metabolic acidosis. Treatment is immediate IV hydrocortisone (100 mg stat then 200 mg per 24 h as infusion or 50 mg six-hourly), isotonic saline resuscitation, and treatment of any precipitant. After acute recovery, double or triple the regular steroid dose during intercurrent illness ('sick day rules'); ensure the patient has an emergency hydrocortisone injection kit and a Medic-Alert.
key_points: Adrenal crisis: hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia.
IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours.
Saline resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia.
Sick day rules: double or triple steroid dose for febrile illness.
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat + 0.9% saline bolus before any other intervention; hyperkalaemia self-corrects with steroid replacement.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia adrenal insufficiency statement

options.rationale: AU adrenal crisis pathway is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 200 mg over 24 hours) plus prompt isotonic saline resuscitation to correct hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Oral steroids and oral rehydration are inappropriate in adrenal crisis with vomiting and hypotension; absorption is unreliable and the patient needs immediate IV access. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Fludrocortisone is not available IV and is unnecessary acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at 100 mg doses. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

The hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis is secondary to cortisol and aldosterone deficiency; it resolves with hydrocortisone and saline, and standard insulin-dextrose risks rebound hypoglycaemia in this already hypoglycaemic patient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Calcium gluconate is used for cardioprotection in life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes; this patient does not yet have ECG features and steroid plus saline are higher priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management in Australia (ADS protocol) follows fluid, insulin, potassium, glucose, and search for precipitant. Critically, when initial potassium is <3.3 mmol/L, insulin must be HELD until potassium is replaced to at least 3.5 mmol/L, because insulin drives further intracellular shift and causes potentially fatal hypokalaemia. Replace potassium at 20-40 mmol per litre of crystalloid; rates above 10 mmol/h need cardiac monitoring. Once potassium ≥3.5, start fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h. Add 5% dextrose to fluids once glucose ≤14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate reserved for pH <6.9 with shock.
key_points: ADS DKA: hold insulin if K <3.3 mmol/L until replaced to ≥3.5.
Replace K at 20-40 mmol/L in crystalloid; cardiac monitor if >10 mmol/h.
Fixed-rate insulin 0.1 unit/kg/h once potassium safe.
Add 5% dextrose to fluid once glucose ≤14 mmol/L.
explanation.pearls: DKA with potassium <3.3 mmol/L: replace potassium first, hold insulin until K ≥3.5 mmol/L (ADS protocol).

sources.label: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.rationale: ADS DKA protocol holds insulin until potassium is at or above 3.5 mmol/L because insulin drives potassium intracellularly and risks fatal hypokalaemia; potassium-replete saline runs first. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.rationale: Insulin in the setting of potassium <3.3 mmol/L precipitates further intracellular potassium shift and can trigger ventricular arrhythmia; the ADS pathway holds insulin until potassium ≥3.5 mmol/L. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is only considered for adult DKA with pH <6.9 and persistent shock; routine use worsens intracellular acidosis and aggravates hypokalaemia, which is already critical here. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.rationale: Aggressive saline without potassium plus immediate insulin will drive potassium even lower from an already 2.9 mmol/L baseline, with ECG changes already present; potassium replacement must come first. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

options.rationale: Subcutaneous insulin and oral potassium are inappropriate in active DKA with hypokalaemia, vomiting and shock; absorption is unreliable and IV therapy is required. (Source: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020)
source_refs: ADS Australian Diabetes Society DKA Guideline 2020

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma requires preoperative alpha-adrenergic blockade for 10-14 days before any beta blockade is added, to prevent unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis. The AU first-line agent is phenoxybenzamine (irreversible non-selective alpha blocker); doxazosin is an alternative. Beta blockade is added only AFTER adequate alpha blockade, to control reflex tachycardia. High sodium and fluid intake during the alpha blockade phase prevents volume contraction-related hypotension. Surgery (typically laparoscopic adrenalectomy) is planned when BP and heart rate targets are met.
key_points: Alpha block first, beta block only after alpha block is established.
Phenoxybenzamine first-line; doxazosin alternative.
10-14 days of alpha block before surgery.
Liberal salt and fluid intake during alpha block to prevent hypotension.
explanation.pearls: Phaeochromocytoma preop: stop any premature beta blocker; start phenoxybenzamine for 10-14 days, then re-add beta blocker only once alpha block is established.

sources.label: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.rationale: Surgery without adequate alpha blockade for 10-14 days carries a high risk of intraoperative hypertensive crisis, arrhythmia and death; pre-operative blockade is mandatory. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.rationale: Continuing beta blockade alongside the start of alpha blockade is not safer than the AU recommended sequence of stopping beta first, then starting alpha, then re-introducing beta once alpha is established. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.rationale: Escalating beta blockade in phaeochromocytoma without alpha blockade worsens the unopposed alpha state and accelerated hypertension risk; calcium channel blockers are adjuncts, not the primary fix here. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.rationale: Beta blockade without prior alpha blockade in phaeochromocytoma causes unopposed alpha vasoconstriction and worsened hypertension; the AU approach is to STOP metoprolol, start phenoxybenzamine, and only add a beta blocker once alpha blockade is established. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

options.rationale: Hydralazine causes reflex tachycardia and is not a controlled choice in phaeochromocytoma; phenoxybenzamine is the AU preferred preoperative alpha blocker. (Source: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement)
source_refs: Endocrine Society of Australia phaeochromocytoma statement

explanation.summary: The CSANZ-endorsed 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm allows rule-out of NSTEMI when 0-hour hs-troponin <5 ng/L OR 0-hour <12 with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L, with non-diagnostic ECG and resolved symptoms. Rule-in is 0-hour ≥52 ng/L OR 1-hour delta ≥5 ng/L. Intermediate values need observation and 3-hour repeat.
key_points: 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm: rule-out <5 at 0h or <12 with delta <3 at 1h
Rule-in: 0h ≥52 ng/L OR 1h delta ≥5 ng/L
Outpatient cardiology stress test or CT coronary angiogram is the post-rule-out pathway
explanation.pearls: The 0/1h algorithm requires assay-specific cut-offs (different for hs-troponin T vs hs-troponin I). Sex-specific 99th percentile cut-offs apply for the rule-in side. Use clinical judgement in patients with renal impairment - the baseline hs-troponin is often above 14 ng/L without acute MI.

options.rationale: 6-hourly serial troponin protocols precede hs-troponin and are no longer the standard. CSANZ accepts the 0/1h hs-troponin algorithm for rule-out, freeing low-risk patients. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)
DAPT for ACS rule-in is not indicated when troponin trajectory rules out NSTEMI; bleeding risk without benefit. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

The European Society of Cardiology 0/1h hs-troponin T rule-out algorithm (also accepted in AU CSANZ pathways) considers a 0-hour value <5 ng/L OR 0-hour <12 with 1-hour delta <3 ng/L as a rule-out for NSTEMI. Her 0-hour 8 with 1-hour delta of 1 ng/L meets rule-out criteria. Symptoms have resolved and ECG is non-diagnostic so outpatient cardiology review with stress test is appropriate. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

Urgent coronary angiography is for STEMI, NSTEMI rule-in with high-risk features (haemodynamic instability, dynamic ECG changes, persistent angina), or unstable angina. She has rule-out troponin trajectory and no high-risk features. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

CT coronary angiogram is useful in intermediate-risk patients to refine the diagnosis but is not the standard immediate step after rule-out by 0/1h algorithm; stress testing is preferred for functional assessment in outpatient cardiology pathways. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP scores Systolic BP, Multilobar, Albumin, Respiratory rate, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygen, pH, and predicts need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support (IRVS). Above 5 has over 50% positive predictive value for IRVS. AU TSANZ guidelines incorporate this for site-of-care decisions.
key_points: SMART-COP ≥5 predicts ICU need; ≥3 is the typical hospital-admission threshold
Severe CAP requires broad cover: piperacillin-tazobactam + azithromycin or per local antibiogram
BiPAP is contraindicated in obtunded patients with aspiration risk
explanation.pearls: AU TSANZ guidelines emphasise that PSI and CURB-65 underestimate severity in younger patients without comorbidity. SMART-COP is calibrated for IRVS prediction. Add gentamicin for atypicals coverage and Pseudomonas in selected patients.

options.rationale: BiPAP is appropriate for COPD-related hypercapnic respiratory failure but he is currently hypoxic and septic with confusion; BiPAP risks aspiration in the obtunded patient and delays intubation. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

Ceftriaxone monotherapy is appropriate empirically only for mild-to-moderate CAP; with SMART-COP 11 and septic shock the patient needs ICU-level care and broader empirical cover (eg piperacillin-tazobactam + azithromycin or as per local antibiogram). (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

Small simple parapneumonic effusions are managed with antibiotics; drainage is reserved for empyema or large effusion compromising oxygenation. The dominant issue is sepsis and respiratory failure, not the effusion. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

SMART-COP: low Systolic BP (2), Multilobar / large effusion (1), low Albumin (1), high Respiratory rate (1), Tachycardia (1), Confusion (1), low Oxygen (2), low pH (2) = 11. Above 5 predicts >65% need for ventilatory or inotropic support and mandates ICU referral. The AU TSANZ pathway uses SMART-COP for site-of-care decisions in addition to severity-of-illness scoring like APACHE. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)
Discharge with oral antibiotics is not an option in septic shock with multilobar pneumonia and respiratory failure. (Source: TSANZ / Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory CAP)

explanation.summary: Subsegmental PE without proximal DVT and without risk factors can be considered for surveillance-only management per CHEST guidelines, but AU practice typically still anticoagulates for 3 months because of false-negative scan rates and elevated D-dimer indicating ongoing clot. Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD is the first-line DOAC for VTE.
key_points: Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days, then 5 mg BD - AU first-line for VTE
Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days, then 20 mg daily - alternative DOAC for VTE
Subsegmental PE surveillance is an alternative only in selected patients with confirmed absence of proximal DVT
explanation.pearls: Indefinite anticoagulation is offered for unprovoked proximal PE with low bleeding risk, recurrent VTE, or cancer-associated VTE. LMWH remains first-line for cancer-associated thrombosis in many AU centres, though apixaban and edoxaban now have growing evidence (eviQ guidelines).

options.rationale: Indefinite (extended) anticoagulation is reserved for unprovoked proximal PE with low bleeding risk or recurrent VTE. A single subsegmental PE without confirmed VTE elsewhere does not yet warrant indefinite therapy; the 3-month course is the standard initial period. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Warfarin is no longer first-line for VTE in AU practice; DOACs are preferred because of fewer monitoring requirements and similar efficacy. Warfarin remains the choice in mechanical valves, antiphospholipid syndrome, and severe renal impairment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Surveillance without anticoagulation is a CHEST guideline option for subsegmental PE with confirmed absence of proximal DVT, low recurrence risk, and patient preference for not taking anticoagulants; however the AU consensus still favours treating because diagnostic accuracy of subsegmental PE on CTPA is limited and elevated D-dimer here suggests ongoing clot. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Single subsegmental PE with no proximal DVT, no risk factors, low cancer risk, and no haemodynamic compromise represents an isolated low-risk PE. AU practice supports a 3-month course of anticoagulation as the standard duration for low-risk PE. Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD is the AU first-line DOAC regimen for VTE; surveillance proximal vein Doppler is an alternative only in selected cases. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
LMWH bridging to warfarin is the alternative but DOACs do not require bridging and are preferred for non-cancer-associated VTE in AU. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Trimethoprim blocks distal tubular potassium secretion and is a common precipitant of severe hyperkalaemia when added to renin-angiotensin blockade and a mineralocorticoid antagonist in chronic kidney disease. Nitrofurantoin is the safer first-line choice here.
key_points: Trimethoprim acts on the epithelial sodium channel in the same way as amiloride.
Nitrofurantoin is avoided when the eGFR falls below about 45 mL/min.
The safest prescription is the one that prevents the electrolyte emergency rather than treating it.
explanation.context: Most hospital presentations of severe hyperkalaemia are iatrogenic and predictable, arising from a combination of drugs acting on the same aldosterone-dependent secretory pathway in the collecting duct in a patient whose nephron reserve is already reduced. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers lower aldosterone, spironolactone blocks its receptor, and trimethoprim closes the sodium channel that generates the electrical gradient for potassium secretion. Each step is tolerable alone. The prescribing decision that matters is usually the last one added to the list, and a short course antibiotic is exactly the sort of addition that is made without a second thought.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Nitrofurantoin is a recommended first-line agent for uncomplicated cystitis and is acceptable at this level of renal function. It avoids the potassium sparing effect that makes the usual alternative hazardous in this combination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Trimethoprim is first-line for uncomplicated cystitis in a woman without renal impairment or potassium raising drugs. It blocks the epithelial sodium channel like amiloride and, with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor and a mineralocorticoid antagonist, is a well described cause of severe hyperkalaemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Amoxicillin with clavulanate is used for cystitis where the isolate is known to be susceptible and first-line options are unsuitable; empirical resistance rates make it a poor initial choice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Ciprofloxacin is kept for pyelonephritis or proven multiresistant infection. Quinolones are reserved in Australia because of resistance and tendon and neurological harms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Doxycycline treats atypical genital tract infection, not cystitis, since urinary concentrations are inadequate against the usual uropathogens. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Status epilepticus is seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes. First-line: IV/IM/buccal benzodiazepine (lorazepam 4 mg IV or midazolam 10 mg IM). Second-line at 20 minutes: levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV, valproate 40 mg/kg IV, or phenytoin 20 mg/kg IV (all similar efficacy per ESETT). Third-line: thiopentone or propofol infusion in ICU.
key_points: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV is AU first-line second-line agent because of safety and few interactions
ESETT trial: levetiracetam, fosphenytoin and valproate equally effective (~50% response rate)
Refractory status epilepticus requires intubation and continuous EEG monitoring in ICU
explanation.pearls: Always check glucose, Na, Mg, Ca, and ammonia (valproate users) in status. Pyridoxine 100 mg IV is added if INH overdose is suspected. Driving cessation rules: minimum 6 months seizure-free in AU under Austroads.

options.rationale: Status epilepticus refractory to first-line benzodiazepines requires a second-line non-benzodiazepine anticonvulsant. The AU TSANZ / ANZAN consensus (post-ESETT trial) is that levetiracetam, valproate and fosphenytoin/phenytoin all show similar response rates (~50%); levetiracetam at 60 mg/kg is often first choice because of fewer interactions, no enzyme induction, and tolerability. He should still get a third line agent if seizure continues past this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Status epilepticus is defined as seizure activity lasting more than 5 minutes; waiting risks worsening neurological injury (proportional to duration) and progression to refractory status. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Fosphenytoin/phenytoin is an acceptable second-line per ESETT and AU TSANZ; either levetiracetam, valproate or phenytoin are reasonable choices. Phenytoin requires cardiac monitoring and is contraindicated in heart block, hypotension, and porphyria; levetiracetam is often preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Repeat benzodiazepine dose is appropriate at 5 to 10 minutes if first dose has not worked, but past the 20 to 30 minute mark a second-line non-benzodiazepine is added because of receptor internalisation reducing further benzodiazepine response. Excessive benzodiazepines also cause respiratory depression. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

Thiopentone or propofol infusions are third-line for refractory status epilepticus after second-line non-benzodiazepine has failed. They require intubation and ICU. Skipping second-line escalates aggressively without an evidence basis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Stanford type A (ascending aorta) dissection is a surgical emergency with high mortality (1% per hour untreated); proceeding to theatre on bedside TTE with intimal flap and AR is appropriate when CT contrast risks AKI. Type B (descending aorta) is medically managed in uncomplicated cases. Bedside TOE is the contrast-free imaging alternative.
key_points: Stanford A = ascending aorta involvement, surgical emergency; Stanford B = descending only, medical management for uncomplicated
TTE with intimal flap and AR is sufficient bedside imaging to mobilise theatre when CT contrast risks AKI
Bilateral arm BP differential >20 mmHg with appropriate clinical features is a hallmark
explanation.pearls: Bridge therapy: titrate to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg with esmolol or labetalol first, then nicardipine if more BP control is needed (vasodilator without rate response is contraindicated alone). IABP is absolutely contraindicated.

options.rationale: MRI is contraindicated by time delay in acute Stanford A dissection. It is reserved for stable Stanford B or follow-up imaging in chronic disease. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

Beta-blockade and BP control are essential bridge therapy but not the definitive management for Stanford A. Type A requires emergency surgery; ward admission is inappropriate. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

Stanford type A dissection with confirmed intimal flap on TTE in the ascending aorta plus aortic regurgitation is a surgical emergency. Definitive imaging is helpful but not mandatory if the diagnosis is established and theatre is ready - delays for CT angiography in the setting of confirmed Stanford A worsens outcome. AU and international cardiothoracic practice supports proceeding to theatre with TOE in theatre to further characterise. Renal impairment is a secondary consideration; transoesophageal echocardiogram is the bedside alternative to CT in renal disease. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)
IABP is contraindicated in aortic regurgitation and aortic dissection because it worsens both. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

CT angiography is the gold standard non-invasive imaging but iodinated contrast in eGFR 28 risks contrast-induced nephropathy, especially in stable haemodynamics; the TTE already shows the intimal flap and AR confirming Stanford A. Going to CT first delays surgery for marginal additional information. (Source: Heart Foundation / CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: HHS is defined by severe hyperglycaemia (>30 mmol/L), effective osmolality >320 mOsm/kg, dehydration, altered mentation, and only minimal ketosis or acidosis. Fluid resuscitation is the dominant therapy. Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride only once intravascular volume is restored and corrected sodium is rising. Insulin is started low at 0.05 unit/kg/hour with target glucose drop of 4 to 5 mmol/L/hour to avoid cerebral oedema.
key_points: HHS osmolality drop should be no more than 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour to avoid cerebral oedema
Insulin rate in HHS is 0.05 unit/kg/hour (half that of DKA)
Switch to 0.45% sodium chloride after volume restoration AND if corrected sodium is rising; otherwise continue isotonic
explanation.pearls: Effective osmolality = 2 x Na + glucose (mmol/L). Mortality is high (5 to 20%), driven by underlying precipitants - sepsis, MI, stroke, drugs (steroids, atypicals). Anti-coagulation is indicated for prevention of arterial thrombosis given hyperviscosity.

options.rationale: Doubling insulin risks dropping glucose too quickly with cerebral oedema risk; HHS is characterised by relative insulin sufficiency to suppress ketogenesis but inadequate for glycaemic control. The slower 0.05 unit/kg/hour rate is standard. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Stopping insulin once the diagnosis is confirmed and resuscitation is underway will not adequately lower glucose. The insulin infusion is run alongside fluids, not in isolation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Switching to dextrose before glucose has dropped below about 14 to 15 mmol/L is premature and would slow glucose correction excessively in someone still at 44. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
There is no significant acidosis (HCO3 22, AG 12, lactate 2.6); bicarbonate is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

HHS with corrected sodium above 150 mmol/L (this patient 162) and an effective osmolality of 348 requires a slow, controlled correction of both glucose and effective osmolality. Lowering osmolality faster than 3 to 8 mOsm/kg/hour and glucose by more than 4 to 5 mmol/L/hour risks cerebral oedema in elderly patients. Hypotonic fluids (0.45% sodium chloride) are switched to once initial volume restoration is achieved AND corrected sodium is rising. AU diabetes society guidelines support this slow correction; the insulin rate is intentionally low (0.05 unit/kg/hour) in HHS, not the 0.1 used in DKA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Infrarenal AAA referral thresholds for elective repair: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women, OR growth above 1 cm per year, OR development of symptoms. Surveillance intervals scale with diameter (24 months for 3.0-3.9 cm, 12 months for 4.0-4.5 cm, 6 months for 4.6-5.4 cm in men). Elective repair (EVAR or open) substantially reduces rupture mortality compared with emergency repair (30 to 50%). Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable factor; aspirin and beta-blockers do not change AAA growth or rupture rates.
key_points: Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm men, 5.0 cm women, OR growth >1 cm/year, OR symptoms
EVAR vs open: anatomy-dependent; EVAR lower short-term mortality but ongoing surveillance
Smoking cessation is the most effective modifiable risk factor for growth and rupture
explanation.pearls: An expanding AAA with new abdominal or back pain in a haemodynamically stable patient is a contained leak until proven otherwise - never reassure these patients home, image urgently and discuss with vascular on call.

options.rationale: Surveillance is appropriate for AAA between 3.0 and 5.4 cm in men with slow growth, but a maximal diameter of 5.5 cm is the recognised threshold for elective repair (in men); growth rate above 1 cm per year also triggers referral. This case is at threshold AND has accelerated growth (0.7 cm in 12 months is the upper end of normal but combined with diameter approaching threshold warrants surgical assessment). (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Aspirin has not been shown to reduce AAA growth or rupture and antithrombotic decisions in AAA are made on cardiovascular risk grounds, not aneurysm-specific. Delaying definitive vascular assessment is inappropriate when approaching repair threshold. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Rupture is suggested by severe back/abdominal pain, hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass. This patient is asymptomatic with normal vital signs; emergency presentation is not warranted. Urgent outpatient referral, however, is. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Australian and international guidance recommends referral for elective AAA repair consideration when maximal infrarenal diameter reaches 5.5 cm in men (5.0 cm in women), OR when growth exceeds 1 cm per year, OR when the patient becomes symptomatic. A 5.4 cm aneurysm with 0.7 cm growth in 12 months is at the surgical threshold and warrants vascular surgical assessment to discuss endovascular (EVAR) versus open repair and patient-specific anatomy/comorbidity. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)
Beta-blockers do not reduce AAA growth or rupture rates in randomised trials. BP control is appropriate but does not replace surgical assessment at threshold. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Suspected pulmonary embolism in pregnancy: start with chest X-ray and bilateral compression ultrasound of lower limbs. If CXR clear and CUS negative, V/Q scan is first-line imaging because of lower maternal breast radiation dose. CTPA reserved for abnormal CXR, underlying lung disease, or non-diagnostic V/Q. Empirical anticoagulation with low-molecular-weight heparin (NOT DOACs) is appropriate during imaging delay. D-dimer is not routinely used because it rises physiologically in pregnancy.
key_points: V/Q first-line in pregnancy with normal CXR (lower breast radiation)
CTPA reserved for abnormal CXR, underlying lung disease, non-diagnostic V/Q
Anticoagulation: LMWH only in pregnancy; DOACs contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Iliac vein DVT in pregnancy is missed on standard compression ultrasound (which scans femoral and popliteal); if clinical suspicion is high with negative routine CUS, request specific iliac vein imaging by Doppler or MRI venogram.

options.rationale: A single negative compression ultrasound does not exclude PE because clot may be confined to the pulmonary or pelvic vasculature. Definitive imaging of the pulmonary vasculature is required when clinical suspicion of PE is moderate-to-high. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)
