In pregnancy with a clear chest X-ray and no underlying lung disease, ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan is preferred over CTPA because of substantially lower maternal breast radiation dose (V/Q approximately 0.28 mGy maternal breast vs CTPA approximately 10-70 mGy maternal breast). Fetal radiation dose is comparable and within safe limits for either modality. CTPA is reserved for patients with chest X-ray abnormalities, underlying lung disease, or where V/Q is unavailable or non-diagnostic. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

CTPA exposes maternal breast tissue (highly radiosensitive in young women) to a much higher radiation dose than V/Q. With a clear chest X-ray, V/Q is preferred first-line. CTPA is reserved for abnormal CXR or non-diagnostic V/Q. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Pulmonary angiogram is invasive, carries higher radiation dose than CTPA or V/Q, and is reserved for cases where non-invasive imaging is non-diagnostic and PE confirmation is needed before catheter-directed therapy. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban) are contraindicated in pregnancy because of placental transfer and inadequate safety data. Empirical anticoagulation in pregnancy uses low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin 1 mg/kg twice daily). However, imaging should be pursued promptly to confirm and guide duration; empirical treatment without imaging is appropriate only as a bridge if imaging delay is likely. (Source: RANZCOG Statements)

explanation.summary: Sodium bicarbonate has a narrow place in hyperkalaemia: as an adjunct when a significant metabolic acidosis is present. It is slower and weaker than insulin with dextrose, and is never the sole treatment.
key_points: Bicarbonate is reserved for hyperkalaemia with significant metabolic acidosis.
Diuretics only help where urine output is preserved.
Dialysis is the definitive answer in oliguric acute kidney injury; everything else is a bridge.
explanation.context: Acidosis and hyperkalaemia travel together for two reasons. Inorganic acidosis drives potassium out of cells as hydrogen ions move in and are buffered intracellularly, and the same failing kidney that cannot excrete acid cannot excrete potassium. Correcting the pH reverses part of that exchange, which is why the benefit of bicarbonate is confined to patients who are actually acidotic and is modest even then. The wider lesson is the four-part structure of hyperkalaemia management: protect the myocardium, shift potassium into cells, remove it from the body, and stop whatever caused it.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Bicarbonate is an adjunct reserved for hyperkalaemia with a significant metabolic acidosis, where correcting the pH shifts potassium intracellularly and buys time until dialysis. It is not used as sole or first-line therapy. (Source: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Furosemide can help where the patient still makes urine and is not volume deplete, so kaliuresis can be driven. It is futile in established oliguria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)

Salbutamol works as an additional shifting agent, especially where intravenous access is difficult, but it adds little once insulin with dextrose is already running and leaves the acidosis untouched. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Sodium polystyrene sulfonate suits slow removal of total body potassium over hours to days in a patient who is not critically unwell, not as the bridge in a decompensated patient awaiting dialysis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Calcium is repeated when electrocardiogram changes persist or recur after the first dose, since calcium lasts under an hour. It is repeated for the rhythm, not for the acidosis. (Source: ANZCOR adult advanced life support)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma hypertensive crisis is treated with non-selective alpha-blockade first. IV phentolamine is the agent of choice for acute control; sodium nitroprusside is an alternative. Beta-blockade is contraindicated until alpha-blockade is established because unopposed alpha-mediated vasoconstriction worsens hypertension. After acute control, transition to oral phenoxybenzamine titrated against postural BP to a target of mild postural drop, followed by beta-blockade for residual tachycardia, with adequate fluid and sodium replacement before surgical resection at 7 to 14 days.
key_points: Alpha-blockade ALWAYS before beta-blockade in phaeochromocytoma
Phentolamine IV first-line for crisis; phenoxybenzamine oral for chronic preop
Beta-blocker monotherapy precipitates hypertensive crisis (unopposed alpha)
explanation.pearls: Pre-operative preparation needs 7 to 14 days of alpha-blockade with deliberate volume expansion (high sodium diet, IV saline if symptomatic postural drop) to prevent profound post-operative hypotension after tumour removal.

options.rationale: Beta-blocker monotherapy (or further beta-blockade) in phaeochromocytoma can paradoxically worsen hypertension by leaving alpha-mediated vasoconstriction unopposed. Beta-blockade must NEVER be added before alpha-blockade is established in phaeochromocytoma. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Phaeochromocytoma hypertensive crisis is managed with non-selective alpha-blockade FIRST. Phentolamine (a short-acting IV non-selective alpha-blocker) is the agent of choice for acute control while transitioning to oral phenoxybenzamine. Sodium nitroprusside or IV nicardipine may be alternative parenteral options where phentolamine is unavailable. Beta-blockade is added LATER, only after alpha-blockade is established and reflex tachycardia emerges. The patient has been on metoprolol without prior alpha-blockade, which is itself a precipitant; this should be paused. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Labetalol is a mixed alpha and beta blocker but its alpha-blocking effect is relatively weak compared with its beta effect, and in phaeochromocytoma the predominant beta effect can worsen hypertension. It is not first-line in phaeochromocytoma crisis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Amlodipine is not available in IV form; it is oral only and has a slow onset (24 to 48 hours). Calcium channel blockers can be used as adjunctive oral therapy in phaeochromocytoma but are not first-line for acute crisis. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Magnesium has been used as an adjunct in phaeochromocytoma anaesthesia and crisis but is not first-line; non-selective alpha-blockade with phentolamine is the standard initial agent. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical diagnosis suggested by pain out of proportion, rapid progression, dusky skin or bullae, systemic toxicity, raised CK, raised lactate and high LRINEC score (6+ high-risk). Empirical antibiotics: piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem PLUS clindamycin (anti-toxin) PLUS vancomycin (MRSA). Urgent surgical debridement is the only intervention that reduces mortality. Polymicrobial type I (diabetic, mixed aerobic/anaerobic) and monomicrobial type II (group A strep) are the two main forms.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity = think necrotising fasciitis
Diagnosis is surgical - do not delay operative debridement for imaging
Clindamycin is essential for anti-toxin effect against group A strep
explanation.pearls: Aeromonas and Vibrio vulnificus necrotising fasciitis follow freshwater and seawater exposure respectively; consider ceftriaxone plus doxycycline or fluoroquinolone in the empirical regimen when the history is consistent with water exposure.

options.rationale: The presentation (pain out of proportion, rapid progression, dusky skin with bullae, foul exudate, systemic toxicity, LRINEC 6+ high-risk, deranged renal function, lactate 4) is highly suspicious for necrotising fasciitis. The diagnosis is surgical, not radiological - imaging delays surgery and a normal CT does not exclude. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam OR meropenem) PLUS clindamycin (anti-toxin effect against group A streptococcus exotoxins) PLUS vancomycin (MRSA cover) are given immediately, but URGENT operative debridement is the only intervention that changes mortality. Australian guidance supports this combination empirically. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Standard cellulitis management understages this presentation. Pain out of proportion, bullae, dusky skin, lactate 4 and LRINEC 9 indicate necrotising fasciitis - delay of even hours increases mortality from approximately 25% to over 50%. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging may show fascial thickening, gas or fluid tracking, but the diagnosis is clinical and imaging delays surgery. Urgent surgical referral does not wait for CT in a patient with classic features. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

IM benzylpenicillin is dose-inappropriate for severe sepsis and does not cover Gram-negative or anaerobic flora seen in necrotising fasciitis (especially after a dog bite). Polymicrobial cover is required while awaiting surgical exploration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Oral antibiotics are inadequate for septic shock from necrotising fasciitis. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics plus immediate surgery are mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Cholinergic crisis from over-treatment with cholinesterase inhibitors produces muscarinic (SLUDGE: salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, GI cramps, emesis, plus miosis, bradycardia, bronchorrhoea) AND nicotinic (weakness, fasciculations) features. Myasthenic crisis presents with weakness alone without muscarinic features. The historical edrophonium test has been replaced by careful clinical assessment and a trial of cholinesterase withdrawal. Management: withhold pyridostigmine, atropine for muscarinic features, intubation for respiratory failure (FVC under 1 L, NIF less negative than -20, rising pCO2), and treat the underlying exacerbation with IVIG or plasma exchange.
key_points: Cholinergic crisis: muscarinic excess + weakness; myasthenic crisis: weakness only
Respiratory intubation thresholds: FVC <1 L, NIF less negative than -20 cmH2O
Treatment of underlying exacerbation: IVIG or plasma exchange after stabilisation
explanation.pearls: Common precipitants of myasthenic crisis: infections (especially respiratory), aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, magnesium, neuromuscular blockade and pregnancy/postpartum - always identify and remove the trigger as part of crisis management.

options.rationale: Increasing pyridostigmine in a patient who has been self-titrating, now showing muscarinic features (miosis, secretions, lacrimation, cramps, diarrhoea, bradycardia, fasciculations) along with weakness suggests cholinergic crisis from over-dosing rather than under-treated myasthenic crisis. Increasing the dose worsens the picture. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Giving more cholinesterase inhibitor in suspected cholinergic crisis is contraindicated; the historical edrophonium (Tensilon) test has fallen out of practice for this reason. Differentiation of myasthenic from cholinergic crisis is now based on clinical features and response to atropine and cessation of pyridostigmine. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

IVIG is appropriate treatment for myasthenic crisis but does not address the cholinergic component here and the muscarinic features (secretions, bradycardia, miosis, cramps) point to over-treatment. Withholding pyridostigmine is appropriate; IVIG can follow once cholinergic features resolve and pure myasthenic weakness is confirmed. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

The combination of weakness with muscarinic excess (miosis, increased oral secretions, lacrimation, bradycardia, abdominal cramps, diarrhoea, fasciculations) in a patient who has been self-escalating pyridostigmine is consistent with cholinergic crisis OR a mixed cholinergic-myasthenic picture. The correct response is to WITHHOLD pyridostigmine, give atropine 0.5 to 1 mg IV titrated for muscarinic features, and intubate given FVC below 1 L, NIF less negative than -20, rising CO2 and clinical respiratory failure. Once intubated and stabilised, treat underlying myasthenic exacerbation with IVIG or plasma exchange, and identify and treat the precipitant (here the chest infection). (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Pralidoxime is used in organophosphate poisoning, not in pyridostigmine-induced cholinergic excess; pyridostigmine causes reversible cholinesterase inhibition that resolves with cessation. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: Guillain-Barre syndrome is treated with IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (or plasma exchange 5 sessions over 2 weeks - equivalent efficacy). Corticosteroids are NOT effective. Monitor for respiratory failure (FVC, NIF, MIP/MEP - 20-30-40 rule: FVC less than 20 mL/kg, MIP less negative than -30, MEP less than 40 triggers intubation) and autonomic dysfunction (cardiac arrhythmia, labile BP) - both are major causes of mortality. Common precipitants: Campylobacter jejuni, CMV, EBV, Mycoplasma, vaccinations (rare). Recovery over weeks to months; residual disability in 20%.
key_points: IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day x 5 days OR plasma exchange; steroids ineffective
20-30-40 rule for ventilatory support thresholds
Autonomic dysfunction is a major mortality contributor - HDU monitoring mandatory
explanation.pearls: The Miller Fisher variant of GBS presents with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia and areflexia without prominent limb weakness; anti-GQ1b antibody is positive in over 85% and is the diagnostic test of choice when this triad is seen.

options.rationale: Corticosteroids are NOT effective in Guillain-Barre syndrome (multiple trials have shown no benefit). Steroids are used in chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP), not in GBS. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Intubation is required when FVC falls below approximately 20 mL/kg (about 1.0 to 1.2 L in adults), MIP less negative than -30, MEP under 40, or there is bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk (the so-called 20-30-40 rule). At FVC 1.4 L with downward trend, immediate intubation is premature; close monitoring with intubation when criteria met is appropriate, alongside specific therapy. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Treating individual autonomic events symptomatically may be necessary but does not address the underlying disease; autonomic instability resolves with treatment of the GBS itself. The fundamental treatment is IVIG or plasma exchange, with cardiac monitoring for arrhythmia. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Plasma exchange is an equally effective treatment to IVIG in GBS but is less practical in many Australian centres, requires central venous access and is generally reserved for patients in whom IVIG is contraindicated or fails. IVIG is the more commonly used first-line. Either is acceptable; the key point is that disease-modifying therapy is needed now. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

Guillain-Barre syndrome with progressive weakness, autonomic instability and falling FVC warrants prompt disease-modifying therapy with IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days (total 2 g/kg). Plasma exchange is an equivalent alternative. Concurrent management includes HDU/ICU level monitoring for autonomic instability (cardiac telemetry), serial FVC and NIF every 2 to 4 hours, DVT prophylaxis, and intubation criteria readiness. Steroids are not effective. Autonomic instability (labile BP, tachy-brady) is a major cause of mortality and necessitates HDU/ICU. (Source: BMJ Best Practice)

explanation.summary: eTG first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in an adult without MRSA risk factors and without severe sepsis is oral flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days. Mark the margin and reassess at 48 hours; escalate to IV if no improvement, sepsis develops, or rapid progression. Clindamycin or TMP-SMX is for non-severe penicillin allergy or MRSA cover. IV therapy is reserved for systemic illness or facial/orbital cellulitis.
key_points: First-line non-purulent cellulitis: flucloxacillin 500 mg QID 5 days
Cefalexin is reasonable but second-choice in AU practice
TMP-SMX or clindamycin if MRSA risk or non-severe penicillin allergy
IV therapy: systemic illness, rapid progression, facial cellulitis
explanation.pearls: Marking the erythema border with a marker and reassessing at 48 hours is an underused practical bedside test that tells you whether the antibiotic is working before changing therapy.

options.rationale: Cefalexin is reasonable but at 500 mg QID covers streptococci adequately but has weaker beta-lactamase stability against community methicillin-susceptible S. aureus than flucloxacillin in AU practice. eTG prefers flucloxacillin first-line for non-purulent cellulitis without MRSA risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

IV antibiotics are indicated when systemic sepsis features are present (sepsis criteria, rapid progression, failure of oral therapy), in immunosuppressed patients, or for facial cellulitis; this patient is systemically well with limited disease and well-controlled diabetes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Clindamycin is reserved for non-severe penicillin allergy or where MRSA cover is needed. It is not first-line in non-purulent cellulitis without MRSA risk factors. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole is used when MRSA is suspected or confirmed and is not standard first-line cover for streptococcal cellulitis where streptococci are the predominant organism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

eTG recommends oral flucloxacillin 500 mg every 6 hours for 5 days as first-line for non-purulent cellulitis in an adult without MRSA risk factors or severe sepsis; it covers Streptococcus pyogenes and methicillin-susceptible Staphylococcus aureus, the predominant causative organisms. Mark the erythema border and reassess at 48 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: A postmenopausal woman with minimal-trauma fracture plus DEXA T-score ≤-2.5 meets PBS criteria for anti-resorptive therapy. Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line in normal renal function with no dental contraindication. Denosumab is preferred for renal impairment or oral intolerance. Teriparatide is for severe disease. MHT is no longer first-line for osteoporosis in older women.
key_points: Minimal-trauma fracture + T ≤-2.5 = anti-resorptive eligible
First-line: alendronate 70 mg weekly if eGFR ≥35 and no dental contraindication
Denosumab if renal impairment or oral intolerance
Calcium 1000 mg/day + vitamin D 800-1000 IU/day
explanation.pearls: PBS osteoporosis criteria in AU include minimal-trauma fragility fracture in adults aged 70+ OR DEXA T-score ≤-2.5; either alone meets the eligibility threshold.

options.rationale: Postmenopausal woman with a minimal-trauma fracture plus DEXA T-score ≤-2.5 meets PBS-funded criteria for anti-resorptive therapy. Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly is first-line in patients with normal renal function and no high-risk dental procedures or oesophageal contraindication; calcium and vitamin D are maintained; falls assessment is added. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

Denosumab is an alternative anti-resorptive and is preferred for renal impairment (eGFR <35) or oral bisphosphonate intolerance. With normal renal function and patient preference for oral therapy, oral alendronate is first-line. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures, very low T-score, or failure of anti-resorptive therapy; it is not first-line in this case. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

Calcium and vitamin D alone are insufficient when osteoporosis is established with a recent minimal-trauma fracture; PBS-funded pharmacotherapy is indicated and delay increases re-fracture risk. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

MHT is no longer first-line for osteoporosis given thromboembolic, stroke, and breast cancer risks in older postmenopausal women, particularly more than 10 years from menopause as in this case. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: The 2017 McDonald criteria allow CSF-specific oligoclonal bands to substitute for dissemination in time. With one clinical attack (optic neuritis) and DIS demonstrated on MRI plus CSF OCBs, the diagnosis advances from CIS to relapsing-remitting MS, allowing earlier initiation of disease-modifying therapy. AQP4 and MOG antibody testing are mandatory in atypical presentations to exclude NMOSD and MOGAD respectively.
key_points: 2017 McDonald: OCBs substitute for DIT
DIS: lesions in ≥2 of 4 typical locations (periventricular, juxtacortical/cortical, infratentorial, spinal)
Test AQP4 and MOG to exclude alternatives
Earlier diagnosis = earlier DMT = better long-term outcome
explanation.pearls: The 2017 McDonald update shifted OCBs from a supportive feature to an accepted substitute for DIT, enabling MS diagnosis at the first clinical event in many patients and earlier DMT initiation.

options.rationale: Subacute combined degeneration causes dorsal column and corticospinal tract signs, often peripheral neuropathy and megaloblastic anaemia. It does not cause optic neuritis with periventricular MRI lesions and OCBs. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MS)

CIS describes a first clinical event without dissemination in time evidence; here CSF oligoclonal bands plus DIS substitute for DIT under the 2017 McDonald criteria, making this MS rather than isolated CIS. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria)

NMOSD typically presents with longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (3+ vertebral segments) or severe optic neuritis with aquaporin-4 IgG positivity; AQP4-IgG is negative here and lesion patterns are consistent with MS. (Source: International NMOSD Criteria)

MOG-IgG is negative; MOGAD typically presents with bilateral optic neuritis, ADEM-like episodes, or longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis, with a different MRI pattern. (Source: MOGAD Criteria)

Dissemination in space is met by typical MRI lesions in two or more CNS locations (here periventricular and juxtacortical plus spinal). Dissemination in time is met by CSF-specific oligoclonal bands (acceptable substitute for a second clinical attack or enhancing lesion under 2017 McDonald criteria). The clinical syndrome of optic neuritis with positive lesion and OCBs supports RRMS diagnosis. (Source: 2017 McDonald Criteria)

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis: FVC <15 mL/kg or <1 L, weak cough, respiratory failure, often triggered by infection or medication. Cholinergic crisis (excess pyridostigmine): SLUDGE/miosis with fasciculations and bronchorrhoea. Pupil size and secretions are the bedside discriminators. Management of myasthenic crisis is airway/ventilation support, withholding pyridostigmine temporarily, and plasmapheresis or IVIG to remove circulating antibodies.
key_points: Myasthenic: normal pupils, dry membranes, no fasciculations
Cholinergic: miosis, fasciculations, SLUDGE
FVC <1 L or <15 mL/kg is crisis threshold
Withhold pyridostigmine, IVIG or plasmapheresis, ICU
explanation.pearls: Cholinergic crisis is rare in modern practice as pyridostigmine doses are usually conservative; assume myasthenic crisis until cholinergic features (miosis, fasciculations, bronchorrhoea) prove otherwise.

options.rationale: Pyrexia, normal troponin, and clinical features of bulbar weakness with ptosis are characteristic of myasthenic crisis, not PE; ABG shows hypercapnia (PE typically hypocapnia with type 1 respiratory failure). (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)

Cholinergic crisis presents with miosis, fasciculations, hypersalivation, lacrimation, diarrhoea, and bradycardia (SLUDGE/miosis), which are absent here. Dry mucous membranes and normal pupil size point to myasthenic, not cholinergic, crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology)

Bilateral ptosis with bulbar weakness, paradoxical breathing, hypercapnia (pCO2 56 mmHg) and FVC under 1 L (or 15 mL/kg) define myasthenic crisis. Initial trigger here was viral illness. Distinguishing from cholinergic crisis: pupils normal-sized, mucous membranes dry (not wet), no fasciculations, bowel sounds normal - all favouring myasthenic rather than cholinergic crisis. Treatment is airway protection (NIV or intubation), withholding pyridostigmine to remove ambiguity, and immunomodulation with plasmapheresis or IVIG. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Neurology)

Asthma exacerbation does not cause bilateral ptosis, dysphagia, or fatigable shoulder weakness, and the respiratory failure here is from neuromuscular weakness not bronchoconstriction. Wheeze is absent. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)
Hyperventilation would cause hypocapnia, not hypercapnia, and would not produce bilateral ptosis or bulbar features. The objective ABG and FVC exclude anxiety as cause. (Source: BMJ Best Practice MG)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is suggested by sudden severe tearing chest/back pain, inter-arm BP differential over 20 mmHg, aortic regurgitation murmur, and widened mediastinum. CT aortogram is the diagnostic standard. Treatment targets rate first (HR under 60 with beta-blockade) then BP (systolic 100-120 mmHg). ACS therapy is contraindicated until dissection is excluded. Type A dissections require emergency cardiothoracic surgery; type B is medical unless complicated.
key_points: Pain quality + BP differential + AR murmur + widened mediastinum
CT aortogram is diagnostic standard
Beta-blocker first (rate, dP/dt), then vasodilator
Avoid ACS treatment until dissection excluded
explanation.pearls: Treating dissection like ACS with antiplatelets and anticoagulants is the high-yield exam disconfirming step; the inter-arm BP differential >20 mmHg with an early diastolic murmur in a hypertensive smoker is the picture that must override the ACS reflex.

options.rationale: Coronary angiography with anticoagulation in dissection causes catastrophic bleeding; dissection must be excluded before any invasive coronary procedure even when troponin rises (which can occur with coronary ostia involvement in dissection). (Source: ESC Aortic Dissection)

Dual antiplatelet therapy and anticoagulation in suspected aortic dissection cause catastrophic bleeding into the false lumen and pericardial space; ACS treatment is contraindicated until dissection is excluded. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

Vasodilators alone increase reflex tachycardia and aortic wall stress; beta-blockade must precede or accompany any vasodilator therapy to control rate and dP/dt before reducing BP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

TTE sensitivity for aortic dissection is limited (especially descending dissection) and discharge of a patient with classical dissection features is unsafe; CT aortogram or TOE is required urgently. (Source: ESC Aortic Dissection)

Sudden tearing interscapular pain, blood pressure differential between arms over 20 mmHg, aortic regurgitation murmur and widened mediastinum strongly suggest acute aortic dissection. Urgent CT aortogram is the diagnostic modality of choice in the haemodynamically stable patient; meanwhile rapid IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) targeting heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100-120 mmHg reduces aortic wall shear stress. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis identified by haemodynamic compromise with tracheal deviation, ipsilateral hyperresonance and absent breath sounds, raised JVP, and hypoxia. Immediate needle decompression in the 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary line is followed by formal intercostal catheter. Positive-pressure ventilation before decompression can precipitate cardiac arrest. Lung ultrasound (absent sliding, barcode sign) confirms the diagnosis at the bedside.
key_points: Clinical diagnosis - decompress before imaging
4th-5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary line preferred in adults (ATLS 10)
Avoid positive-pressure ventilation pre-decompression
Formal intercostal catheter follows needle decompression
explanation.pearls: ATLS 10th edition moved adult needle decompression from 2nd ICS midclavicular to 4th-5th ICS anterior/mid-axillary because the lateral chest wall is consistently thinner and the needle more reliably reaches the pleural space.

options.rationale: Cardiac tamponade produces muffled heart sounds, equal breath sounds bilaterally, and pulsus paradoxus; the clinical picture and ultrasound here are pneumothorax, not tamponade. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis; waiting for imaging delays life-saving decompression and risks cardiac arrest. Bedside ultrasound has already confirmed pneumothorax (absent sliding, barcode sign). (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

Positive-pressure ventilation in tension pneumothorax can convert a simple pneumothorax to tension and rapidly worsens haemodynamics; decompression must precede intubation when tension is suspected. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)
Fluids and vasopressors do not address the obstructive cause of shock; chest decompression is the only effective intervention. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

Tension pneumothorax with haemodynamic compromise requires immediate decompression. AU and ATLS now recommend the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line as the preferred site in adults (replacing the 2nd ICS midclavicular site for higher reliability in adult chest wall thickness), followed by formal intercostal catheter for definitive drainage. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

explanation.summary: Chylothorax presents as milky pleural fluid from thoracic duct injury, often after thoracic, oesophageal, or cardiac surgery. Diagnosis is by pleural fluid triglyceride: above 1.24 mmol/L confirms; below 0.56 mmol/L excludes; intermediate requires chylomicron electrophoresis. Pseudochylothorax (cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L, low triglyceride) is seen in chronic inflammatory effusions. Management is dietary fat restriction with medium-chain triglycerides, octreotide, and thoracic duct ligation or embolisation for refractory cases.
key_points: Pleural triglyceride >1.24 mmol/L = chylothorax
Cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L + low triglyceride = pseudochylothorax
Post-thoracic surgery is a classic chylothorax setting
Treatment: MCT diet, octreotide, then duct ligation/embolisation
explanation.pearls: Pleural cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L with low triglyceride distinguishes pseudochylothorax from true chylothorax - the two milky-effusion entities that look identical at the bedside but have entirely different aetiologies and management.

options.rationale: Raised pleural amylase suggests pancreatic effusion or oesophageal rupture, neither of which is supported by the post-thoracic-surgery context with milky lymphocytic fluid. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

High cholesterol with low triglyceride is the signature of pseudochylothorax (chronic effusions from RA, TB, old empyema), not true chylothorax. Triglyceride is the discriminator for chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)
ADA is useful in suspected TB pleural effusion but the milky appearance and post-thoracic-surgery context point to chylothorax; ADA does not confirm chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

Empyema fluid is purulent with pH below 7.20, glucose below 2.2 mmol/L, and high neutrophils; this fluid has normal pH, normal glucose, and lymphocyte predominance, excluding empyema. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

Milky pleural fluid with high lymphocyte count after thoracic surgery is highly suspicious for chylothorax from thoracic duct injury. Pleural fluid triglyceride above 1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) confirms chylothorax; below 0.56 mmol/L (50 mg/dL) excludes it. The intermediate range requires lipoprotein electrophoresis for chylomicrons. Cholesterol level differentiates pseudochylothorax (cholesterol >5.18 mmol/L with low triglyceride) from true chylothorax. (Source: BTS Pleural Disease)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP stratifies community-acquired pneumonia by need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support. Score 0-2: low severity, outpatient amoxicillin plus doxycycline. Score 3-4: moderate severity, ward admission with IV benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline. Score 5+: severe, ICU consideration with IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin (and anti-pseudomonal cover if structural lung disease). Step-down to oral amoxicillin or doxycycline when clinically stable; total duration 5-7 days.
key_points: SMART-COP 0-2 outpatient, 3-4 ward, 5+ ICU consideration
Ward AU first-line: IV benzylpenicillin + oral doxycycline (or azithromycin)
ICU CAP: IV ceftriaxone + IV azithromycin; add anti-pseudomonal if at risk
Total duration 5-7 days; step down when clinically stable
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP gives 2 points for systolic BP under 90 mmHg, multilobar CXR, low albumin under 35 g/L, RR raised, tachycardia over 125 bpm; and 2 points for confusion, oxygen low, low pH - a score of 3 or 4 is moderate severity requiring admission.

options.rationale: Oral monotherapy or oral combination is appropriate for low-severity CAP (SMART-COP 0-2) without admission; SMART-COP 3 in this patient (low SpO2, low pH-neutral with low PaO2 less than 70 mmHg, plus low albumin) is moderate severity warranting admission and intravenous therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Moderate-severity CAP (SMART-COP 3-4, admitted to ward) is treated with AU first-line intravenous benzylpenicillin plus oral doxycycline (or oral azithromycin) to cover Streptococcus pneumoniae and atypicals (Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila). Step-down to oral amoxicillin when stable. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam plus macrolide combination is reserved for severe CAP (SMART-COP 5+), severe sepsis, or specific risk factors for resistant organisms (structural lung disease, recent broad-spectrum antibiotics); SMART-COP 3 with ward admission does not need this. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin empirical cover is reserved for MRSA-suspected pneumonia (severe necrotising, post-influenza secondary bacterial, intravenous drug use, or community MRSA prevalence high); none apply here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Fluoroquinolone monotherapy in CAP is reserved for penicillin allergy with anaphylaxis or other contraindication; AU stewardship discourages fluoroquinolone first-line because of resistance and tendinopathy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; AMH)

explanation.summary: Iron-deficiency anaemia in adults over 50 (any sex), or in postmenopausal women, mandates urgent gastrointestinal investigation for occult malignancy. Combined upper endoscopy and colonoscopy under one anaesthetic is the AU standard. Premenopausal women with menstrual losses can be treated empirically with iron, but those with persistent or severe deficiency, family history of colorectal cancer, or other red flags warrant endoscopic workup. Once a cause is found, treat with oral iron (or IV iron if oral intolerant) and recheck at 6-12 weeks.
key_points: Adults over 50 with iron deficiency: dual endoscopy until proven otherwise
Premenopausal: treat empirically with iron unless red flags
Oral iron first-line; IV iron if oral failed or intolerant
Recheck Hb and ferritin at 6-12 weeks of treatment
explanation.pearls: Oral iron is best absorbed when taken second-daily on an empty stomach (the hepcidin rebound from daily dosing reduces absorption), often with vitamin C; treat for 3 to 6 months past haemoglobin normalisation to refill stores.

options.rationale: Empirical iron treatment without investigating the source of loss in an adult over 50 (and any postmenopausal woman) is unsafe; colorectal malignancy must be excluded. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines; NHMRC NBCSP)

Inherited haemoglobinopathy is unlikely in an adult whose haemoglobin was 142 g/L three years ago; ferritin of 8 micrograms/L is diagnostic of iron deficiency. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)

Iron-deficiency anaemia in an adult over 50 (or any postmenopausal woman) is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise. AU practice is dual upper endoscopy and colonoscopy on the same anaesthetic to identify upper gastrointestinal pathology (peptic ulcer, malignancy) and lower gastrointestinal cancer or angiodysplasia. Empirical iron without endoscopy delays diagnosis. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines; NHMRC NBCSP)

CT colonography misses small adenomas and cannot biopsy or treat; colonoscopy is preferred when the index of suspicion for malignancy is high. Upper endoscopy is also needed. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)
H. pylori may contribute to iron deficiency via gastritis but does not exclude malignancy; endoscopy with biopsy is required. (Source: GESA Iron Deficiency Guidelines)

explanation.summary: New atrial fibrillation is managed with stroke prophylaxis (CHA2DS2-VA-based anticoagulation) and either rate or rhythm control. Direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban, rivaroxaban, dabigatran, edoxaban) are AU first-line; warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves or moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Rate control (beta-blocker first, calcium channel blocker if beta-blocker contraindicated) targets resting heart rate under 110 bpm (lenient) or 80 bpm (strict). Cardioversion in unscreened AF over 48 hours requires either TOE-guided or 3-4 weeks of anticoagulation first.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA replaces CHA2DS2-VASc in AU - drops sex points
DOAC first-line; warfarin only for mechanical valve / moderate-severe MS
Rate control: bisoprolol first, target HR under 110 bpm
Cardioversion in AF over 48 hours: TOE-guided or 3-4 weeks anticoagulation first
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily is the AU first-line DOAC for stroke prevention in non-valvular AF; reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily if any two of age over 80, weight under 60 kg, or creatinine over 133 micromol/L are present.

options.rationale: Aspirin is not adequate stroke prophylaxis in atrial fibrillation; CHA2DS2-VA score over 1 in this patient (age, hypertension, diabetes, prior TIA) mandates oral anticoagulation. Cardioversion in unscreened AF over 48 hours requires either transoesophageal echo to exclude thrombus or 3-4 weeks of anticoagulation first. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

TOE-guided cardioversion is a reasonable strategy when prompt rhythm control is needed, but rate control with oral anticoagulation is the AU first-line for newly diagnosed AF of uncertain duration; rhythm strategy is decided at outpatient follow-up. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
Ablation is reserved for symptomatic paroxysmal or persistent AF refractory to medical therapy; first-line is rate or rhythm control and oral anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)
Bisoprolol is for rate control, not rhythm control; anticoagulation is missing from this option and is the priority for stroke prevention. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline)

CHA2DS2-VA score of 5 (age, hypertension, diabetes, prior TIA - the VA scheme drops sex; under AU practice this score mandates anticoagulation). Apixaban is AU first-line DOAC, well-tolerated, no INR monitoring required. Bisoprolol provides rate control. Cardiology decides on rhythm vs rate strategy at outpatient review; if rhythm control is desired and AF is over 48 hours, anticoagulation precedes cardioversion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism is risk-stratified by haemodynamic status, right ventricular strain, and cardiac biomarker elevation. High-risk (massive) PE - shock or sustained hypotension - is treated with systemic thrombolysis unless absolute contraindication, in which case catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy is considered. Intermediate-risk PE - normotensive with RV strain - is treated with anticoagulation alone, with close monitoring; rescue thrombolysis if deterioration occurs. Low-risk PE is treated outpatient with DOAC in selected patients.
key_points: Massive PE (shock): systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours
Intermediate-risk PE: anticoagulation, monitor for deterioration
Avoid fluid overload in RV failure; small judicious bolus only
Catheter-directed lysis or surgical embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated
explanation.pearls: Alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours is the AU thrombolytic regimen for massive PE; followed by unfractionated heparin infusion once thrombin time or APTT confirms adequate clearance.

options.rationale: Haemodynamically unstable PE (systolic BP under 90 mmHg or vasopressor requirement) with confirmed embolus and no absolute contraindication is treated with systemic thrombolysis. The AU regimen is alteplase 100 mg intravenously over 2 hours, then anticoagulation. Reduced dose or catheter-directed thrombolysis is considered in high bleeding-risk patients. Surgical embolectomy is reserved for failed thrombolysis or absolute contraindications. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Heparin alone is the standard for haemodynamically stable PE; with shock (systolic BP under 90 mmHg), thrombolysis or thrombectomy is the AU intervention; heparin is given alongside but is not sufficient on its own. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

IVC filters are reserved for absolute contraindication to anticoagulation or recurrent PE despite therapeutic anticoagulation; they do not treat the embolus already in situ. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

Therapeutic-dose LMWH is appropriate for haemodynamically stable PE; shock features (hypotension, low SpO2 needing oxygen) place this in the high-risk category requiring thrombolysis. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

Aggressive fluid loading in obstructive shock from PE can worsen right ventricular overload and reduce cardiac output; small judicious volume is acceptable while reperfusion therapy is given, not as primary treatment. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ VTE Guideline)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency. Empirical hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously stat, followed by 50-100 mg every 6 hours, is the AU first-line - given before biochemical confirmation when crisis is clinically suspected. Paired cortisol and ACTH samples can be drawn beforehand for later interpretation. Aggressive isotonic saline (1-2 L initially) and glucose correction address hypovolaemia and hypoglycaemia. Hyperpigmentation in light-exposed areas plus hyperkalaemia and hyponatraemia points to primary adrenal failure (Addison disease); secondary adrenal insufficiency lacks hyperpigmentation and hyperkalaemia.
key_points: Treat first, confirm second - hydrocortisone 100 mg IV stat
Paired cortisol and ACTH before first dose if feasible
Hyperpigmentation + hyperkalaemia = primary (Addison); think autoimmune adrenalitis in AU
Sick-day rules: triple hydrocortisone dose for febrile illness or major stress
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously stat then 50-100 mg every 6 hours covers both glucocorticoid and adequate mineralocorticoid receptor activity in acute crisis; fludrocortisone is added on transition to maintenance oral therapy.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is life-threatening and treatment must not wait for biochemical confirmation; the paired sample can be drawn before steroid administration but treatment proceeds. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH)

Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid effect (important in primary adrenal failure) and is less preferred in established crisis where mineralocorticoid replacement is needed; hydrocortisone is the AU first-line. Dexamethasone is acceptable only when needing to preserve cortisol assay for short ACTH stimulation. (Source: AMH)

Glucose correction alone does not address adrenal failure and the patient remains in crisis; steroid is the priority intervention alongside fluid and glucose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis (hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, hypotension, hyperpigmentation suggesting primary adrenal failure) is treated empirically with intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg stat, followed by 50-100 mg every 6 hours, alongside isotonic saline resuscitation and glucose correction. Paired cortisol and ACTH can be drawn before the first dose. Mineralocorticoid is not needed acutely at hydrocortisone doses of 50 mg or more (sufficient mineralocorticoid activity). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; AMH)
Surgical referral is irrelevant in acute adrenal crisis from primary adrenal failure; immediate steroid is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Diabetic ketoacidosis in adults is treated with fluid first, insulin second, and aggressive potassium replacement. Open with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour. Start insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/hour once potassium is known; withhold if under 3.5 mmol/L and replace potassium first. Add 5% dextrose to the fluid when glucose falls to around 14 mmol/L (continue insulin until ketones cleared). Treat the precipitant and convert to subcutaneous insulin only when acidosis and ketones have resolved and the patient can eat.
key_points: Fluid first, insulin within the first hour, potassium replacement priority
Withhold insulin if potassium under 3.5 mmol/L until replaced
Add 5% dextrose when glucose under 14 mmol/L while continuing insulin to clear ketones
Bicarbonate reserved for pH under 6.9 with shock or hyperkalaemic instability
explanation.pearls: AU DKA pathway: insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour without bolus; the priority is volume restoration and potassium replacement, not rapid glucose correction.

options.rationale: Starting insulin before adequate fluid resuscitation worsens hypovolaemia (osmotic diuresis is the primary driver of dehydration) and can precipitate hypoglycaemia and hypokalaemia faster; AU pathways open with fluid first then insulin within the first hour. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adult DKA management opens with intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over the first hour to restore intravascular volume. Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/hour is started within the first hour once potassium is known (over 3.5 mmol/L can give insulin without potassium replacement first; under 3.5 mmol/L withhold insulin and replace potassium). Potassium is added to the second litre of fluid unless K is over 5.5 mmol/L. Add 5% dextrose when glucose reaches 14 mmol/L while continuing insulin to clear ketones. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Subcutaneous insulin in established DKA is unreliable due to peripheral vasoconstriction; intravenous infusion is the AU first-line. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)

Bicarbonate is reserved for pH under 6.9 with shock or hyperkalaemia-related cardiac instability; routine use in DKA worsens intracellular acidosis and prolongs ketosis. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)
Empirical antibiotics are not part of the DKA bundle unless infection is clinically suspected; the trigger here is pump failure. (Source: ADS/ADIPS DKA Guideline)

explanation.summary: Warfarin-associated major bleeding (intracerebral haemorrhage, ongoing major bleeding, or pre-emergency surgery) requires rapid reversal with prothrombin complex concentrate plus intravenous vitamin K. The AU agent (Prothrombinex-VF) contains factors II, IX, and X and works within minutes; vitamin K provides sustained factor synthesis as prothrombin complex clears. Fresh frozen plasma is second-line due to slow speed, large volume, and incomplete factor profile. In mechanical valve patients, recommencement of anticoagulation is balanced against rebleed risk; typically restart at 1 to 4 weeks based on imaging stability and valve type.
key_points: Major bleed on warfarin: prothrombin complex concentrate 50 IU/kg + IV vitamin K 10 mg
Prothrombinex-VF is the AU agent (3-factor: II, IX, X) - works within minutes
FFP is second-line: slow, volume burden, incomplete factor coverage
Mechanical mitral valve: restart anticoagulation at 1 to 4 weeks based on bleed stability
explanation.pearls: Prothrombinex-VF 50 IU/kg combined with intravenous vitamin K 10 mg restores warfarin-suppressed factors II, IX, and X within minutes while vitamin K secures sustained correction - the AU rapid-reversal pair for warfarin-associated intracerebral haemorrhage.

options.rationale: Fresh frozen plasma reverses warfarin slowly (large-volume infusion limits rate), provides incomplete factor replacement, and risks transfusion-associated circulatory overload in the elderly; AU guidelines prefer prothrombin complex concentrate. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus; HSANZ)

Intravenous vitamin K alone takes 6 to 12 hours for full effect, far too slow for ongoing intracerebral haemorrhage; rapid factor replacement is required first. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)
Watchful waiting in major bleeding with INR over 4 is contraindicated; rapid reversal is the AU standard. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)

Recombinant factor VIIa is not the AU first-line for warfarin-associated ICH and carries arterial thrombosis risk; prothrombin complex concentrate is preferred for warfarin reversal. (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus)

Warfarin-associated major bleeding (intracerebral haemorrhage is the highest-risk category) is reversed with three- or four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (Prothrombinex-VF in AU) at 50 IU/kg plus intravenous vitamin K 10 mg. Prothrombinex restores factors II, IX, and X within minutes; vitamin K provides sustained factor synthesis to prevent rebound coagulopathy as the prothrombin complex concentrate clears. Mechanical mitral valve thrombosis risk in the short term is acceptable in the context of active ICH; restart anticoagulation when imaging stabilises (typically 1 to 4 weeks). (Source: NBA Warfarin Reversal Consensus; HSANZ; ANZSBT)

explanation.summary: The Surviving Sepsis Campaign 1-hour bundle (adapted in Australia by ANZICS) includes measuring lactate, blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour, 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, and vasopressor (noradrenaline) to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg if fluid-refractory. Repeat lactate guides response. Empirical antibiotic choice is by source. Urinary tract sepsis is treated with piperacillin-tazobactam or third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone or cefotaxime), with gentamicin added when severity warrants and renal function permits. Source control (drainage, removal of foreign material) is essential.
key_points: Lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg fluid, vasopressor if refractory - the hour-1 elements
Antibiotic delay raises mortality - empirical cover starts immediately
Source control completes the bundle
Noradrenaline first-line vasopressor; vasopressin second
explanation.pearls: Noradrenaline is the first-line vasopressor in septic shock targeting MAP 65 mmHg; vasopressin 0.03 IU/min is added to reduce noradrenaline requirements when high doses are needed.

options.rationale: Crystalloid resuscitation for sepsis-induced hypotension or lactate above 4 mmol/L targets 30 mL/kg within 3 hours, not a single 1 L bolus; gentamicin dose is reasonable but needs review in CKD and is paired with a broader-spectrum agent for urosepsis with shock. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Hydrocortisone is added when shock persists despite adequate fluid resuscitation and vasopressor therapy; it is not the first-line step. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

Surviving Sepsis adapted hour-1 bundle: measure lactate, take blood cultures before antibiotics if no delay, administer broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics within 1 hour (piperacillin-tazobactam covers Gram-negative urosepsis), give 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate over 4 mmol/L, repeat lactate, start vasopressors to maintain MAP at least 65 mmHg if hypotension persists after fluids. Early ICU communication is part of escalation. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Antibiotic delay in septic shock increases mortality by approximately 7% per hour; empirical broad-spectrum therapy is given before culture results. CVP-guided resuscitation has been superseded by dynamic measures. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

Noradrenaline is initiated when fluid resuscitation has been inadequate to restore MAP to 65 mmHg, not before initial fluid loading; in undifferentiated shock, fluid resuscitation precedes vasopressor in the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Surviving Sepsis Adaptation)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a deep soft tissue infection along the fascial planes with rapid progression and high mortality. Hallmarks: pain out of proportion to examination, dusky discoloration, haemorrhagic blisters, crepitus, systemic toxicity, and a tense oedematous limb with reduced sensation over the affected area. LRINEC score 6 or higher raises suspicion (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) but does not exclude the diagnosis at lower scores. Management is urgent surgical debridement, broad-spectrum empirical antibiotics (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for toxin suppression, and aggressive fluid resuscitation. Source control is essential and re-look debridement is the rule.
key_points: Pain out of proportion plus dusky skin plus crepitus is a surgical emergency
LRINEC over 6 raises suspicion; under 6 does not exclude
Empirical cover: meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam PLUS clindamycin
Repeat debridement is the rule, not the exception
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin is added to standard broad-spectrum cover because it suppresses streptococcal toxin production and remains effective in the stationary growth phase where beta-lactams are inoculum-limited.

options.rationale: Imaging is supportive but should not delay surgical referral and exploration when clinical features are characteristic; the operating theatre is the diagnostic and therapeutic destination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Empirical cover for necrotising fasciitis requires broad spectrum including anaerobic and protein synthesis inhibitor for toxin suppression; surgical debridement is the priority. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC over 6, pain out of proportion, dusky skin, haemorrhagic blisters, crepitus, systemic toxicity) is a surgical emergency. Empirical broad-spectrum cover (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin (for streptococcal and clostridial toxin suppression) and fluid resuscitation accompany urgent surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
This is a surgical emergency; outpatient management has a high mortality. Cefalexin does not cover the spectrum needed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Topical agents have no role in deep soft tissue infection requiring debridement; this is a surgical emergency. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Postmenopausal osteoporosis is diagnosed by DEXA T-score under -2.5 OR by a minimal-trauma fracture regardless of T-score in a woman over 50 (or man over 50). Australian PBS-funded therapy for women aged 70 or over uses T-score under -2.5 OR T-score under -1.5 with minimal-trauma fracture. First-line pharmacotherapy is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly, risedronate 35 mg weekly, or zoledronic acid 5 mg IV annually). Denosumab is second-line or first-line when bisphosphonates contraindicated. Anabolic agents (teriparatide, romosozumab) are reserved for severe disease. Calcium 1300 mg daily, vitamin D supplementation, weight-bearing exercise, fall-risk modification, and smoking abstinence are universally recommended.
key_points: Diagnosis: T-score under -2.5 OR minimal-trauma fracture over 50
First-line: oral bisphosphonate (alendronate or risedronate) or IV zoledronic acid
Denosumab second-line; severe rebound on cessation
Anabolics (teriparatide, romosozumab) for severe disease only
explanation.pearls: Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV once yearly is an alternative to weekly oral bisphosphonate when oesophageal pathology, swallow difficulty, or adherence is the issue; pre-treat with paracetamol to reduce the post-infusion flu-like reaction.

sources.label: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis

options.rationale: A minimal-trauma fracture in a woman over 50 with T-score under -1.5 is established osteoporosis under the AU MBS criteria; pharmacological treatment is indicated now, not deferred. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis

options.rationale: Raloxifene is a SERM reserved for selected patients with vertebral fracture risk and no peripheral fracture concern; it does not reduce non-vertebral or hip fractures and is not first-line. (Source: AMH; Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis

options.rationale: Denosumab is an alternative when bisphosphonates are contraindicated or not tolerated, or with eGFR under 30 mL/min/1.73 m squared; it is not the AU first-line. Stopping denosumab abruptly causes rapid rebound bone loss, so the agent is best reserved for patients who can adhere indefinitely. (Source: AMH)

Teriparatide (recombinant PTH 1-34) is anabolic and reserved for patients with severe osteoporosis (T-score under -3 with multiple fractures or where antiresorptive therapy has failed); it is not first-line. (Source: AMH)

A minimal-trauma fracture and T-score under -2.5 in a postmenopausal woman meets PBS criteria for an oral bisphosphonate. Alendronate 70 mg orally once weekly is first-line. Adequate dietary calcium (1300 mg daily) and vitamin D (with supplementation if level under 50 nmol/L), smoking abstinence, weight-bearing exercise, and fall-risk modification are co-prescribed. Bone health is reviewed at 12 months and treatment duration reviewed at 5 years. (Source: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis; AMH)
source_refs: Royal Australian College of General Practitioners Osteoporosis

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion is the transfusion of large volumes of blood products typically defined as 10 or more units of red cells in 24 hours, 4 or more units in 1 hour with ongoing need, or replacement of more than half the blood volume in 4 hours. Indications include uncontrolled haemorrhage with haemodynamic compromise (shock index over 1, lactate over 4 mmol/L, ongoing visible blood loss). Balanced product ratios (close to 1:1:1 red cells:plasma:platelets) reduce mortality compared to red cells alone. Tranexamic acid 1 g IV is given within 3 hours of injury, followed by 1 g over 8 hours. Calcium gluconate prevents citrate-induced hypocalcaemia after multiple units. Avoid hypothermia, acidosis, and hypocalcaemia (the lethal triad with coagulopathy).
key_points: Activation indicators: shock index over 1, lactate over 4 mmol/L, ongoing haemorrhage
Balanced ratios 1:1:1 reduce mortality
Permissive hypotension (SBP around 90 mmHg) until haemorrhage controlled
Calcium gluconate prevents citrate-induced hypocalcaemia
explanation.pearls: Tranexamic acid 1 g IV given within 3 hours of trauma onset followed by 1 g over 8 hours reduces all-cause mortality; later than 3 hours it may increase mortality and is not given.

sources.label: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Module

options.rationale: Crystalloid above 1-2 L worsens trauma-induced coagulopathy by dilution and cooling; uncrossmatched red cells and balanced product ratios are the next step in major haemorrhage. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management; National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Module)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Module

options.rationale: Major haemorrhage protocols use balanced product ratios (close to 1:1:1 red cells:plasma:platelets) to reduce trauma-induced coagulopathy mortality; red cells alone exacerbate dilutional coagulopathy. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)

The shock index (HR over SBP) above 1, ongoing haemorrhage with pelvic and lower limb sources, and lactate over 5 mmol/L are indications for massive transfusion protocol activation. Balanced product ratios (close to 1:1:1) reduce mortality compared to red cells alone. The pelvic binder is already applied; permissive hypotension (target SBP around 90 mmHg until haemorrhage controlled) and damage control surgery follow. Calcium gluconate is given after multiple units to prevent citrate-induced hypocalcaemia. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management; National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Module)
source_refs: National Blood Authority Massive Transfusion Module

options.rationale: Major haemorrhage requires empirical balanced product transfusion immediately; awaiting laboratory results delays correction and increases mortality. Targeted product replacement is added later guided by laboratory or viscoelastic testing. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management)
Prothrombinex is used for warfarin reversal or significant coagulopathy with factor deficiency, not as primary haemostatic resuscitation in undifferentiated trauma. (Source: AMH)

explanation.summary: Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis is empirically treated with IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly, with benzylpenicillin or amoxicillin 2 g 4-hourly added when listeria is a consideration (age over 50, immunocompromise, pregnancy). Vancomycin is added in regions with high penicillin/ceftriaxone-resistant pneumococcal prevalence. Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is given immediately before or with the first antibiotic dose and continued for 4 days; greatest benefit is in pneumococcal disease, reducing mortality and hearing loss. CT head is performed before lumbar puncture only when clinical features suggest raised intracranial pressure risk (altered consciousness, focal deficit, papilloedema, seizure in the past week, immunocompromise), and never delay antibiotics for imaging. Public health notification, contact tracing, and chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin or rifampicin) for close contacts of meningococcal cases are mandatory.
key_points: Empirical: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly +/- benzylpenicillin for listeria
Dexamethasone 10 mg IV immediately before or with first antibiotic
CT before LP only with high-risk features; do not delay antibiotics
Notifiable disease - public health, contacts, chemoprophylaxis
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone benefit is greatest if given before or with the first antibiotic dose; once antibiotics have been running for hours, the survival and hearing-loss benefit of dexamethasone is no longer demonstrable and it is not started late.

options.rationale: Antibiotic delay in bacterial meningitis raises mortality; empirical therapy starts immediately after blood cultures and before imaging if any delay is anticipated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Dexamethasone 10 mg IV is given immediately before or with the first dose of antibiotic in adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis (most benefit demonstrated in pneumococcal disease); deferring loses the chance for adjunctive benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin is added to ceftriaxone in areas of higher penicillin/ceftriaxone-resistant pneumococcus prevalence, not as monotherapy; the combination ensures Gram-negative and resistant pneumococcal cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Adult community-acquired bacterial meningitis empirical therapy in Australia is IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly; benzylpenicillin 2.4 g 4-hourly is added when listeria is a consideration (age over 50, immunocompromise, pregnancy). Dexamethasone 10 mg IV 6-hourly is given immediately before or with the first antibiotic dose to reduce mortality and hearing loss, particularly for pneumococcal disease. Public health notification is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; CDNA Meningococcal Disease)
Outpatient management is unsafe in suspected bacterial meningitis; inpatient empirical therapy is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Intravenous alteplase is offered within 4.5 hours of stroke onset (and selected patients up to 9 hours by perfusion imaging) with strict eligibility. BP must be under 185/110 mmHg before treatment and under 180/105 mmHg in the 24 hours after. AU first-line antihypertensive for pre-thrombolysis BP control is IV labetalol 10-20 mg over 1-2 minutes (with repeated doses or infusion) or IV glyceryl trinitrate. Direct oral anticoagulant within 48 hours is a relative contraindication. Endovascular thrombectomy is offered for confirmed large vessel occlusion (anterior circulation up to 24 hours by perfusion imaging) and reduces disability when added to alteplase. Tenecteplase is increasingly used in Australia and may be preferred where available.
key_points: BP under 185/110 mmHg before alteplase; under 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after
Labetalol IV 10-20 mg over 1-2 min is AU first-line
DOAC within 48 hours: anti-Xa or thrombin level guides decision
Large vessel occlusion: thrombectomy referral alongside alteplase
explanation.pearls: Tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg as a single bolus is non-inferior to standard alteplase 0.9 mg/kg infusion in selected stroke patients in the AU pathway and is increasingly the preferred fibrinolytic where available.

options.rationale: Blood pressure above 185/110 mmHg is a contraindication to IV alteplase; antihypertensive control to under that threshold is required first. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

This option is close to correct but the AU thresholds differ: BP must be under 185/110 mmHg before alteplase and is then maintained under 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours. Aiming at 180/105 mmHg as a single pre-thrombolysis target risks borderline non-compliance with the AU criterion. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

Direct oral anticoagulant within 48 hours is a relative contraindication, but a normal anti-Xa level (or a level below the assay-specific safe-threshold) can permit thrombolysis under stroke neurology guidance, particularly when balanced against major large-vessel occlusion benefit. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

AU stroke pathway: blood pressure must be under 185/110 mmHg before IV alteplase and maintained under 180/105 mmHg for 24 hours after. IV labetalol 10-20 mg over 1-2 minutes (repeated as needed) or IV glyceryl trinitrate is the AU choice. With a confirmed large vessel occlusion (left M1 MCA) and a NIHSS over 6, endovascular thrombectomy referral is indicated alongside alteplase within the time window. The low anti-Xa level removes the apixaban barrier in this case. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines; AHA Stroke Guideline)

Full-dose heparin acutely after stroke increases haemorrhagic transformation; secondary prevention with oral anticoagulation is deferred typically 4-14 days depending on stroke size. (Source: Stroke Foundation Living Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Phaeochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumour of the adrenal medulla (or chromaffin tissue elsewhere - paraganglioma). Hallmark triad: episodic headache, palpitations, sweating. Diagnosis is by plasma metanephrines (most sensitive) or 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines, with localisation by CT or MRI. Hereditary syndromes (MEN2A and 2B, von Hippel-Lindau, NF1, SDHx mutations) drive 30-40% of cases and routine genetic testing is offered. Preoperative blockade prevents intraoperative hypertensive crisis: alpha-blocker first (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) titrated to mild postural hypotension and nasal congestion with salt and fluid liberalisation, then beta-blocker added only after alpha-blockade for reflex tachycardia, then surgery 10-14 days later. Acute hypertensive crisis intraoperatively is treated with IV phentolamine, sodium nitroprusside, or magnesium sulfate.
key_points: Alpha first, beta second: never beta-blocker alone
Salt and fluid liberalisation to expand contracted volume
Surgery 10-14 days after adequate blockade
Hereditary testing for all confirmed phaeochromocytoma
explanation.pearls: Doxazosin 2 mg orally daily, titrated up to 16 mg, is an alternative to phenoxybenzamine, with a shorter half-life that allows easier postoperative blood pressure management at the cost of less intraoperative haemodynamic stability.

options.rationale: Beta-blocker monotherapy in phaeochromocytoma is dangerous because unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation provokes severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis; alpha-blockade is initiated first. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline; AMH)

Calcium channel blocker monotherapy is insufficient; alpha-blockade is mandatory preoperatively to control hypertensive crises and prepare for intraoperative catecholamine surge. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

This sequence is correct in principle - alpha first, then beta if reflex tachycardia emerges - but the dose initiation, salt/fluid liberalisation, and orthostatic monitoring framework are best captured by the more complete option that titrates phenoxybenzamine to a mild postural drop with salt and fluid liberalisation before the beta blocker. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

Phaeochromocytoma preoperative blockade in Australia uses an alpha blocker first (phenoxybenzamine 10 mg BD titrated up by 10-20 mg every few days until BP targets are met with mild postural drop and nasal stuffiness). Salt and fluid liberalisation expands the contracted intravascular volume. A beta blocker (atenolol or metoprolol) is added 2-3 days before surgery only after alpha-blockade is established, to address reflex tachycardia. Calcium channel blocker is an adjunct. Surgery is typically deferred 10-14 days for blockade. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline; AMH)

Magnesium sulfate is an intraoperative adjunct for catecholamine surge but is not the preoperative blockade strategy; alpha-blockade is the AU standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Phaeochromocytoma Guideline)

explanation.summary: Empirical antibiotic regimens for endocarditis depend on valve type and time since implantation. Native valve endocarditis: benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin (or vancomycin plus gentamicin if penicillin-allergic or MRSA suspected). Early prosthetic valve endocarditis (within 12 months of implantation): vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin (rifampicin added after 3-5 days of vancomycin). Late prosthetic valve endocarditis (after 12 months): similar to native valve. Diagnosis uses the modified Duke criteria. Surgical indications include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation (over 10 mm) with embolic events, perivalvular abscess, and fungal endocarditis.
key_points: Native valve: benzylpenicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin
Early prosthetic (under 12 months): vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin
Add rifampicin after 3-5 days of vancomycin
Surgical indications: heart failure, abscess, large vegetation
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin is added late (not at the start) to prosthetic valve endocarditis regimens because monotherapy or front-loaded rifampicin can select rifampicin-resistant staphylococci before the bactericidal partner reduces the bacterial load.

options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA) or coagulase-negative staphylococci that dominate early prosthetic valve endocarditis; empirical regimen needs to be broader. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Flucloxacillin monotherapy lacks MRSA, coagulase-negative staphylococcal, and enterococcal cover required for empirical prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Prosthetic valve endocarditis within 12 months of implantation is treated empirically with vancomycin (for MRSA and coagulase-negative staphylococci), gentamicin (synergistic against staphylococci and streptococci), and rifampicin (penetrates biofilm on prosthetic material). Rifampicin is started AFTER 3-5 days of vancomycin to reduce the chance of selecting rifampicin resistance. The regimen is rationalised when blood cultures speciate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ESC Endocarditis Guideline)

Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin covers viridans group streptococci endocarditis but misses staphylococci and Enterococcus faecium; not appropriate for prosthetic valve empirical cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Piperacillin-tazobactam covers many gram-positives and gram-negatives but is not the AU first-line for prosthetic valve endocarditis and does not address biofilm; vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin is the regimen. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Aortic dissection is classified by the Stanford system: type A involves the ascending aorta (surgical) and type B is distal to the left subclavian artery (medical first, surgical for complications). Uncomplicated type B is treated with prompt impulse and pressure control: intravenous labetalol or esmolol to heart rate under 60 bpm first, then vasodilator added if systolic still above 120 mmHg. Target systolic is 100-120 mmHg. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, aneurysmal dilatation) is referred for endovascular repair (TEVAR), which has displaced open surgery for most complicated cases. Long-term management includes lifelong antihypertensive therapy with a beta-blocker base and serial imaging.
key_points: Type A: ascending, surgical emergency
Type B: distal to left subclavian, medical first
HR <60 bpm before vasodilator; SBP 100-120 mmHg
Complicated type B: endovascular TEVAR
explanation.pearls: Beta-blocker before vasodilator: starting with a pure vasodilator (e.g. nitroprusside, hydralazine) causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic wall stress that can extend the dissection.

options.rationale: Vasodilator monotherapy causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic shear stress; beta-blockade must precede or accompany vasodilator therapy. (Source: ANZSCTS-CSANZ TAD position statement)

Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection is managed medically; emergent surgery is reserved for complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, aneurysmal dilatation, refractory pain or hypertension). (Source: ANZSCTS-CSANZ TAD position statement)

Aortic dissection requires admission to a monitored setting with aggressive intravenous antihypertensive therapy and serial imaging; outpatient management is unsafe. (Source: ANZSCTS-CSANZ TAD position statement)
AU targets are heart rate under 60 bpm and systolic 100-120 mmHg; HR under 80 and SBP 130-140 mmHg are too permissive and risk dissection extension. (Source: ANZSCTS-CSANZ TAD position statement)

Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection is managed medically with prompt control of impulse (heart rate) and pressure. Intravenous labetalol or esmolol is titrated to a heart rate under 60 bpm first (reducing dP/dt and aortic shear stress); a vasodilator is added if systolic remains above 120 mmHg. The target systolic is 100-120 mmHg. Admission to a high-acuity setting with arterial line and repeat imaging at 24-48 hours is required. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, aneurysm progression) is referred for endovascular repair (TEVAR). (Source: ANZSCTS-CSANZ TAD position statement; eviQ guideline)

explanation.summary: Primary spontaneous pneumothorax occurs without underlying lung disease, typically in tall thin young males. Secondary spontaneous pneumothorax has underlying lung disease (COPD, cystic fibrosis, asthma, ILD). Size is measured as the gap at the hilum on plain chest X-ray (large = 2 cm or more) or CT. Small primary pneumothorax (under 2 cm) without breathlessness is managed conservatively with oxygen and review. Large primary pneumothorax or any symptomatic patient receives intervention: needle aspiration is an acceptable first step but intercostal catheter is more reliable in the breathless patient. Recurrence prevention (VATS pleurodesis) is offered after a second event, persistent air leak over 5-7 days, or in high-risk occupations.
key_points: Primary: no underlying lung disease; tall thin young males
Large = 2 cm or more gap at hilum
Small primary without breathlessness: oxygen and review
Large or symptomatic: aspiration or intercostal catheter; ICC for the breathless patient
explanation.pearls: Patients with primary pneumothorax should not fly for 7 days after radiological resolution and should never SCUBA dive again because of the high risk of recurrence at depth.

options.rationale: Oxygen alone is reserved for small primary pneumothorax (under 2 cm gap) without significant breathlessness; 3.5 cm with breathlessness is large and requires drainage. (Source: TSANZ Pneumothorax position statement; BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)

AU and BTS guidance treat large primary spontaneous pneumothorax (defined as gap 2 cm or more at the hilum) with active intervention. Needle aspiration is an alternative first step but recurrence and persistent leak rates favour intercostal catheter insertion for the breathless patient. An 8-14 French catheter is acceptable; large bore (28 French) is reserved for haemopneumothorax or air leak management. Observation in a monitored setting with serial chest X-rays continues until air leak resolves and the lung expands fully. (Source: TSANZ Pneumothorax position statement; BTS Pleural Disease Guideline)

Large bore is reserved for haemopneumothorax or persistent air leak; an 8-14 French catheter has equivalent efficacy with less pain and complication. Suction is added only if the lung fails to re-expand on underwater seal alone. (Source: TSANZ Pneumothorax position statement)

VATS pleurodesis is the recurrence prevention strategy after a second pneumothorax, persistent air leak over 5-7 days, or for high-risk occupations (diver, pilot); first-line management of the first episode is intercostal catheter drainage. (Source: TSANZ Pneumothorax position statement)

Needle aspiration is one acceptable first step for primary pneumothorax in selected patients, but in a breathless patient with a 3.5 cm gap and ongoing symptoms, intercostal catheter is the AU first-line. (Source: TSANZ Pneumothorax position statement)

explanation.summary: Early rheumatoid arthritis (symptoms under 12 months) requires prompt diagnosis and DMARD start to prevent joint damage. The 2010 ACR/EULAR classification criteria use joint involvement, serology (rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP), acute-phase reactants, and symptom duration. Poor prognostic markers include high disease activity, anti-CCP positivity, early erosions, and high inflammatory markers. AU first-line conventional synthetic DMARD is methotrexate 10-15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly 24-48 hours after methotrexate. Bridge prednisolone is used until DMARD effect.
