Biologic step-up (PBS eligibility) requires failure of two conventional DMARDs (one being methotrexate) at adequate doses for 3 months. Treat-to-target aims for DAS28 under 3.2 within 6 months.
key_points: Symptoms under 12 months: start DMARD promptly
Methotrexate 10-15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg weekly
Bridge prednisolone until DMARD effect
Treat-to-target: DAS28 under 3.2 in 6 months
explanation.pearls: An Australian review of coronial records found 7 deaths linked to methotrexate dosing errors, all of them preventable.

sources.label: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis
MJA: A decade of Australian methotrexate dosing errors

options.rationale: NSAID monotherapy delays disease-modifying therapy and risks irreversible joint damage; methotrexate is usually first-line therapy for rheumatoid arthritis. An NSAID is a symptom-relief adjunct alongside a DMARD, not a substitute for one. (Source: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis; ARA Recommendations on Early RA)
source_refs: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis

options.rationale: ANZMUSC positions glucocorticoids as a short bridge while a DMARD takes effect, not as a standalone strategy, and 50 mg daily is far above the lowest effective dose. A short course at the lowest effective dose, started alongside methotrexate, is the supported use. (Source: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis)
source_refs: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis

options.rationale: Methotrexate for rheumatoid arthritis is taken once a week (7.5 to 25 mg weekly), and accidental daily dosing causes life-threatening toxicity, with serious harm reported after as little as 3 consecutive days. The referral, folic acid, bridging prednisolone and 12-week review in this plan are all appropriate; only the daily schedule is wrong. (Source: MJA: A decade of Australian methotrexate dosing errors)
source_refs: MJA: A decade of Australian methotrexate dosing errors

options.rationale: Early rheumatoid arthritis (symptoms under 12 months, persistent synovitis, seropositive, raised inflammatory markers, no erosions yet) is treated with prompt conventional synthetic DMARD therapy to prevent joint damage. Methotrexate is usually first line, given weekly with folic acid, and ANZMUSC conditionally recommends a short course of glucocorticoid at the lowest effective dose until the DMARD takes effect, with a shared plan to taper it; review at 12 weeks guides treat-to-target escalation. ANZMUSC also conditionally recommends considering methotrexate in combination (usually triple therapy) as initial therapy. (Source: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis; ARA Recommendations on Early RA)
source_refs: ANZMUSC Australian Living Guideline for Inflammatory Arthritis

options.rationale: Hydroxychloroquine is reasonable in mild disease without poor prognostic features; this patient has high DAS28, anti-CCP positive, and active synovitis on Doppler, all favouring methotrexate first-line. (Source: ARA Recommendations on Early RA)

explanation.summary: Stevens-Johnson syndrome (under 10% BSA detachment) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (over 30% BSA detachment) are severe cutaneous drug reactions with mortality 5-50% depending on extent. The SCORTEN score (age over 40, malignancy, heart rate over 120, BSA over 10%, urea over 10 mmol/L, glucose over 14 mmol/L, bicarbonate under 20 mmol/L) predicts mortality. Common culprits are anticonvulsants (lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin), allopurinol, sulfonamides, beta-lactams, NSAIDs, and nevirapine. Immediate withdrawal of the offending drug is the single most effective intervention. Supportive care in a burns or specialist unit includes fluid resuscitation, wound care, ophthalmology (corneal scarring prevention), nutrition, and analgesia. Adjunctive therapies (IVIG, ciclosporin, etanercept) are considered case-by-case with limited evidence.
key_points: SJS under 10% BSA; TEN over 30% BSA; overlap 10-30%
Suspect drug withdrawal is the single most effective step
Burns or specialist supportive care
Ophthalmology essential to prevent corneal scarring
explanation.pearls: Lamotrigine SJS/TEN risk is highest in the first 8 weeks; rapid dose escalation (faster than the AMH-approved 2-weekly schedule) substantially increases risk, particularly in patients on concurrent valproate.

options.rationale: Continuing the offending agent worsens SJS/TEN mortality; immediate cessation of the suspect drug is the single most effective intervention. Oral steroids alone do not replace withdrawal. (Source: ANZCA Drug Reaction Statement)

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (under 10% BSA detachment) and toxic epidermal necrolysis (over 30%) are drug reactions; SJS/TEN overlap is 10-30%. Immediate withdrawal of the offending drug (most often anticonvulsants - lamotrigine, carbamazepine, phenytoin; allopurinol; sulfonamides; nevirapine) is the most important intervention and reduces mortality. Supportive care is provided in a burns unit or specialist setting with intravenous fluid replacement, wound care, ophthalmology, urology, and nutrition input. Adjunctive therapies (IVIG, ciclosporin, etanercept) are considered case-by-case; evidence is limited. (Source: ANZCA Drug Reaction Statement; ANZBA Burns Statement)

Sertraline has been on for 6 months and is unlikely to be the cause; lamotrigine started 3 weeks ago is the classic culprit and has the established association with SJS/TEN. (Source: ANZCA Drug Reaction Statement)
Lamotrigine continuation is the wrong direction; sertraline is unlikely to be the cause; IVIG is not principal therapy and the evidence is mixed. (Source: ANZCA Drug Reaction Statement)
Discharge with antibiotics misses the need for specialist supportive care and risks rapid progression; prophylactic antibiotics are not routine in SJS/TEN. (Source: ANZCA Drug Reaction Statement)

explanation.summary: Potassium based salt substitutes are a common and easily missed cause of hyperkalaemia in patients on renin-angiotensin blockade with chronic kidney disease. Removing the exposure is preferable to stopping a prognostically valuable drug.
key_points: Ask specifically about salt substitutes, potassium supplements and complementary medicines.
Other potassium rich exposures include coconut water, dried fruit and vegetable juices.
Dose reduction of the culprit drug is preferred to cessation where the load can be removed instead.
explanation.context: The kidney excretes about 90% of a dietary potassium load, and it does so through aldosterone-driven secretion in the principal cells of the collecting duct. Chronic kidney disease reduces the number of functioning nephrons available to do that, and angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, mineralocorticoid antagonists, trimethoprim and calcineurin inhibitors each interrupt the same final pathway. A patient with any one of those usually copes; stack a large potassium load on top and the reserve is gone. This is why a medication and dietary history, taken specifically, is more useful in a stable hyperkalaemic outpatient than any further blood test.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Salt substitutes replace sodium chloride with potassium chloride and deliver a large daily potassium load. With renin-angiotensin blockade and reduced excretory reserve, removing the load corrects the problem without sacrificing a drug that improves his survival. (Source: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Reducing the perindopril dose is appropriate where no reversible dietary or drug load can be found and the potassium stays high, since dose reduction is preferred to outright cessation in heart failure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
A potassium binder is added when potassium remains raised after reversible contributors are removed and the treatment that is raising it must continue. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Emergency referral is needed for potassium above about 6.5 mmol/L, or any level with electrocardiogram change, symptoms or rapidly worsening renal function. (Source: ANZCOR adult advanced life support)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Routine three-monthly review suits a stable potassium in the upper reference range on established therapy with no new exposure. A rise from 4.6 to 6.0 mmol/L needs action now. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

explanation.summary: Myasthenic crisis is respiratory or bulbar failure requiring intubation or non-invasive ventilation, typically precipitated by infection, surgery, medication change, or pregnancy. Cholinergic crisis is the rare overdose state of cholinesterase inhibitors with weakness PLUS muscarinic excess (lacrimation, miosis, salivation, sweating, bradycardia, diarrhoea). The two can be indistinguishable in late phases; the unifying first step is to PAUSE pyridostigmine, secure the airway with NIV or intubation (triggers: vital capacity under 1 L, single-breath count under 10, rising pCO2), and start IVIG (2 g/kg over 2-5 days) or plasma exchange (5 sessions every other day). Edrophonium (Tensilon) testing has been superseded. Precipitants are addressed in parallel (drug review: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, beta-blockers, magnesium sulfate, neuromuscular blockers all worsen MG). Long-term immunomodulation continues (prednisolone, azathioprine, mycophenolate, rituximab, eculizumab).
key_points: Pause pyridostigmine in either crisis
NIV/intubate: vital capacity under 1 L OR single-breath count under 10
Disease-modifying: IVIG 2 g/kg or PLEX 5 sessions
Edrophonium test superseded
explanation.pearls: Single-breath count is a quick bedside marker of vital capacity: a patient who can count to 50 in one breath has roughly 4 L vital capacity; under 20 is severe respiratory weakness needing airway plan and high-acuity care.

options.rationale: Continuing or escalating pyridostigmine in cholinergic crisis worsens secretions and weakness; in any crisis the first step is airway protection planning, then disease-modifying therapy with IVIG or plasma exchange. (Source: ANZAN MG guidelines)

This patient may be in cholinergic crisis (excess cholinergic features: lacrimation, miosis, secretions, bradycardia after self-titration) or in myasthenic crisis with overlap. AU and ANZAN guidance for severe crisis hold pyridostigmine temporarily, secure the airway (NIV trial then intubation if vital capacity under 1 L, single-breath count under 10, or rising pCO2), and start disease-modifying therapy with IVIG (2 g/kg over 2-5 days) or plasma exchange (5 sessions every other day). Tensilon (edrophonium) testing has been superseded; the differentiation is clinical and pyridostigmine is paused in both crises. (Source: ANZAN MG guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Edrophonium testing has been superseded by bedside clinical features and is no longer routinely performed because of risk of precipitating arrhythmia or worsening cholinergic crisis. (Source: ANZAN MG guidelines)
Atropine treats cholinergic excess but does not treat the myasthenic component; pyridostigmine hold and airway management are the unifying first steps in either crisis. (Source: ANZAN MG guidelines)

Acute high-dose oral steroids in MG can transiently worsen weakness in the first week and pyridostigmine should be paused in suspected cholinergic crisis; IVIG or plasma exchange is the disease-modifying treatment for crisis. (Source: ANZAN MG guidelines)

explanation.summary: Mixed acid-base disorders are identified by checking whether respiratory compensation matches the expected formula. Winter's formula for metabolic acidosis: expected pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 (±2). If measured pCO2 is higher than expected, a concurrent respiratory acidosis exists; if lower, a concurrent respiratory alkalosis exists. Acute respiratory acidosis is expected to raise HCO3 by 1 mmol/L per 10 mmHg rise in pCO2; chronic raises by 3-4 per 10 mmHg. The delta-delta ratio (delta anion gap over delta HCO3) detects additional disorders: 1-2 = pure high-AG acidosis; under 1 = additional non-AG acidosis; over 2 = additional metabolic alkalosis. Post-arrest patients commonly have mixed lactic acidosis (hypoperfusion) plus respiratory acidosis (inadequate ventilation, exhausted respiratory drive). The bedside response is to address ventilation AND restore perfusion in parallel.
key_points: Winter's: expected pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 (range ±2)
Higher measured pCO2 = additional respiratory acidosis
Lower measured pCO2 = additional respiratory alkalosis
Post-arrest: commonly mixed lactic + respiratory acidosis
explanation.pearls: The delta-delta ratio is calculated as (anion gap minus 12) divided by (24 minus bicarbonate). A ratio between 1 and 2 is pure high-anion-gap acidosis; outside that range there is a coexisting disorder.

options.rationale: Winter's formula predicts expected pCO2 = 1.5 x HCO3 + 8 (with range ±2). Expected pCO2 = 1.5(18) + 8 = 35 mmHg (range 33-37). Measured pCO2 60 mmHg is much higher than expected; this means a concurrent respiratory acidosis, not appropriate compensation. (Source: Stewart Acid-Base; Boron and Boulpaep)
Bicarbonate is REDUCED at 18 mmol/L; chronic respiratory acidosis would raise bicarbonate. The picture is mixed metabolic plus respiratory acidosis. (Source: Stewart Acid-Base)
pH is 7.10 (acidaemia, not alkalaemia); the picture is acidosis. (Source: Stewart Acid-Base)

pH 7.10 is acidaemia. Metabolic component: HCO3 18 mmol/L (reduced), anion gap 24 mmol/L (raised) - high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. The driver is lactate (8.2 mmol/L) from post-arrest tissue hypoperfusion. Respiratory component: Winter's formula expected pCO2 for HCO3 18 = 1.5(18) + 8 = 35 mmHg; measured pCO2 60 mmHg is far higher, indicating inadequate compensation (respiratory acidosis). This is a mixed high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis PLUS respiratory acidosis. The bedside response is to increase minute ventilation (raise rate or tidal volume) to drive pCO2 toward 35 mmHg while addressing the lactic acidosis with perfusion restoration. (Source: Stewart Acid-Base; Boron and Boulpaep)

There is no evidence of a second metabolic alkalosis component (delta-delta is within range for pure high-AG acidosis) and pCO2 is high not low; triple disorder is not the best fit. (Source: Stewart Acid-Base)

explanation.summary: Latent TB infection is diagnosed by a positive interferon-gamma release assay (QuantiFERON-TB Gold Plus) or tuberculin skin test in someone with no clinical or radiological evidence of active disease. The NTAC currently endorses several first-line regimens: 4 months daily rifampicin, 3 months weekly isoniazid plus rifapentine (3HP, supply limited in Australia), or 9 months isoniazid plus pyridoxine. Four-month rifampicin has better completion and lower hepatotoxicity than 9 months isoniazid. Treatment is prioritised in recent migrants, contacts, immunocompromised hosts and those starting biologic therapy. Baseline ALT, hepatitis serology and HIV are checked. Untreated latent TB carries 5-10% lifetime reactivation risk (much higher with HIV, biologics or transplant).
key_points: First-line LTBI: rifampicin 4 months daily, or isoniazid 9 months, or 3HP weekly
Active TB excluded by symptom screen + chest radiograph
Pyridoxine 25 mg added to isoniazid to prevent peripheral neuropathy
Lifetime reactivation risk 5-10%; higher with HIV or biologics
explanation.pearls: Four-month daily rifampicin is the NTAC first-line LTBI regimen because it has equivalent efficacy to nine-month isoniazid with about half the hepatotoxicity and significantly better completion; check for major drug interactions (warfarin, OCP, opioids) given rifampicin's CYP3A4 induction.

options.rationale: Isoniazid monotherapy for 6 to 9 months is effective for latent TB but is no longer first-line in Australia given longer duration and higher hepatotoxicity than shorter rifamycin-containing regimens. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee NTAC)

4-month daily rifampicin is endorsed by the National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee as a first-line latent TB infection regimen with non-inferior efficacy to 9 months isoniazid plus better completion rates and lower hepatotoxicity. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee NTAC; eTG Antibiotic)

Four-drug RIPE therapy is for active TB; he is asymptomatic with a clear chest radiograph and treating him as active overtreats and exposes to greater toxicity. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee NTAC)

A positive QuantiFERON in a recent immigrant from a high-prevalence country with clear chest radiograph already confirms latent TB infection; treatment is offered now to reduce reactivation risk. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee NTAC)

Untreated latent TB carries a 5 to 10% lifetime reactivation risk; treatment is the standard offer for recent migrants from high-prevalence regions. (Source: National Tuberculosis Advisory Committee NTAC)

explanation.summary: Suspected acute bacterial meningitis is managed by immediate empiric IV antibiotic plus adjunctive dexamethasone, then prompt CT (if features of raised intracranial pressure or focal deficit), then lumbar puncture for diagnosis. Adult empiric therapy in Australia is IV dexamethasone 10 mg every 6 hours plus IV ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours, with the addition of IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours (or amoxicillin) when Listeria risk is present (age >50 years, immunocompromised, pregnancy). Antibiotic delay independently predicts mortality. Dexamethasone reduces mortality in pneumococcal meningitis but must be given with or before the first antibiotic dose. Confirmed N. meningitidis requires single-dose chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally) for close contacts.
key_points: Adult empiric: dexamethasone 10 mg IV + ceftriaxone 2 g IV
Add benzylpenicillin/amoxicillin if Listeria risk (>50, immunocompromise, pregnancy)
Dexamethasone must be given with or before first antibiotic dose
Antibiotics before CT/LP if any delay risk
explanation.pearls: Dexamethasone benefits meningitis only when given with or before the first dose of antibiotic; once antibiotics are running, late steroid addition does not change outcome - the timing window is the rate limiter.

options.rationale: Dexamethasone alone does not treat infection; it is adjunctive to and must accompany the first antibiotic dose. Withholding antibiotics is the dangerous part. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Antibiotic delay in bacterial meningitis increases mortality by approximately 10% per hour; empiric antibiotics are given immediately and CT/LP follow without delay. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Empiric antibiotic plus adjunctive corticosteroid must be given immediately when bacterial meningitis is suspected; dexamethasone reduces mortality and neurological sequelae but only when given with or before the first antibiotic dose. Adding benzylpenicillin maintains Listeria cover in those over 50 or with risk factors, but in young adults the eTG combination is dexamethasone plus ceftriaxone; if Listeria risk exists, add benzylpenicillin (or amoxicillin). (Source: eTG Antibiotic; ANZICS Sepsis)

Aciclovir is appropriate empirical cover for HSV encephalitis but is not a substitute for antibacterial cover when bacterial meningitis is the leading diagnosis; both can be given. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Ciprofloxacin is a post-exposure prophylaxis option for contacts of meningococcal disease; it does not treat the index patient who needs full IV antibiotic therapy. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection. Septic shock is the subset with circulatory and cellular metabolic dysfunction requiring vasopressors and lactate above 2 mmol/L. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign hour-1 bundle is: measure lactate (repeat if initial >2), take blood cultures before antibiotics, administer broad spectrum antibiotics within an hour, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid (balanced solution preferred over saline) for hypotension or lactate above 4, and start vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) if MAP remains under 65 after fluid resuscitation. Source control follows. Norepinephrine is initiated through a central line ideally but may be started peripherally if needed.
key_points: Hour-1 bundle: lactate, cultures, antibiotics, 30 mL/kg crystalloid, vasopressors if MAP <65
Noradrenaline is first-line vasopressor; adrenaline second
Empirical antibiotics within 1 hour; source control follows
Mortality rises about 7% per hour of antibiotic delay in septic shock
explanation.pearls: Each hour of delay in antibiotic administration in septic shock raises mortality by approximately 7%; the hour-1 bundle is the most evidence-supported intervention package in adult sepsis care.

options.rationale: This is septic shock (sepsis plus lactate >2 mmol/L despite resuscitation OR hypotension requiring vasopressors). The Surviving Sepsis hour-1 bundle and ANZICS recommendation are: measure lactate, take cultures, give broad spectrum antibiotics, give 30 mL/kg crystalloid, start vasopressors if MAP <65 despite fluids; antibiotics for urosepsis with gram-negative growth follow eTG sepsis empirical pathway. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis; eTG Antibiotic; Surviving Sepsis Campaign)

Tazocin is an acceptable empirical agent for complicated urosepsis but should follow cultures and accompany fluid resuscitation; imaging must not delay the hour-1 bundle. (Source: eTG Antibiotic; ANZICS Sepsis)
A 250 mL bolus undertreats septic shock; the hour-1 bundle calls for 30 mL/kg of balanced crystalloid as the initial resuscitation in adults. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

Vasopressors are escalated after fluid resuscitation has failed to restore MAP; starting vasopressors first does not address the relative hypovolaemia and is not the bundle sequence. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)
Time to antibiotics is the strongest modifiable predictor of mortality in septic shock; empiric therapy starts within the first hour. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic syndrome encompasses dissection (type A: ascending; type B: descending), intramural haematoma and penetrating aortic ulcer. Type A is a surgical emergency. Uncomplicated type B is managed medically with anti-impulse therapy targeting HR <60/min and SBP 100-120 mmHg, achieved with IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) plus vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or GTN) if needed after HR is controlled. TEVAR is indicated for complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, rapid expansion, persistent hypertension on maximum medical therapy, or aortic diameter >5.5 cm). Pain control with opioids, calm environment, transfer to monitored bed and arterial line placement complete the acute management.
key_points: Type B uncomplicated: medical anti-impulse therapy
Targets: HR <60/min, SBP 100-120 mmHg
Labetalol IV combines alpha and beta blockade (Australian first-line)
TEVAR for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, expansion
explanation.pearls: Beta-blockade must precede any vasodilator in aortic dissection - reflex tachycardia from unopposed vasodilatation raises wall shear (dP/dt) and can extend the dissection.

options.rationale: Furosemide does not provide acute BP or rate control; it has no role in acute aortic syndrome management. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

Vasodilator without prior beta-blockade triggers reflex tachycardia which increases shear stress on the dissection flap; beta-blockade must precede or accompany vasodilatation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)
Oral antihypertensives do not titrate fast enough for acute dissection; IV infusion that can be adjusted minute-to-minute is required. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

Uncomplicated type B dissection management is medical anti-impulse therapy: lower shear stress (dP/dt) by first achieving HR <60/min with beta-blockade, then add vasodilator if SBP remains >120; IV labetalol's combined alpha and beta blockade achieves both in one agent and is the Australian first-line. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes; eTG Cardiovascular)

Uncomplicated type B dissection is managed medically with optimal anti-impulse therapy and surveillance; TEVAR is reserved for malperfusion, rupture, refractory pain, or rapid aortic expansion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Aortic Syndromes)

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with a mortality of 20-40%. The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine and glucose; scores >=6 suggest probable necrotising fasciitis, >=8 makes it highly likely. The score is supportive only - clinical features (pain out of proportion, systemic toxicity, rapid progression, skin signs evolving over hours, gas, crepitus, necrosis) drive decisions and should not be overridden by a low score. Empirical antibiotics are broad: piperacillin-tazobactam (or meropenem) plus clindamycin (anti-toxin effect at the ribosome reducing streptococcal exotoxin production) plus vancomycin for MRSA cover. IVIG is considered for streptococcal toxic shock. Surgical debridement is mandatory, with relooks every 24 hours until source-controlled.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + systemic toxicity = NSTI until proven otherwise
LRINEC >=6 probable, >=8 highly likely (supportive only)
Empirical: piperacillin-tazobactam + clindamycin + vancomycin
Surgical debridement must not be delayed for imaging
explanation.pearls: Hyponatraemia (sodium <135) plus tachycardia plus pain out of proportion in a limb cellulitis is the classic triad that should trigger surgical referral for necrotising fasciitis exclusion regardless of LRINEC score.

options.rationale: MRI can show fascial enhancement and gas but is not specific and must not delay urgent surgical exploration when the clinical picture is concerning. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

Flucloxacillin alone is appropriate for uncomplicated cellulitis but inadequate for necrotising soft tissue infection which is polymicrobial or group A streptococcal; the syndrome requires both surgery and broad spectrum cover. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

Conservative observation is appropriate for stable uncomplicated cellulitis; with systemic toxicity, hyponatraemia and disproportionate pain, delay is dangerous. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)

Pain out of proportion to visible signs, systemic toxicity, hyponatraemia and high LRINEC score (>=6 here) are the bedside red flags for necrotising fasciitis; the LRINEC score is supportive but should not delay surgical exploration which is both diagnostic and therapeutic. (Source: ANZSA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection; eTG Antibiotic; LRINEC score)
Discharge home with oral antibiotics in a systemically unwell diabetic with red flags is unsafe; admission is mandatory. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Durable virological suppression prevents sexual transmission of HIV. The Australian position, consistent with the international consensus, is that a person on antiretroviral therapy with an undetectable viral load sustained for at least six months and confirmed on regular testing does not pass HIV on to sexual partners. The practical requirements are adherence, six monthly viral load monitoring and prompt review if a result becomes detectable. Conception by timed condomless intercourse is appropriate, with the usual preconception care for both partners. In context, this changes what serodiscordant couples are told: pre-exposure prophylaxis, sperm washing and mandatory condom use belong to the era before reliable suppression, and offering them now implies a risk that no longer exists.
key_points: Undetectable sustained for six months means HIV is not transmitted sexually.
Adherence and six monthly viral load monitoring underpin the advice.
Condoms still have a role for other infections and contraception.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis is for partners of people who are not reliably suppressed.
explanation.pearls: The advice rests on a sustained record of undetectable results, not on a single result; a newly suppressed patient still needs the six month track record before the counselling changes.

options.rationale: Sustained viral suppression for at least six months with ongoing adherence and monitoring means there is effectively no risk of sexual transmission, so they can conceive by timed intercourse without antiretroviral prophylaxis. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Condoms remain the advice while suppression is not yet established, when doses are being missed, or for preventing other sexually transmissible infections and unplanned pregnancy, none of which apply to a couple seeking conception. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Pre-exposure prophylaxis is for a partner whose viral load is not reliably suppressed, who has other partners, or where adherence is uncertain, and it adds nothing once suppression is durable. (Source: ASHM PrEP Guidelines)
Sperm washing was standard before effective therapy and is now reserved for couples with a detectable viral load or a separate fertility problem. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines)

Intensifying a regimen is considered for virological failure with documented resistance, not for a suppressed patient, and extra agents add toxicity without benefit. (Source: ASHM HIV Management Guidelines; AMH)

explanation.summary: Treatment failure in community-acquired pneumonia at 72 hours is defined as worsening clinical status or absence of improvement and prompts re-evaluation. Causes include inadequate antimicrobial cover (atypical pathogens such as Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydophila), resistant organism, complication (empyema, abscess), wrong diagnosis (PE, vasculitis, eosinophilic pneumonia, malignancy) or host factor (immunosuppression). Legionnaires disease classically presents with hyponatraemia, transaminitis, diarrhoea, relative bradycardia and progressive multilobar consolidation; the urinary antigen is sensitive for serogroup 1 (most common). First-line therapy in Australia is azithromycin or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (moxifloxacin); doxycycline has less activity against severe Legionella. Source identification (cooling towers, spa pools, warm water systems) triggers public health notification.
key_points: CAP non-response at 72 h: rethink pathogen, complication, diagnosis, host
Legionella triad: hyponatraemia + transaminitis + diarrhoea
Urinary antigen sensitive for serogroup 1
First-line: azithromycin IV or moxifloxacin; doxycycline weaker
explanation.pearls: The classic Legionella signature in an otherwise typical-looking CAP is the combination of hyponatraemia under 130 mmol/L, ALT above 100 U/L and gastrointestinal symptoms; presence of a warm-water exposure (cooling tower, spa, hot tub) clinches the suspicion even before urinary antigen returns.

options.rationale: Bronchoscopy is useful in non resolving pneumonia but should not delay empiric escalation when clinical and biochemical clues already strongly suggest Legionella; urinary antigen and BAL can be sent in parallel. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

She has community-acquired pneumonia (presented from home) and there is no evidence of pseudomonal or MRSA risk; broad spectrum nosocomial cover does not address suspected atypical Legionella infection. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)
Corticosteroids may have benefit in severe CAP but do not substitute for adequate antimicrobial cover when an atypical pathogen is being missed by the current regimen. (Source: eTG Antibiotic)

The triad of hyponatraemia, transaminitis and gastrointestinal symptoms in a patient with progressive multifocal pneumonia and recent exposure to a warm-water source is highly suggestive of Legionella pneumophila, which requires azithromycin (or a fluoroquinolone such as moxifloxacin) for adequate coverage; doxycycline has weaker activity against severe Legionella infection and the urinary antigen test should be sent immediately to confirm. (Source: eTG Antibiotic: Community-acquired pneumonia; CDNA Legionellosis SoNG)

Oxygen requirements may indeed warrant higher level care, but escalation of respiratory support without addressing the inadequately covered pathogen perpetuates clinical failure. (Source: ANZICS Sepsis)

explanation.summary: Acute gout is treated with NSAIDs (first-line if no contraindication), low-dose colchicine, or short course corticosteroid (oral 30 mg prednisolone for 5 days, or intra-articular if mono articular). Low-dose colchicine 1 mg now followed by 500 mcg 1 hour later (maximum 1.5 mg in 24 hours) is preferred over the historical high-dose regimen, which caused unacceptable diarrhoea. Colchicine is safe at this dose in eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 but contraindicated with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin) and P-glycoprotein inhibitors (ciclosporin). Urate lowering therapy (allopurinol or febuxostat) is started 2 to 4 weeks after the flare settles with colchicine 500 mcg daily prophylaxis for 6 months to prevent flare from urate mobilisation. Target serum urate is under 0.36 mmol/L (under 0.30 mmol/L if tophaceous or recurrent).
key_points: Acute gout first-line: NSAID, low-dose colchicine, or short steroid
Colchicine 1 mg + 500 mcg in 1 hour, max 1.5 mg/24 hours
Start urate lowering 2 to 4 weeks after flare with colchicine cover
Target serum urate under 0.36 mmol/L (under 0.30 if tophaceous)
explanation.pearls: Colchicine has narrow therapeutic index and interacts with CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, diltiazem) and P-glycoprotein inhibitors; check for these in elderly patients before prescribing per AMH.

options.rationale: Probenecid is a urate lowering agent for chronic management, not acute flare treatment, and is contraindicated in the acute flare and in moderate renal impairment. (Source: AMH)
Pulse intravenous steroid is excessive; a short oral prednisolone course or intra-articular steroid is appropriate when colchicine is unsuitable. (Source: eTG: Rheumatology)
NSAIDs are first-line in many but contraindicated by his recent ibuprofen reaction and his duodenal ulcer history; colchicine or intra-articular steroid is preferred here. (Source: eTG: Rheumatology)

Low-dose colchicine 1 mg followed by 500 mcg 1 hour later is the recommended first-line in acute gout when NSAIDs are contraindicated or not tolerated, with eGFR over 30 mL/min/1.73 m2 supporting safe use. (Source: AMH; eTG: Rheumatology)
Urate lowering therapy is initiated AFTER the acute flare settles, not during it; starting urate lowering during a flare can precipitate further gout attacks. (Source: AMH; eTG: Rheumatology)

explanation.summary: Stable angina is managed with both prognostic therapy (aspirin, high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor in selected patients) and antianginal therapy (beta blocker or non dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker first-line). When monotherapy is inadequate, dual antianginal therapy with a beta blocker and a dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine or felodipine) is preferred; non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are NOT combined with beta blockers due to AV node block. Refractory symptoms may justify addition of nicorandil, ivabradine (sinus rhythm only), or ranolazine. Revascularisation is considered for symptoms refractory to optimal medical therapy or for prognostic indications (left main, three vessel disease with reduced left ventricular function). All patients receive cardiovascular risk factor optimisation.
key_points: Dual antianginal: beta blocker + DHP-CCB (amlodipine)
AVOID non-DHP-CCB (diltiazem, verapamil) with beta blocker
Third-line: nicorandil, ivabradine (SR), ranolazine
Revascularisation for refractory symptoms or prognostic indications
explanation.pearls: Ivabradine 5 mg twice daily is an alternative third-line antianginal in patients with sinus rhythm and heart rate over 70 beats per minute on maximally tolerated beta blockade; it has no effect on blood pressure unlike calcium channel blockers per NHFA guidance.

options.rationale: Nicorandil is a third-line agent reserved for patients intolerant of beta blockers or calcium channel blockers; it is not first dual therapy. (Source: eTG: Cardiovascular)
Non dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers are contraindicated with beta blockers due to AV node conduction block and risk of bradycardia or asystole. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina; AMH)

He has already been assessed as a non revascularisation candidate; medical therapy optimisation is the agreed pathway and dual antianginal therapy has not been tried yet. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina)
Ranolazine is a third-line agent on PBS authority for refractory angina; it is added after first-line dual therapy fails, not before. (Source: PBS)

Beta blocker plus dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (amlodipine) is the recommended dual antianginal therapy in stable angina with inadequate symptom control on monotherapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Stable Angina; eTG: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Primary hypothyroidism is treated with once daily oral levothyroxine taken on an empty stomach to minimise food and calcium or iron interaction. Full replacement is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day; lower starting doses (25 to 50 mcg) are used in elderly or coronary artery disease patients. TSH is the marker of replacement adequacy: target lower half of the reference range (0.4 to 2.5 mIU/L). Dose adjustments are made in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks because the half-life of levothyroxine is 7 days. Persistent fatigue with adequate TSH suggests a parallel diagnosis (depression, vitamin D deficiency, anaemia) rather than under-replacement. Pregnancy or planned pregnancy requires a 25 to 50% dose increase to maintain TSH under 2.5 mIU/L.
key_points: Full replacement approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day
TSH target lower half reference range (0.4 to 2.5 mIU/L)
Dose adjust in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks
Pregnancy: increase dose 25 to 50%, target TSH under 2.5
explanation.pearls: In pregnancy, levothyroxine dose typically needs to rise by 25 to 50% from preconception baseline; women on stable therapy should add 2 extra tablets per week as soon as pregnancy is confirmed per RANZCOG and Endocrine Society guidance, until the trimester-specific TSH is checked.

options.rationale: Full replacement for primary hypothyroidism is approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day (around 100 mcg for this patient at 65 kg); titrate in 25 mcg increments every 6 to 8 weeks until TSH is in the lower half of the reference range. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)
Combination T4 plus T3 is not first-line because trials show no consistent symptom benefit; adequate levothyroxine titration should be tried first. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)
TSH 12.5 mIU/L is above target; under-replacement should not be left for 6 months because it perpetuates symptoms and adverse effects on lipids and cardiac function. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)
A large dose increment of 50 mcg risks overshoot to subclinical hyperthyroidism; 25 mcg titration with 6 to 8 week re-check is the standard. (Source: eTG: Endocrinology)
Desiccated thyroid extract has variable hormone content batch to batch and is not recommended over levothyroxine in evidence-based practice. (Source: AMH; eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Acromegaly is caused by a growth hormone secreting pituitary adenoma in over 95% of cases, with insidious onset and average diagnostic delay of 7 to 10 years. Cardinal features include coarse facial features, prognathism, macroglossia, soft tissue and acral enlargement, hyperhidrosis, headache, sleep apnoea, hypertension, glucose intolerance, and arthropathy. Biochemical diagnosis is by raised serum IGF-1 for age and sex plus failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 mcg/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test. After biochemical confirmation, MRI pituitary defines the adenoma (microadenoma under 10 mm or macroadenoma 10 mm and over), and the rest of pituitary function is assessed. First-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery for microadenomas and most macroadenomas; medical therapy (somatostatin analogues, pegvisomant, dopamine agonists) and radiotherapy are second and third line.
key_points: Screen with IGF-1 for age and sex; random GH alone is unreliable
Confirm with OGTT-GH suppression below 1 mcg/L failure
MRI pituitary defines anatomy AFTER biochemical confirmation
First-line treatment: transsphenoidal surgery
explanation.pearls: Cardiovascular disease drives excess mortality in acromegaly (heart failure, hypertension, coronary disease); standardised mortality ratio falls from approximately 1.7 in untreated disease to 1.0 with adequate biochemical control of IGF-1 and growth hormone.

options.rationale: Pituitary hormone screening is appropriate as part of workup after diagnosis but does not confirm acromegaly itself; the diagnostic step is OGTT-GH suppression. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)

Failure of growth hormone to suppress below 1 mcg/L during a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test confirms acromegaly biochemically; IGF-1 plus failed OGTT suppression is the diagnostic gold standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly; eTG: Endocrinology)
Urinary IGF-1 is not part of the diagnostic algorithm; serum IGF-1 already screened is the standard measure of growth hormone exposure. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)
Insulin tolerance test is used to confirm growth hormone DEFICIENCY (lack of rise); it is not the test for growth hormone excess in acromegaly. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly)

MRI confirms the anatomical lesion but does not confirm hormonal hypersecretion biochemically; OGTT with serial growth hormone is the biochemical confirmation that defines active disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Acromegaly; eTG: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Multiple myeloma is suspected when CRAB features (hypercalcaemia over 2.75 mmol/L, renal impairment, anaemia, lytic bone disease) are present in an older patient with normochromic normocytic anaemia and raised ESR or rouleaux on film. Initial workup is serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) with immunofixation, serum free light chain assay, and 24-hour urine for Bence Jones protein. Approximately 97% of myelomas have a detectable paraprotein. Confirmation requires bone marrow showing clonal plasma cells over 10% plus end-organ damage (CRAB) or biomarkers of malignancy (clonal plasma cells over 60%, light chain ratio over 100, MRI focal lesions over 1). Whole body low-dose CT or PET-CT or whole body MRI staging follows. Treatment depends on transplant eligibility but typically involves bortezomib-based induction with dexamethasone plus lenalidomide.
key_points: CRAB: hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions
First test: SPEP + immunofixation + serum free light chains + urine Bence Jones
Confirm with marrow plus CRAB or biomarkers (SLiM-CRAB)
Stage with whole body low-dose CT, PET-CT, or whole body MRI
explanation.pearls: In Australia, low-dose whole body CT has largely replaced traditional skeletal survey for myeloma staging because it detects more lytic lesions at lower radiation dose; whole body MRI is the more sensitive alternative for marrow involvement when CT is equivocal per HSANZ guidance.

options.rationale: PET-CT is more useful in solitary plasmacytoma and treatment response monitoring than in initial diagnosis of suspected myeloma; serum and urine paraprotein detection are the first step. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)
Bone marrow is part of myeloma workup but follows demonstration of paraprotein; jumping to marrow without paraprotein screen is not standard. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)

In CRAB-pattern clinical picture (hypercalcaemia, renal impairment, anaemia, bone lesions), the diagnostic step is to detect monoclonal protein with SPEP plus immunofixation, serum free light chain assay and Bence Jones protein in urine; bone marrow follows. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma; MSAG Clinical Practice Guidelines)
Renal biopsy is reserved for cases where paraprotein workup is negative or the cause of kidney injury remains uncertain; in classic CRAB the paraprotein screen comes first. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma)

Imaging staging follows biochemical confirmation; serum protein electrophoresis, free light chains and Bence Jones are the initial diagnostic step for suspected myeloma. (Source: HSANZ Myeloma; MSAG Clinical Practice Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is the most common idiopathic interstitial pneumonia, characterised by progressive fibrosis with a usual interstitial pneumonia pattern on HRCT. Diagnosis requires exclusion of known causes (connective tissue disease, asbestos, hypersensitivity pneumonitis, drug induced) and a definite UIP HRCT pattern confirmed at multidisciplinary meeting. Antifibrotic therapy with pirfenidone or nintedanib slows annual FVC decline by approximately half and reduces mortality; both are subsidised on the PBS for definite IPF with FVC 50 to 90% predicted. Long-term steroids are harmful in IPF per the PANTHER-IPF trial and N-acetylcysteine monotherapy is not effective. Supportive care includes pulmonary rehabilitation, supplemental oxygen, GORD treatment, vaccination, and consideration of lung transplantation in eligible candidates.
key_points: Definite UIP HRCT + exclusion of secondary causes = IPF
Antifibrotic: pirfenidone or nintedanib slows FVC decline approximately 50%
Long-term steroids are HARMFUL in IPF (PANTHER-IPF)
Supportive: oxygen, pulmonary rehab, transplantation, palliative care
explanation.pearls: PBS subsidy for pirfenidone and nintedanib in Australia requires definite IPF on multidisciplinary review, FVC 50 to 90% predicted, and DLCO 30 to 79% predicted at initiation; FVC threshold for ongoing PBS subsidy requires demonstrated stabilisation or decline less than 10% per year on therapy.

options.rationale: N-acetylcysteine monotherapy showed no benefit over placebo in the PANTHER-IPF and INSTAGE trials and is not standard care. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)
Cyclophosphamide is used in severe connective tissue disease ILD (scleroderma ILD) but is not recommended in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)

Mycophenolate is reserved for connective tissue disease-associated ILD which has been excluded by negative rheumatology screen; it is not the recommended IPF therapy. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement)

Antifibrotic therapy with pirfenidone (or nintedanib) is the recommended disease modifying therapy in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis; it slows decline in forced vital capacity and reduces mortality. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement; ATS/ERS IPF Guidelines)

Long-term steroids are NOT recommended in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis because the PANTHER-IPF trial demonstrated harm with prednisolone, azathioprine and N-acetylcysteine combination. (Source: TSANZ IPF Position Statement; ATS/ERS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Carcinoid syndrome occurs in approximately 20% of patients with midgut neuroendocrine tumours when serotonin and vasoactive metabolites reach the systemic circulation - usually after liver metastases bypass first-pass hepatic clearance. The classic triad is episodic flushing, watery diarrhoea and bronchospasm; right heart valve fibrosis (tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonary stenosis) is the late carcinoid heart disease. Biochemical confirmation is 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) on a low amine diet for 2 consecutive collections; sensitivity over 75% and specificity over 90%. Imaging staging is 68-Ga DOTATATE PET. Treatment of carcinoid syndrome is somatostatin analogue (octreotide LAR or lanreotide) for symptoms, liver-directed therapy (resection, embolisation, radiofrequency ablation, Y-90 radioembolisation) for liver burden, and peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (177-Lu DOTATATE) for refractory disease. Carcinoid crisis is precipitated by anaesthesia, biopsy or tumour manipulation and is prevented with peri-procedure octreotide infusion.
key_points: Classic triad: flushing, watery diarrhoea, bronchospasm
Tricuspid regurgitation plus pulmonary stenosis = carcinoid heart disease
Confirm with 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on low amine diet x 2
Stage with 68-Ga DOTATATE PET; treat with somatostatin analogue
explanation.pearls: Carcinoid crisis (severe flushing, hypotension, bronchospasm, arrhythmia) is precipitated by anaesthetic induction, biopsy or tumour manipulation; peri-procedural octreotide 500 mcg subcutaneous before induction and 100 mcg/hour intra-operative infusion is recommended by eviQ to prevent crisis.

options.rationale: Plasma chromogranin A is supportive but non-specific and serum serotonin is not a primary diagnostic test in Australia; 24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on a low amine diet is the established Australian biochemical confirmation. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; eviQ Cancer Treatments)

Liver biopsy carries risk of carcinoid crisis from serotonin release and requires somatostatin analogue cover; biochemical confirmation should precede biopsy. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)
MIBG imaging is used in phaeochromocytoma and neuroblastoma diagnosis; it is not the test of choice for serotonin-secreting carcinoid tumours. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)

DOTATATE PET is the staging imaging of choice in neuroendocrine tumour after biochemical confirmation; it identifies somatostatin receptor expression but does not establish the diagnosis. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines)

24-hour urinary 5-HIAA on a low amine diet (no banana, walnut, tomato, avocado, kiwifruit, pineapple, paracetamol, caffeine) for 2 consecutive collections is the diagnostic standard for carcinoid syndrome; serotonin metabolism via 5-HIAA correlates with tumour load. (Source: AGS Neuroendocrine Tumour Guidelines; eviQ Cancer Treatments)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management aims to reduce aortic shear stress (dP/dt) by first controlling heart rate with a beta-blocker, then adding a vasodilator if BP remains above target. Starting with vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia and propagates the dissection. Targets are heart rate under 60 and systolic BP 100-120 mmHg with adequate organ perfusion.
key_points: First beta-blocker (esmolol, labetalol), then vasodilator (GTN, nicardipine).
Heart rate target under 60; systolic BP 100-120 mmHg.
Type A dissection (proximal) is a surgical emergency; type B is initially medical unless complicated.
Avoid pure vasodilator without prior beta-blockade due to reflex tachycardia.
explanation.pearls: The sequence in aortic dissection BP control is rate first, pressure second; the order matters because reflex tachycardia accelerates the tear.

options.rationale: Labetalol alone is acceptable as both rate and BP control but the target MAP is too low and would risk end-organ ischaemia; usual target is SBP 100-120 with HR 60-80, not aggressively low MAP. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Pure vasodilator without prior rate control causes reflex tachycardia and increased aortic shear stress, propagating the dissection; rate control with beta-blocker must precede vasodilator. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
GTN without prior beta-blockade causes reflex tachycardia and propagates dissection; rate control comes first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

AU and international guidance for type B aortic dissection is rate control with beta-blocker first (esmolol or labetalol) to a heart rate under 60, then add a vasodilator if BP remains elevated; this sequence prevents reflex tachycardia and dissection propagation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
Oral therapy lacks the titration speed and reliability required in acute dissection; IV titratable agents are mandatory in the initial hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia during an intercurrent illness is usually transient. Once the precipitant has resolved and renal function has recovered, renin-angiotensin blockade is reintroduced cautiously rather than abandoned, one drug at a time with a potassium check.
key_points: Reintroduce one agent at a time at a reduced dose, with potassium and creatinine at one to two weeks.
The angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor is reinstated before the mineralocorticoid antagonist.
Give sick day advice to withhold both during vomiting, diarrhoea or dehydration.
explanation.context: Permanent discontinuation after a single episode of hyperkalaemia is one of the more consequential prescribing errors in heart failure, because the drugs that raise potassium are the same ones that reduce mortality. The rational response is to distinguish a transient prerenal insult, which resolves, from a fixed ceiling on excretory capacity, which does not. Sick day rules, dose reduction, dietary review and, where necessary, a potassium binder all exist to keep the patient on therapy. The same logic applies to metformin and to sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors: withhold during acute illness, then deliberately resume.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: The precipitant was transient and both potassium and creatinine have returned to baseline. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibition carries the larger mortality benefit and the smaller hyperkalaemia risk, so it is reintroduced first at a lower dose with a potassium check in one to two weeks. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)

Restarting both drugs at full dose is reasonable only where the hyperkalaemia was clearly explained by a single removable exposure and renal function never changed. Reintroducing two potassium raising drugs at full dose at once removes any way of telling which one causes a recurrence. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Increasing the furosemide treats congestion, which he does not have. Abandoning disease modifying therapy after a single reversible episode costs survival benefit and is a common error after discharge. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
A beta blocker belongs in the four pillar regimen, but it complements rather than substitutes for renin-angiotensin blockade and does not address the omission. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Spironolactone alone is reasonable where an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor is not tolerated for another reason. Of the two, the mineralocorticoid antagonist carries the greater hyperkalaemia risk, so it is not the one reintroduced first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)

explanation.summary: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma, vomiting) is treated with bolus 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL over 10 minutes, repeated up to 3 times if needed, aiming to raise serum sodium 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour. Overcorrection above 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination syndrome. SSRIs and TCAs are common precipitants of SIADH in older adults.
key_points: Hypertonic saline bolus dose: 150 mL of 3% saline over 10 min, up to 3 doses.
Target sodium rise: 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, then a maximum of 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours.
SSRIs, TCAs, thiazides, and carbamazepine are common medication precipitants.
Overcorrection risk: osmotic demyelination syndrome (former central pontine myelinolysis).
explanation.pearls: Seizure plus sodium of 112 mmol/L on a new SSRI gets 3% saline bolus 150 mL now, not 0.9% saline maintenance; the target is up by 5 in the first hour, then slow.

sources.label: European Society of Endocrinology Hyponatraemia Guideline

options.rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizure, coma) is treated with bolus 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL over 10 minutes, repeated to raise sodium 4-6 mmol/L in the first hour, with strict caution not to exceed 8-10 mmol/L in 24 hours to prevent osmotic demyelination; the SSRI is a likely precipitant. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Isotonic saline corrects too slowly for symptomatic severe hyponatraemia with seizure and can worsen SIADH-driven hyponatraemia; bolus hypertonic is required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Fluid restriction is for chronic asymptomatic SIADH; severe acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizure mandates immediate hypertonic saline. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Tolvaptan is oral, not IV; it is reserved for sub-acute SIADH management, not acute symptomatic severe hyponatraemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Mannitol is not used for hyponatraemia-related cerebral oedema; the specific treatment is hypertonic saline to raise serum sodium directly. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is treated with immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg, IV 0.9% saline 1 L bolus, and IV dextrose if hypoglycaemic. Hydrocortisone has both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid activity at high dose, sufficient for the acute phase. Dexamethasone is reserved for when biochemical confirmation is needed (it does not interfere with cortisol assay) but hydrocortisone is the preferred treatment in known adrenal insufficiency.
key_points: First hour: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat + IV 0.9% saline 1 L + dextrose if hypoglycaemic.
Maintenance: IV hydrocortisone 50 mg every 6 hours or 200 mg/24 h infusion until oral tolerated.
Do not delay treatment for cortisol or ACTH result.
Dexamethasone is used when biochemical confirmation pending; otherwise hydrocortisone.
explanation.pearls: A vomiting patient on long-term hydrocortisone gets 100 mg IV in resus before bloods come back, not after; the sick-day rules trump the cortisol level.

options.rationale: Anti-emetics and oral rehydration alone do not address adrenal crisis; immediate IV hydrocortisone and saline are required. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis is treated with IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat (then 50 mg every 6 hours or infusion), 0.9% saline 1 L bolus for hypovolaemia, and dextrose if hypoglycaemic; this is the AU first-hour bundle and should not wait for the cortisol result. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Fludrocortisone is for chronic mineralocorticoid replacement; high-dose IV hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity in the acute phase, and oral fludrocortisone is irrelevant when vomiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
Oral therapy is unreliable in a vomiting patient with adrenal crisis; IV hydrocortisone is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dexamethasone has no mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for when biochemical confirmation of adrenal insufficiency is required (will not interfere with cortisol assay); in known adrenal insufficiency, hydrocortisone is preferred. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Adult anaphylaxis is treated with IM adrenaline 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into the anterolateral mid-thigh as the first action, repeated every 5 minutes if no improvement. IV adrenaline boluses are reserved for refractory anaphylaxis. Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts that do not act in time and must not delay adrenaline.
key_points: Adult IM adrenaline dose: 0.5 mg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) into anterolateral mid-thigh.
Repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement; move to IV infusion if multiple IM doses fail.
Steroids and antihistamines are adjuncts only; they do not act fast enough as primary therapy.
Promethazine is contraindicated due to vasodilation and sedation.
explanation.pearls: The needle should be in the anterolateral thigh within 30 seconds of recognising adult anaphylaxis; IV access can come after the IM dose.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: IV adrenaline boluses are reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after IM doses fail and only by clinicians with critical care familiarity due to arrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia risk; IM is first-line. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is an adjunct for upper airway oedema after IM dosing; it is not first-line treatment for systemic anaphylaxis. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Adult anaphylaxis with hypotension, airway, and circulatory features is treated with IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral mid-thigh as the first action; repeat every 5 minutes if no improvement. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Steroids do not act in time and are an adjunct, not first-line; their use as primary therapy delays the only proven life-saving step. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

options.rationale: Promethazine causes vasodilation and sedation in anaphylaxis and is contraindicated; antihistamines treat skin symptoms only and have no primary role. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for acute management of anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: Trauma haemorrhage with shock and a positive FAST scan triggers Massive Transfusion Protocol activation with fixed 1:1:1 ratio of red cells, FFP, and platelets, plus IV tranexamic acid 1 g within 3 hours of injury (and a further 1 g infusion over 8 hours). TXA mortality benefit was established by the CRASH-2 trial and is sustained when given inside the window. Crystalloid is minimised to limit dilutional coagulopathy.
key_points: TXA mortality benefit window: within 3 hours of trauma; loading dose 1 g IV over 10 minutes.
MTP fixed ratio 1:1:1 PRBC:FFP:platelets reduces dilutional coagulopathy.
Crystalloid is restricted (no more than 1 L) once MTP active.
Cease MTP when haemodynamically stable, surgical control achieved, and lactate trending down.
explanation.pearls: TXA mortality benefit in trauma is preserved up to 3 hours from injury; this patient at 90 minutes is well within the window and gets 1 g IV alongside the first MTP pack.

options.rationale: Slow ratio transfusion in active haemorrhage worsens dilutional coagulopathy and hypothermia; massive transfusion protocol with rapid 1:1:1 ratio is the standard. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

Crystalloid worsens dilutional coagulopathy in trauma haemorrhage and is restricted to a minimum; FFP and platelets are given empirically as part of the MTP. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)
Whole blood is an option where available but is not the universal standard; the MTP fixed ratio with TXA addresses both shock and coagulopathy. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

Trauma haemorrhage at 90 minutes from injury still falls within the 3 hour TXA window where CRASH-2 demonstrated mortality benefit; MTP with 1:1:1 ratio plus TXA is the AU NBA standard. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines, CRASH-2)

Recombinant factor VIIa is not first-line in trauma haemorrhage, raises thrombosis risk, and is reserved for selected refractory cases; MTP and TXA come first. (Source: NBA Patient Blood Management Guidelines)

explanation.summary: ATLS 10th edition updated the recommended adult tension pneumothorax needle decompression site from the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line to the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line, reflecting evidence that adult chest wall thickness at the 2nd ICS frequently exceeds standard cannula length. Needle decompression is a temporising measure that must be followed by definitive intercostal catheter insertion. Finger thoracostomy is an alternative in intubated patients.
key_points: ATLS 10e adult site: 4th-5th ICS anterior or mid-axillary line, not 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
Paediatric site is still 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line.
Needle decompression is temporising; intercostal catheter follows.
Finger thoracostomy is an alternative, especially in intubated patients.
explanation.pearls: If you teach the 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line as the only adult site, you risk the needle not reaching pleura; ATLS 10e moved adults to the 4th-5th ICS anterior axillary line.

options.rationale: The 2nd ICS mid-clavicular line is the historical landmark but adult chest wall thickness commonly exceeds the needle length; ATLS 10th edition and AU practice now prefer the 4th-5th ICS in the anterior or mid-axillary line, and a chest tube must follow needle decompression. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)
Pericardiocentesis treats tamponade, not tension pneumothorax; the clinical picture is decompensated lung collapse, not cardiac tamponade. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

Definitive chest drain is the end-point but in true tension pneumothorax with cardiovascular collapse, immediate needle or finger thoracostomy is performed first to relieve the pressure, then the formal drain is inserted. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)
Bag-mask ventilation worsens tension pneumothorax by adding positive pressure through a non-intact pleura; immediate decompression is mandatory. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition)

ATLS 10th edition and AU practice updated the recommended needle decompression site to the 4th-5th intercostal space anterior or mid-axillary line because adult chest wall thickness at the 2nd ICS often exceeds the needle length; needle decompression must be followed by definitive chest drain insertion. (Source: ATLS 10th Edition; Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: Pulmonary embolism is risk-stratified into high (shock or sustained hypotension), intermediate (RV dysfunction by imaging or biomarkers without shock), and low (no RV dysfunction, no biomarker rise) categories. Intermediate-risk PE is further divided into intermediate-high (both imaging RV dysfunction AND biomarker rise) and intermediate-low (one or other). Anticoagulation with IV UFH or LMWH or DOAC is the foundation; systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 h or weight-based 0.6 mg/kg) is RESERVED for high-risk PE (with shock) or intermediate-risk PE that deteriorates haemodynamically on anticoagulation. The PEITHO trial showed routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE prevented haemodynamic decompensation but doubled major bleeding without mortality benefit. Catheter-directed therapies are an alternative when systemic thrombolysis is contraindicated or fails.
key_points: Risk stratify: high (shock), intermediate (RV dysfunction), low.
Anticoagulation foundation: UFH, LMWH, or DOAC.
Systemic thrombolysis reserved for high-risk PE or intermediate that decompensates.
PEITHO: routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk doubles major bleeding.
UFH preferred when bleeding risk uncertain (reversible with protamine).
explanation.pearls: PEITHO trial: routine alteplase in intermediate-risk PE doubles major bleeding without reducing mortality - reserve thrombolysis for the patient who actually decompensates on heparin.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism 2019

options.rationale: Intermediate-risk (submassive) PE with normal BP is treated with anticoagulation alone and close monitoring; systemic thrombolysis is reserved for haemodynamic decompensation (PEITHO showed thrombolysis prevents deterioration but increases major bleeding). UFH preferred over LMWH in renal impairment and possible bleeding need. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

Routine thrombolysis in intermediate-risk PE (without shock) increases major bleeding (PEITHO) without improving mortality; reserved for haemodynamic deterioration on heparin. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

LMWH at therapeutic dose is acceptable in low-risk PE but in intermediate-risk PE with renal impairment and possible need to switch to thrombolysis, IV UFH (rapidly reversible) is preferred in HDU. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)
Catheter-directed therapies are reserved for high-risk PE with shock or contraindication to thrombolysis; not first-line in intermediate-risk PE. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

IVC filter without anticoagulation in established PE has no role unless absolute contraindication to anticoagulation; this patient has none, and bleeding risk from a knee replacement at day 3 is acceptable for UFH. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute PE position statement)

explanation.summary: Adult diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is defined by hyperglycaemia (>11 mmol/L), ketonaemia (>3 mmol/L) or ketonuria, and metabolic acidosis (pH <7.30 or HCO3 <15). Management has 4 pillars: (1) fluid first - 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride over 1 h, then 1 L over 2 h, then 1 L over 4 h with adjustments for haemodynamic state; (2) insulin infusion at 0.1 U/kg/h started AFTER first fluid bag; (3) potassium replacement guided by serum K - K <3.3 hold insulin and replace K first, K 3.3-5.5 add KCl to fluid (40 mmol/L), K >5.5 no replacement; (4) dextrose added when glucose <14 mmol/L. Bicarbonate only if pH <6.9. Hourly bloods until anion gap resolves. Look for precipitant (infection, pump failure, non-adherence, MI). Transition to subcut insulin only when anion gap resolved and patient eating.
key_points: Fluid first (1 L 0.9% saline over 1 h), then insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h.
K <3.3 hold insulin; 3.3-5.5 replace; >5.5 no replacement.
Add 10% dextrose when glucose <14 mmol/L.
Bicarbonate only for pH <6.9.
Look for precipitant: infection, pump failure, non-adherence, MI.
explanation.pearls: In adult DKA, fluid comes first, insulin second, and potassium replacement waits until serum K drops below 5.5 - the insulin infusion will drop K within 2 hours.

sources.label: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.rationale: Insulin before fluid resuscitation in DKA can precipitate cardiovascular collapse and worsen intracellular potassium shift; fluid is started first per Australian DKA guidelines. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.rationale: AU adult DKA protocol: 1 L 0.9% saline over 1 h first, then insulin infusion 0.1 U/kg/h; K replacement only when serum K <5.5 (high risk of arrhythmia from hypokalaemia as insulin drives K intracellularly). (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.rationale: Bicarbonate in DKA does not improve outcomes and may worsen hypokalaemia and paradoxical CSF acidosis; reserved for pH <6.9 only. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.rationale: Dextrose is added only when glucose falls below 14 mmol/L during DKA treatment; SC intermediate insulin is not appropriate for acute DKA management. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

options.rationale: Oral rehydration and SC insulin alone is inadequate for established DKA with pH 7.10 and significant ketonaemia; IV protocol is required. (Source: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management)
source_refs: ADIPS / RACP Diabetes Australia: Adult DKA Management

explanation.summary: NSTE-ACS is risk-stratified by GRACE score (or TIMI) into very high, high, intermediate, and low risk. Invasive timing: VERY HIGH risk (haemodynamic instability, refractory chest pain, life-threatening arrhythmia, mechanical complication) - immediate angiography (<2 hours). HIGH risk (GRACE >140, dynamic ST/T changes, troponin rise) - early invasive (<24 hours). INTERMEDIATE risk (diabetes, renal dysfunction, EF <40%, prior PCI/CABG, GRACE 109-140) - delayed invasive (<72 hours). LOW risk - ischaemia-guided strategy with non-invasive testing. All NSTE-ACS get dual antiplatelet loading (aspirin + ticagrelor or prasugrel or clopidogrel), parenteral anticoagulation (fondaparinux for non-immediate PCI, UFH or enoxaparin for PCI), statin, beta-blocker, ACEI.
key_points: GRACE >140 = high-risk NSTEMI, early invasive within 24 hours.
Aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg dual antiplatelet loading.
Fondaparinux 2.5 mg SC preferred when PCI not immediate.
Thrombolysis CONTRAINDICATED in NSTE-ACS (no transmural occlusion).
Very high risk (instability) needs immediate angiography <2 hours.
explanation.pearls: GRACE over 140 is the 24 hour gate to the cath lab for NSTEMI - ticagrelor 180 mg load is preferred over clopidogrel unless oral anticoagulant on board or high bleeding risk.

options.rationale: GRACE score >140 categorises as high risk; conservative ischaemia-guided strategy is for low-risk NSTEMI; high risk warrants early invasive within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

Primary PCI within 90 min is for STEMI (or NSTE-ACS with refractory chest pain, electrical/haemodynamic instability, mechanical complication, or VT/VF). NSTEMI with high GRACE without these features is invasive within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

GRACE >140 = high-risk NSTEMI; AU protocol is dual antiplatelet loading (aspirin 300 mg + ticagrelor 180 mg) plus parenteral anticoagulant (fondaparinux preferred over enoxaparin in stable AU practice unless undergoing immediate PCI) and invasive angiography within 24 hours. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)
Thrombolysis is contraindicated in NSTE-ACS (no transmural occlusion to lyse); inappropriate and would increase bleeding without benefit. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)
Discharge of a high-risk NSTEMI (GRACE >140) for outpatient CT-CA risks recurrent infarction and death; inpatient invasive workup is mandatory. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline)

explanation.summary: Tumour lysis syndrome is defined by Cairo-Bishop criteria: any 2 of K >6.0, urate >476 micromol/L, phosphate >1.45 mmol/L, calcium <1.75 mmol/L, OR a 25% change from baseline, within 3 days before or 7 days after chemotherapy commencement. CLINICAL TLS adds creatinine >1.5x ULN, arrhythmia, seizure, or sudden death. High-risk malignancies: Burkitt lymphoma, T-cell ALL, blastic phase CML, AML with high WBC. Prevention in high-risk: rasburicase prophylaxis, aggressive hydration. Established TLS: aggressive IV hydration targeting UO 100 mL/h, rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV (drops urate within hours by enzymatic oxidation to soluble allantoin), correction of hyperkalaemia (calcium gluconate, insulin/dextrose, salbutamol), do NOT correct asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (causes calcium phosphate precipitation), urinary alkalinisation NO LONGER recommended. Dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguria, or fluid overload.
key_points: Cairo-Bishop: any 2 of K/urate/PO4/Ca derangement.
Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV - drops urate within hours.
Do NOT correct asymptomatic hypocalcaemia (precipitates calcium phosphate).
Urinary alkalinisation no longer recommended (worsens Ca-PO4 precipitation).
Dialysis for refractory hyperK, oliguria, or fluid overload.
explanation.pearls: Asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in TLS gets the phosphate treated, not the calcium - injecting calcium gluconate into a high-phosphate state precipitates calcium phosphate in the kidneys and worsens the AKI.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Tumour lysis syndrome

options.rationale: Maintenance fluids alone are inadequate in established TLS (Cairo-Bishop criteria met); rasburicase, aggressive hydration to UO 100 mL/h, and dialysis criteria review are required. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

Asymptomatic hypocalcaemia in TLS should NOT be corrected with calcium - it precipitates as calcium phosphate causing AKI and worsens metastatic calcification; treat the hyperphosphataemia instead. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

Urinary alkalinisation is no longer recommended in TLS - it worsens calcium phosphate precipitation when phosphate is high; rasburicase is the AU first-line in established TLS. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

Established TLS in high-risk haematological malignancy: aggressive hydration (UO 100 mL/h), rasburicase (recombinant urate oxidase) drops urate within hours; dialysis for refractory hyperkalaemia, oliguria, or fluid overload. G6PD result not required to give first dose if otherwise indicated and the patient is not in a known G6PD-deficient demographic. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

Waiting for G6PD result delays critical urate lowering; in emergent TLS, give first dose of rasburicase and accept the small risk if G6PD-deficient (haemolysis), particularly in non-African/Mediterranean ancestry; alkalinisation harms calcium-phosphate handling. (Source: HSANZ TLS prevention and management)

explanation.summary: Cushing syndrome workup proceeds in 3 stages: (1) BIOCHEMICAL CONFIRMATION of hypercortisolism using ANY 2 of 3 first-line tests (1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression, 24-hour urinary free cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol); single test has insufficient specificity. (2) ACTH-DEPENDENT vs ACTH-INDEPENDENT differentiation by plasma ACTH (low <2 pmol/L = adrenal cause, normal/high = pituitary or ectopic). (3) LOCALISATION by pituitary MRI (Cushing disease), inferior petrosal sinus sampling if discordant, CT chest/abdomen for ectopic ACTH or adrenal mass. Pseudo-Cushing causes (obesity, depression, alcoholism, pregnancy) may give false positives; exogenous steroid use is the most common false positive cause overall. Skipping straight to imaging causes misdiagnosis from incidentalomas.
key_points: Confirm hypercortisolism FIRST with 2 of 3: DST, UFC, salivary cortisol.
Then ACTH to differentiate ACTH-dependent vs independent.
Pituitary MRI for ACTH-dependent; CT abdomen for ACTH-independent.
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling if pituitary MRI normal but ACTH-dependent.
Exclude exogenous steroid use as the most common false positive cause.
explanation.pearls: 2-of-3 screening (1 mg DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol) confirms Cushing biochemically before any imaging - pituitary incidentalomas in 10-20% mean MRI-first invites misdiagnosis.

options.rationale: Pituitary incidentalomas occur in 10-20%; imaging before biochemical confirmation cannot distinguish hormone-secreting from non-secreting lesions. Biochemistry first to confirm hypercortisolism is the AU standard. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Short Synacthen tests for adrenal INsufficiency (Addison's), not Cushing syndrome (hypercortisolism); inappropriate test for the clinical question. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Random ACTH alone cannot diagnose or differentiate Cushing syndrome aetiologies; it has a role AFTER hypercortisolism is biochemically confirmed to differentiate ACTH-dependent vs independent disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)
