Renin-aldosterone workup investigates Conn's syndrome; the clinical phenotype here (wide striae, central obesity, proximal weakness, glucose intolerance) is Cushing syndrome and demands cortisol-axis workup. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

Endocrine Society first-line: any 2 of 3 (1 mg overnight DST, 24 h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol) positive to confirm hypercortisolism; ACTH then differentiates ACTH-dependent (pituitary, ectopic) vs ACTH-independent (adrenal) disease. (Source: Endocrine Society Cushing Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: NHFA/CSANZ recommends direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) as first-line stroke prevention in non-valvular atrial fibrillation with CHA2DS2-VASc 2 or higher (women) or 1 or higher (men). Apixaban is preferred in elderly patients with renal impairment because of its lower renal clearance. The apixaban dose reduction criteria require 2 of: age 80 years or older, weight 60 kg or less, serum creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. Dabigatran is contraindicated below CrCl 30 mL/min. Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves and moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Aspirin is NOT recommended for stroke prevention. HAS-BLED informs bleeding-risk modification (BP control, alcohol, drugs) rather than withholding anticoagulation.
key_points: DOACs are first-line for non-valvular AF in Australia
Apixaban dose reduction: 2 of age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133+ micromol/L
Dabigatran contraindicated below CrCl 30 mL/min
Warfarin reserved for mechanical valves and moderate-severe MS
Aspirin not recommended for AF stroke prevention
explanation.pearls: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily is the AU standard dose when any 2 of 3 criteria are met (age 80+, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher); under-dosing without meeting criteria reduces stroke protection without lowering bleeding.

options.rationale: She meets 2 of the 3 dose-reduction criteria (weight 58 kg and creatinine 138 micromol/L); the correct dose is 2.5 mg twice daily, not the standard 5 mg twice daily. (Source: AMH)

Apixaban reduced dose criteria require 2 of: age 80 or older, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher; she meets weight and creatinine criteria, so 2.5 mg twice daily is correct. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular; AMH; NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)
Dabigatran is 80% renally cleared and is contraindicated in CrCl below 30 mL/min and used with caution in 30-50 mL/min; apixaban (less renal clearance) is preferred at her eGFR of 32. (Source: AMH)

Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves, moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, and ESRF on dialysis; DOACs are first-line in non-valvular AF including with stage 3b CKD per AU guidance. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)

Aspirin is NOT recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation - the benefit is small and bleeding risk approaches that of full anticoagulation. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guideline)

explanation.summary: Hyperkalaemia management proceeds in 3 sequential steps when ECG changes are present: (1) membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate (10 mL 10% IV over 2 minutes; works in 1-3 min, lasts 30-60 min); (2) intracellular shift with insulin 10 units in 50 mL of 50% dextrose IV over 15 min plus nebulised salbutamol 10 mg plus sodium bicarbonate 50 mmol IV (if metabolic acidosis); (3) total body removal via loop diuretic (with intact kidney function), patiromer or zirconium cyclosilicate, or dialysis. Identify and stop the precipitant: ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, beta-blockers, heparin. Calcium chloride is more potent than calcium gluconate but requires central access.
key_points: Sequence: stabilise (calcium), shift (insulin-dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate), remove (loop, binder, dialysis)
Calcium gluconate works within 1-3 minutes and lasts 30-60 minutes
Trimethoprim plus ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone is a classical pharmacological triad of hyperkalaemia
Resonium and patiromer are slow GI removers (hours), not for immediate use
Dialysis is definitive in refractory or CKD/AKI cases
explanation.pearls: Trimethoprim added to background ACE inhibitor plus spironolactone in CKD is a classical hyperkalaemia precipitant; the trimethoprim blocks the renal tubular ENaC channel similarly to amiloride and can raise serum potassium by 1-2 mmol/L within days.

options.rationale: Nebulised salbutamol is an adjunct to insulin-dextrose for potassium shifting but is not the first step when ECG changes are present; membrane stabilisation precedes shifting. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

Insulin-dextrose shifts potassium effectively but takes 15-30 minutes to start working; calcium gluconate must precede it when ECG changes are present to stabilise the myocyte membrane. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

Hyperkalaemia with broadened QRS and peaked T waves requires immediate myocyte membrane stabilisation with calcium gluconate before insulin-dextrose; calcium stabilises within 1-3 minutes and lasts 30-60 minutes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

Resonium removes potassium slowly (hours) and has GI side effects including necrosis; it has no role in immediate management of life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

Dialysis is the definitive treatment in refractory hyperkalaemia or CKD/AKI without rapid response; immediate calcium gluconate plus insulin-dextrose precedes dialysis preparation and bridges to RRT. (Source: UpToDate Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: SMART-COP severity tool (Systolic BP, Multilobar, Albumin, Respiratory rate, Tachycardia, Confusion, Oxygen, pH) stratifies CAP. A score of 0-2 indicates outpatient management with oral antibiotics; 3-4 indicates admission for moderate disease; 5 or higher indicates severe CAP requiring IV antibiotics, HDU/ICU consideration, and assessment for invasive ventilation or vasopressors. AU Therapeutic Guidelines first-line for severe CAP is ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily plus azithromycin 500 mg IV daily, escalating to a wider regimen (add gentamicin or pip-taz) for septic shock, immunocompromise, or specific exposures. Moxifloxacin monotherapy is the alternative in severe beta-lactam allergy.
key_points: SMART-COP 5+ is severe CAP requiring IV antibiotics and HDU/ICU assessment
AU first-line severe CAP: ceftriaxone 1 g + azithromycin 500 mg IV daily
Moxifloxacin monotherapy only for severe beta-lactam allergy
Pip-taz plus vancomycin reserved for HAP, aspiration, post-influenza
Atypical organisms (Legionella, Mycoplasma) covered by macrolide
explanation.pearls: SMART-COP score of 5 or higher predicts a need for intensive respiratory or vasopressor support in CAP and triggers IV ceftriaxone PLUS IV azithromycin; the macrolide cover for Legionella is the change from moderate-severity therapy.

sources.label: TSANZ/ATS Guidelines for the Management of Community-Acquired Pneumonia

options.rationale: This is the standard moderate severity AU regimen; with SMART-COP 6 (severe) the recommended Tx Guidelines pathway uses ceftriaxone plus azithromycin (or moxifloxacin monotherapy if beta-lactam allergic). (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

SMART-COP 5 or higher is severe CAP; empirical IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily PLUS IV azithromycin 500 mg daily is the AU Therapeutic Guidelines first-line for severe CAP, covering S pneumoniae and atypical organisms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Pip-taz plus vancomycin is reserved for healthcare-associated or aspiration pneumonia or post-influenza pneumonia where Pseudomonas or MRSA are suspected; not standard CAP cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Moxifloxacin monotherapy is the AU alternative ONLY for severe beta-lactam allergy; in non-allergic patients ceftriaxone plus azithromycin is preferred and has better antimicrobial stewardship. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Oral outpatient therapy is the AU regimen for low-severity CAP (CRB-65 0 or SMART-COP 0-2); SMART-COP 6 is severe and requires IV antibiotics with admission and HDU/ICU review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Contrast-induced acute kidney injury (CI-AKI) risk rises with CKD, diabetes, heart failure, advanced age, hypovolaemia, repeat contrast exposure, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors/ARBs at high doses, and high-volume or hyperosmolar contrast. KDIGO and KHA-CARI recommend isotonic saline IV (1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-contrast) as the only evidence-based pharmacological prophylaxis. The PRESERVE trial definitively refuted N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate. Adjuncts include: minimise contrast volume, use iso-osmolar or low-osmolar contrast, stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides), and hold metformin if eGFR less than 30 (or recheck creatinine 48-72 h post-contrast at moderate CKD). Statins have a small protective effect.
key_points: Isotonic saline 1 mL/kg/hour for 12h pre- and 12h post-contrast
PRESERVE trial: no benefit from N-acetylcysteine or bicarbonate
Stop nephrotoxins (NSAIDs) pre-procedure
Withhold metformin only for lactic acidosis concern, not CIN prevention
Forced diuresis worsens CIN risk
explanation.pearls: Isotonic 0.9% saline 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-contrast is the only proven CIN prophylaxis; PRESERVE trial 2018 ended the use of N-acetylcysteine and sodium bicarbonate.

sources.label: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD

options.rationale: Isotonic IV crystalloid pre- and post-contrast is the only AU-recommended pharmacological prophylaxis with consistent evidence; KHA-CARI and KDIGO recommend 1 mL/kg/hour for 12 hours pre- and 12 hours post-procedure. (Source: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD; KDIGO AKI)
source_refs: KHA-CARI Guideline: Use of Contrast Agents in Patients with CKD

options.rationale: The PRESERVE trial (NEJM 2018) showed no benefit from N-acetylcysteine for contrast-induced AKI prevention versus placebo; AU and international guidelines no longer recommend it. (Source: PRESERVE trial; KDIGO AKI)
PRESERVE trial also showed no benefit from sodium bicarbonate over isotonic saline; the simpler regimen of 0.9% saline is now standard. (Source: PRESERVE trial; KDIGO AKI)

Withholding metformin reduces lactic acidosis risk (separate concern from CIN) but does NOT prevent contrast-induced acute kidney injury; standard practice is to withhold metformin in eGFR less than 30 OR check creatinine 48-72 h post-contrast in moderate CKD. (Source: AMH)

Forced diuresis with furosemide and mannitol INCREASES contrast-induced AKI risk by reducing intravascular volume; isotonic hydration alone is the only proven prophylactic intervention. (Source: KDIGO AKI)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency precipitated by infection, gastroenteritis (vomiting prevents oral steroid absorption), trauma, surgery, or sudden cessation of glucocorticoid. Classical presentation: hypotension, dehydration, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, fever, abdominal pain. Treatment is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus immediately, followed by 200 mg over 24 hours (or 50 mg every 6 hours), plus IV 0.9% saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia, dextrose for hypoglycaemia, treat precipitant, and continue at stress dose for 24-48 hours before titrating down. Mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is added when daily glucocorticoid drops below 50 mg because hydrocortisone has intrinsic mineralocorticoid activity at high doses. Education on sick-day rules (double oral dose for febrile illness, IM hydrocortisone 100 mg for vomiting) is the cornerstone of prevention.
key_points: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is the priority intervention
Followed by 200 mg/24 h infusion or 50 mg IV 6-hourly
Saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia, dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Fludrocortisone added only when daily steroid is below 50 mg
Sick-day rules: double oral dose for fever, IM hydrocortisone for vomiting
explanation.pearls: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV is the immediate priority in adrenal crisis; mineralocorticoid (fludrocortisone) is only added when total daily hydrocortisone drops below 50 mg because high-dose hydrocortisone has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity at the kidney.

sources.label: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus is the single most important intervention in adrenal crisis; do not wait for cortisol results. Saline 1 L over 1 hour for hypovolaemia; dextrose for hypoglycaemia; treat precipitant. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Primary Adrenal Insufficiency; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Dexamethasone is preferred when the diagnosis is uncertain to preserve cortisol assay; this patient has known established Addison disease so hydrocortisone is the correct agent and starts within minutes. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Fludrocortisone is not required acutely because high-dose hydrocortisone (>50 mg/day) has sufficient mineralocorticoid activity; oral fludrocortisone is added when daily steroid drops below 50 mg. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia in adrenal crisis resolves with cortisol replacement and saline; calcium gluconate is only indicated if ECG changes present. Hydrocortisone bolus is the priority and corrects the underlying cause. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

options.rationale: Source-control and empirical antibiotics are appropriate but the immediate priority is glucocorticoid replacement; sepsis without cortisol replacement in Addison disease is rapidly fatal. (Source: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline)
source_refs: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline: Primary Adrenal Insufficiency

explanation.summary: New left bundle branch block in the setting of chest pain is not automatically a STEMI equivalent; the modified Sgarbossa criteria (Smith) identify which patients have acute coronary occlusion. Positive criteria are: (1) concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more in any lead; (2) concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1, V2, or V3; (3) discordant ST elevation with proportionally excessive elevation (ST/S ratio of -0.25 or worse). Any one positive feature classifies as STEMI equivalent. Reperfusion strategy in Australia: primary PCI if first medical contact to balloon time is 90-120 minutes or less; otherwise fibrinolysis with tenecteplase, then transfer for rescue PCI if no resolution in 60-90 minutes (pharmaco-invasive strategy). Time-to-reperfusion is the dominant predictor of outcome.
key_points: New LBBB is not automatically a STEMI equivalent
Modified Sgarbossa criteria identify acute coronary occlusion in LBBB
Concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more is the most specific criterion
Reperfusion: primary PCI if under 120 min, otherwise thrombolysis plus transfer
Pharmaco-invasive strategy: thrombolysis then rescue PCI if no resolution
explanation.pearls: Modified Sgarbossa criteria - concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more in any lead is the most specific criterion (over 90%) for acute coronary occlusion in new LBBB; this is the key discriminator that drives the reperfusion decision.

options.rationale: Waiting for serial troponin or repeat ECG in a STEMI-equivalent loses myocardium; positive Sgarbossa criteria with new LBBB warrant immediate reperfusion. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

Primary PCI is preferred when transfer time is under 90-120 minutes from first medical contact; with 80 minutes transfer plus angiography prep time the total exceeds the 120 minute window and thrombolysis is preferred. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

Treating this as NSTEMI ignores positive Sgarbossa with new LBBB; classifying it as a STEMI-equivalent is the standard of care and time-to-reperfusion drives outcome. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

Modified Sgarbossa criteria are positive (concordant ST elevation 1 mm or more, OR concordant ST depression 1 mm or more in V1-V3, OR excessive discordant ST elevation); new LBBB plus positive Sgarbossa with 80 minute PCI transfer is a STEMI equivalent and requires thrombolysis. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndromes 2016; Sgarbossa criteria)

Analgesia and GTN are appropriate adjuncts but do not address the time-critical reperfusion need; symptomatic management without reperfusion is a major error in suspected STEMI. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ ACS Guideline 2016)

explanation.summary: Australian paracetamol poisoning guideline 2020 distinguishes acute single ingestion (use Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 hour level) from staggered ingestion (ingestion over more than 1 hour) and repeated supratherapeutic ingestion. Staggered ingestion thresholds: 200 mg/kg or 10 g (whichever is less) in 24 hours, or 150 mg/kg over 48 hours, or 100 mg/kg daily over 72 hours. The 2-bag IV acetylcysteine regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) has replaced the older 3-bag regimen due to fewer anaphylactoid reactions. Indications for continued infusion past 20 hours include rising ALT, INR over 2, lactic acidosis, or ongoing detectable paracetamol. King's College criteria (arterial pH less than 7.30 after fluid resuscitation; OR all of: PT over 100 seconds, creatinine over 300 micromol/L, grade 3-4 hepatic encephalopathy) trigger liver transplantation discussion.
key_points: Staggered paracetamol ingestion: do not use nomogram
Threshold: 200 mg/kg or 10 g in 24 hours plus hepatotoxic features
AU 2-bag IV acetylcysteine regimen replaces older 3-bag
Continued infusion if ALT rising, INR over 2, lactic acidosis, paracetamol detected
King's College criteria trigger transplant discussion
explanation.pearls: The 2-bag intravenous acetylcysteine regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours) has replaced the older 3-bag regimen because it gives the same dose with fewer anaphylactoid reactions; AU practice since 2020.

options.rationale: The nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion but acetylcysteine is started anyway if the cumulative dose exceeds 200 mg/kg or 10 g (whichever is less) in 24 hours OR if there are signs of hepatotoxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology; AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

Acetylcysteine is started immediately; King's College criteria are reassessed at 48-72 hours and beyond, not before initial antidote. Acetylcysteine plus transplant referral run in parallel, not sequentially. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

Charcoal is only useful within 2 hours of acute ingestion; this presentation is 26 hours after the start of ingestion. Nomogram does not apply to staggered ingestion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Toxicology)

Active hepatotoxicity (ALT 1280, INR 2.1) and metabolic acidosis (lactate 3.2, bicarbonate 18) indicate severe paracetamol toxicity in progress and discharge would be catastrophic. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

Staggered ingestion exceeding 200 mg/kg in 24 hours plus evidence of hepatotoxicity (ALT 1280, INR 2.1) mandates IV acetylcysteine using the 2-bag regimen (200 mg/kg over 4 hours then 100 mg/kg over 16 hours); King's College criteria triage for liver transplantation. (Source: AU Paracetamol Poisoning Guideline 2020)

explanation.summary: First unprovoked PE requires a minimum 3 months of treatment-dose anticoagulation. The decision at 3 to 6 months is whether to stop or continue indefinitely at reduced dose. Current Australian (THANZ) guidance supports extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely in patients with low bleed risk (HAS-BLED score less than 3, no anaemia, no recent bleeding), based on AMPLIFY-EXT trial showing reduction in recurrence without significant excess of major bleeding. Recurrence risk without extended therapy after first unprovoked PE is approximately 10 percent at 1 year and 30 percent at 5 years. Aspirin is inferior to DOACs for secondary prevention.
key_points: First unprovoked PE: minimum 3 months treatment dose
Extended therapy with apixaban 2.5 mg BD indefinitely halves recurrence (AMPLIFY-EXT)
Low bleed risk and ongoing tolerance favour extended therapy
Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for secondary VTE prevention
explanation.pearls: After 3 to 6 months treatment-dose apixaban for first unprovoked PE, continue apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely if bleed risk is low (AMPLIFY-EXT).

sources.label: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Three months is the minimum to treat the initial event but stopping after a first unprovoked PE carries approximately 10 percent recurrence in year 1 and 30 percent at 5 years; the question of extended therapy must be addressed. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: A defined 6-month total is appropriate for provoked PE; first unprovoked PE warrants either stopping at 3 months or extending indefinitely at reduced dose, not an arbitrary 6-month duration. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: After 3 to 6 months treatment-dose anticoagulation for first unprovoked PE in a patient with low bleed risk, current Australian and AMPLIFY-EXT trial guidance is extended apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely, which roughly halves recurrence without substantially increasing major bleeding. (Source: THANZ; AMPLIFY-EXT trial)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Apixaban is non-inferior to warfarin for VTE prevention with less major bleeding; switching to warfarin would require INR monitoring without benefit. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

options.rationale: Aspirin is inferior to DOAC for VTE recurrence prevention (WARFASA and ASPIRE trials showed approximately 35 percent reduction vs DOAC 80 percent), and is no longer preferred as extended VTE prophylaxis. (Source: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand)
source_refs: Thrombosis and Haemostasis Society of Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: First-line pharmacotherapy for postmenopausal osteoporosis in Australia is an oral bisphosphonate (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) with background calcium 1000 to 1300 mg daily and vitamin D sufficient to maintain 25-hydroxyvitamin D above 50 nmol/L. Denosumab 60 mg SC 6-monthly is second-line, reserved for intolerance to oral bisphosphonate (oesophagitis, dysphagia), eGFR less than 35, or malabsorption. Denosumab carries a meaningful rebound vertebral fracture risk if missed or stopped, requiring continuous adherence or transition to bisphosphonate before discontinuation. Zoledronic acid 5 mg IV annually is an alternative for those who cannot manage weekly dosing. Teriparatide is reserved for severe disease with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of first-line therapy.
key_points: First-line: weekly alendronate or risedronate plus calcium and vitamin D
Denosumab is second-line; rebound vertebral fracture risk after stopping
Zoledronic acid IV annually if oral bisphosphonate not tolerated or adherence concerns
Teriparatide reserved for severe disease or failure of first-line therapy
explanation.pearls: First-line osteoporosis: alendronate 70 mg weekly with calcium and vitamin D; denosumab 6-monthly is second-line because of vertebral rebound risk if missed.

options.rationale: Calcium, vitamin D, and exercise are necessary background therapy but do not alone reduce fracture risk in established osteoporosis with prior minimal-trauma fracture. Pharmacotherapy is indicated. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

Raloxifene reduces vertebral but not non-vertebral fracture risk and carries a VTE risk; it is not first-line for a 68-year-old with established osteoporosis and recent wrist fracture. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

Teriparatide is reserved by PBS for severe osteoporosis with multiple vertebral fractures or failure of antiresorptive therapy; she has not yet had a trial of first-line bisphosphonate. (Source: PBS criteria; RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

Weekly oral alendronate is the Australian first-line agent for postmenopausal osteoporosis in a patient who can sit upright for 30 minutes and has no upper GI contraindication. With background calcium and vitamin D it reduces vertebral, hip, and non-vertebral fracture risk. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Denosumab is reserved as second-line when oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated or contraindicated (severe oesophageal disease, malabsorption, eGFR below 35) because of the rebound vertebral fracture risk if missed or stopped. (Source: RACGP Osteoporosis prevention and management)

explanation.summary: Initial pharmacotherapy in Parkinson's disease is informed by age, motor severity, and side-effect profile. In older patients (over 65 to 70) with functional motor impairment, levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) is the most effective and best-tolerated first-line agent. Dopamine agonists (pramipexole, ropinirole) provide adequate symptomatic relief in younger patients but carry higher rates of impulse control disorder, sleep attacks, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension; they are avoided as first line in older patients. Start levodopa low (50/12.5 mg three times daily) and titrate to balance motor benefit against the onset of motor fluctuations and dyskinesias.
key_points: Levodopa + decarboxylase inhibitor: first-line in older patients with motor impairment
Dopamine agonists in younger patients only because of older-age adverse effects
Anticholinergics avoided over 70 (falls, cognition, urinary retention)
Start low and titrate to symptomatic control and minimise dyskinesia
explanation.pearls: Start older Parkinson's patients on levodopa-carbidopa 50/12.5 mg three times daily and titrate; dopamine agonists carry higher impulse-control and orthostatic risk after 70.

options.rationale: MAO-B inhibitors provide modest symptomatic benefit but are less effective than levodopa for moderate motor symptoms in an older patient with functional impairment, and the neuroprotective claim is not established. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)
Amantadine is primarily used for levodopa-induced dyskinesias and is not a robust first-line monotherapy for established motor symptoms in older patients. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Dopamine agonists carry higher rates of impulse control disorders, sleep attacks, hallucinations, and orthostatic hypotension, and are not preferred in patients over 70 because of these adverse effects. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Anticholinergics worsen cognition, urinary retention, constipation, and falls risk in older adults and should be avoided in patients over 70 with parkinsonism. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

Levodopa combined with a peripheral decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa or benserazide) is the most effective antiparkinsonian agent and the preferred first-line therapy in older patients (over 65 to 70) where dopamine-agonist adverse effects predominate. Start low and titrate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology; MDS Levodopa Recommendations)

explanation.summary: The modified Duke criteria (2023 update) classify suspected infective endocarditis as definite, possible, or rejected. Two major criteria, OR one major plus three minor, OR five minor support definite IE. Major criteria: (a) typical IE organism from two separate cultures OR persistent bacteraemia with any organism OR single positive culture for Coxiella burnetii or phase I IgG titre at least 1:800; (b) imaging evidence of endocardial involvement (echocardiographic vegetation, abscess, prosthetic dehiscence, or PET-CT abnormal uptake on prosthetic valve more than 3 months post-implant). Minor criteria: predisposing condition, fever 38 degrees or more, vascular phenomena, immunological phenomena, microbiology that does not meet major. Vegetation on a prosthetic valve with two positive culture sets meets two majors and is definite IE.
key_points: Definite IE: 2 major OR 1 major + 3 minor OR 5 minor criteria
Major: typical organism in 2 cultures + echo or PET-CT evidence on prosthetic valve
PET-CT added in 2023 for prosthetic valves more than 3 months post-implant
Empirical antibiotics started after cultures, not deferred for PET-CT
explanation.pearls: Two positive cultures for typical organism plus echo vegetation on prosthetic valve equals definite IE by modified Duke 2023; PET-CT is added imaging only when echo is equivocal.

options.rationale: Two sets of blood cultures positive for a typical IE organism (viridans group streptococcus) plus echocardiographic evidence of vegetation on a prosthetic valve constitute two Duke major criteria, which alone make definite IE. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023; Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Two of three positive culture sets with a typical organism already satisfies the major criterion (persistent bacteraemia with typical organism), particularly with prosthetic valve involvement. Further cultures are valuable but the diagnosis is already definite. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

Rejected IE requires a firm alternative diagnosis or resolution of symptoms with 4 days or less of antibiotics; this case meets the major criteria for definite IE. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

While he does meet some minor criteria (fever, vascular phenomena via splinters, prosthetic valve as predisposing factor), the strongest classification is two majors (cultures plus echocardiogram) which by itself reaches definite. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

PET-CT (an imaging modality added to the 2023 modified Duke criteria for prosthetic valves more than 3 months post-implant) is helpful when echo is equivocal but is not required when echo and cultures already satisfy major criteria. (Source: Modified Duke Criteria 2023)

explanation.summary: First-line screening for Cushing's syndrome uses one of three tests (Endocrine Society Guideline): 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), late-night salivary cortisol (two samples on different nights), or overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test. The 1 mg DST is taken at 23:00 with cortisol measured at 08:00 next morning; a failure to suppress to less than 50 nmol/L is abnormal. If one test is abnormal, perform a second different test to confirm. Once Cushing's is confirmed biochemically, ACTH measurement determines whether ACTH-dependent (raised) or independent (suppressed), and imaging (pituitary MRI or adrenal CT) follows accordingly.
key_points: First-line screen: 24-h UFC, late-night salivary cortisol, OR overnight 1 mg DST
1 mg DST: dexamethasone at 23:00, cortisol next morning at 08:00, target less than 50 nmol/L
Confirm with a second different test before proceeding
ACTH and imaging come AFTER biochemical confirmation, not before
explanation.pearls: Cushing's screening: overnight 1 mg DST suppresses 08:00 cortisol to less than 50 nmol/L if normal; ACTH and pituitary MRI follow biochemical confirmation, not precede it.

options.rationale: A single random morning cortisol shows substantial overlap between Cushing's and non-Cushing's states because of episodic secretion and stress reactivity, and is not a screening test for Cushing's syndrome. (Source: ESE Cushing's Guideline; RACGP Endocrinology)

An overnight 1 mg DST (1 mg dexamethasone at 23:00 with serum cortisol measured 08:00 next morning) is one of three first-line screening tests endorsed by the Endocrine Society. A failure to suppress cortisol to less than 50 nmol/L is abnormal and prompts further investigation. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

ACTH is used after diagnosis is confirmed to determine the source (pituitary versus ectopic versus adrenal), not as the initial screening test for Cushing's syndrome itself. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

Imaging the pituitary before establishing Cushing's syndrome generates incidentaloma noise (10 percent of normal adults have pituitary lesions on MRI) and does not constitute screening. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

ARR screens for primary aldosteronism, not Cushing's syndrome. Although hypokalaemia is present, the clinical phenotype here is overwhelmingly Cushing's and screening should target that diagnosis. (Source: ESE Cushing's Syndrome Guideline)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection management depends on Stanford classification. Type A (involves ascending aorta) requires emergent surgical repair due to risk of cardiac tamponade, aortic regurgitation, and coronary occlusion. Type B (distal to left subclavian only) is medically managed if uncomplicated, with IV beta-blockade first (labetalol 20 mg bolus then infusion titrated, OR esmolol infusion) to target heart rate around 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg. Vasodilator (sodium nitroprusside or glyceryl trinitrate) is added only after rate is controlled, to prevent reflex tachycardia raising shear stress. Complicated type B (malperfusion, rupture, rapid expansion, refractory pain) requires TEVAR or surgery.
key_points: Type A dissection: emergent surgery (ascending aorta involved)
Type B uncomplicated: medical management with IV beta blockade FIRST
Targets: heart rate around 60, SBP 100 to 120 mmHg
Vasodilator added only after rate control to avoid reflex tachycardia
explanation.pearls: Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection: IV labetalol or esmolol first to HR 60 and SBP 100 to 120 mmHg; only then add vasodilator to avoid reflex tachycardia raising aortic shear stress.

options.rationale: Starting a pure vasodilator first causes reflex tachycardia which raises shear stress (dP/dt) on the aortic wall and risks dissection extension. Beta blockade must precede vasodilator therapy. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline; eTG: Cardiovascular)
Diuresis is not the issue here and morphine alone is inadequate; the priority is rate and pressure control with beta blockade to reduce aortic wall stress. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

Uncomplicated type B aortic dissection (no branch-vessel compromise, no rupture, no rapidly expanding aorta) is managed medically. The priority is reducing aortic wall shear stress with IV beta-blockade first (labetalol or esmolol) to heart rate around 60 and systolic blood pressure 100 to 120 mmHg, with adjunct vasodilator (nitroprusside or GTN) added if pressure target not met. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline; eTG: Cardiovascular)

TEVAR is indicated for COMPLICATED type B (malperfusion, rupture, rapidly expanding aneurysm, refractory pain) or for those who fail medical therapy. Uncomplicated type B is medically managed first. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

This is a type B dissection (distal to the left subclavian artery), not type A. Surgical replacement is for type A dissections, which involve the ascending aorta and risk cardiac tamponade. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guideline)

explanation.summary: Pituitary apoplexy is haemorrhage or infarction within a pituitary tumour. Classic presentation is sudden severe retro-orbital headache, visual loss (chiasmal compression causes bitemporal hemianopia), cranial nerve III/IV/VI palsies (cavernous sinus extension), nausea, vomiting, and acute hypopituitarism with hypoadrenalism (hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia). Immediate management is stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg IV BEFORE any imaging or surgery to prevent cardiovascular collapse. Resuscitate with IV saline, treat hypoglycaemia, then urgent MRI to confirm and neurosurgical referral. Surgery (transsphenoidal decompression) is indicated within 7 days for severe visual loss or rapid deterioration; conservative management with steroids alone is reasonable for those with stable mild visual changes.
key_points: Pituitary apoplexy triad: thunderclap headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia
Acute hypoadrenalism causes hypotension, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV BEFORE imaging or surgery to prevent crisis
Surgery within 7 days for severe visual loss or rapid deterioration
explanation.pearls: Pituitary apoplexy: give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV before MRI or theatre to prevent adrenal crisis; transsphenoidal decompression within 7 days for severe visual loss.

options.rationale: Surgical decompression is the definitive treatment but is delayed by minutes-to-hours of imaging and theatre availability. Untreated adrenal insufficiency in this window causes cardiovascular collapse and death; hydrocortisone goes first. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

Waiting for imaging confirmation before stress-dose steroid risks adrenal crisis in the imaging suite. The diagnosis is strongly suspected on clinical grounds (known macroadenoma plus thunderclap headache plus visual loss plus cranial nerve palsy plus hypotension plus hyponatraemia) and treatment is empiric. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

The hyponatraemia here is secondary to glucocorticoid deficiency and resolves with hydrocortisone replacement plus isotonic saline. Hypertonic saline is not the first or appropriate intervention. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

Mannitol may have a role in raised ICP but does not address the underlying adrenal insufficiency, and aggressive osmotic diuresis in a hypotensive hypovolaemic patient worsens haemodynamics. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline)

Pituitary apoplexy with hypotension, hyponatraemia, and hypoglycaemia indicates acute hypoadrenalism. Stress-dose hydrocortisone 100 mg IV must precede imaging and surgery to prevent cardiovascular collapse. Then urgent MRI confirms diagnosis and neurosurgery decides on decompression timing. (Source: ESE Pituitary Apoplexy Guideline; AMH)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection (necrotising fasciitis, gas gangrene, Fournier gangrene) is a surgical emergency. Clinical hallmarks are pain out of proportion to skin findings, rapid progression over hours, dusky or mottled skin, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia over the affected area, and systemic toxicity. The LRINEC score (CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) supports diagnosis: 6 or more intermediate probability, 8 or more high probability. Plain X-ray or CT may show subcutaneous gas. The single most important intervention is urgent surgical debridement within 6 hours; every hour of delay increases mortality. Empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression) accompany but do not replace surgery. Resuscitation, source control, and ICU support run in parallel.
key_points: LRINEC 6 to 7 intermediate, 8 or more high probability of necrotising fasciitis
Time to surgical debridement is the dominant mortality determinant
Empirical: meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (toxin suppression)
Bullae, crepitus, pain out of proportion, subcutaneous gas are late signs
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis with LRINEC of 8 or more plus subcutaneous gas: surgical debridement within 6 hours dominates mortality; meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin accompany but do not replace surgery.

sources.label: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.rationale: Necrotising soft tissue infection (LRINEC at least 8 high probability, subcutaneous gas, crepitus, bullae, pain out of proportion, septic shock) requires urgent operative debridement within hours. Time to surgery is the single biggest determinant of mortality. Empirical antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin) accompany but do not replace surgery. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic; ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.rationale: MRI may add diagnostic certainty in equivocal cases but the clinical and biochemical picture here is unambiguous; waiting for MRI delays definitive surgery by hours and worsens mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Flucloxacillin alone does not cover the polymicrobial flora (Streptococcus pyogenes, anaerobes, Gram-negative rods) typical of type I necrotising fasciitis. Watchful waiting in any necrotising infection costs lives. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

HBO has an adjunctive role in some institutions but never replaces or precedes surgical debridement. Time-to-surgery dominates mortality in necrotising fasciitis above all else. (Source: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

options.rationale: Fluid resuscitation begins in parallel and is essential, but it does not address the source which is necrotic tissue that must be excised. Without source control, sepsis progresses despite optimal fluid management. (Source: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines)
source_refs: ANZBA Necrotising Soft Tissue Infection Guidelines

explanation.summary: Acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant adults requiring admission is empirically treated with IV gentamicin (5 to 7 mg/kg once-daily, calculated by ideal body weight) plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly per Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic. Mild pyelonephritis suitable for outpatient management can be treated with oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate guided by local resistance. Always send urine and blood cultures before antibiotics. Step-down to a culture-directed oral agent for a total 10 to 14 day course. Consider imaging (CT or US) if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours or if anatomic abnormalities are suspected.
key_points: Moderate to severe pyelonephritis: IV gentamicin once-daily plus IV amoxicillin first-line
Mild outpatient pyelonephritis: oral ciprofloxacin or amoxicillin-clavulanate
Always urine and blood cultures before antibiotics; step-down to oral by sensitivity
Imaging at 48 to 72 hours if no improvement to exclude complications
explanation.pearls: Adult acute pyelonephritis (admission): IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg once-daily plus IV amoxicillin 2 g six hourly per Therapeutic Guidelines. Step-down to culture-directed oral for total 10 to 14 days. Image if no improvement at 48 to 72 hours.

options.rationale: Oral ciprofloxacin is reserved for mild pyelonephritis suitable for outpatient management. Significant fever, rigors, and raised inflammatory markers warrant initial IV therapy and observation under Therapeutic Guidelines. Fluoroquinolone resistance in E. coli is also a regional issue. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic recommends IV gentamicin plus amoxicillin (or ampicillin) as first-line empirical therapy for moderate to severe acute pyelonephritis in non-pregnant adults requiring admission. Gentamicin covers gram-negative uropathogens including most E. coli; amoxicillin extends cover for enterococci. Step-down to oral guided by culture and sensitivity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Trimethoprim is appropriate for uncomplicated lower UTI when local resistance is low. It does not provide adequate parenteral cover for pyelonephritis and oral monotherapy is insufficient at this severity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Vancomycin targets gram-positive organisms (MRSA, enterococci) and does not cover the dominant gram-negative uropathogens. It is not an empirical choice for pyelonephritis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Meropenem is reserved for severe sepsis with risk factors for multi-drug resistance, ESBL exposure, or failure of first-line. Routine first-line use drives carbapenem resistance and is not Therapeutic Guidelines first-line. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: GOLD 2024 and Lung Foundation Australia's COPD-X guideline use exacerbation history and eosinophil count to direct ICS use. Patients with two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation per year on LAMA or LABA monotherapy should escalate to LAMA plus LABA, with ICS added if eosinophils are 300 cells per microlitre or higher (or 100 to 300 with frequent exacerbations). Triple therapy in a single inhaler improves adherence. After 3 to 6 months of triple therapy, ICS can be considered for withdrawal if no exacerbations and eosinophils remain low; long-term azithromycin is added for ongoing frequent exacerbators despite triple therapy.
key_points: Two or more moderate exacerbations per year on LAMA: escalate to LAMA plus LABA plus ICS if eosinophils 300 or higher
ICS benefit is greatest at eosinophils 300 cells per microlitre or higher
Long-term azithromycin reserved for frequent exacerbators despite triple inhaler
ICS monotherapy is not used in COPD; pneumonia risk and inferior outcomes
explanation.pearls: GOLD/COPD-X COPD escalation: two or more exacerbations on LAMA, escalate to LAMA+LABA+ICS especially if eosinophils 300 cells per microlitre or higher. Long-term azithromycin only for frequent exacerbators on triple therapy. ICS monotherapy is not used in COPD.

options.rationale: Long-term macrolide prophylaxis is considered for frequent exacerbators on optimal inhaled therapy including triple inhaler; it is not the next step before escalating inhalers. Cardiac and hearing screening are required. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

LAMA plus LABA (no ICS) is appropriate if eosinophils are below 100 cells per microlitre and exacerbations are infrequent. With eosinophils 380 and three exacerbations in a year, ICS is indicated under GOLD and COPD-X. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

GOLD 2024 and Lung Foundation Australia recommend escalating to triple therapy (LAMA plus LABA plus ICS) for patients with two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation per year despite LAMA monotherapy, particularly when blood eosinophils are 300 cells per microlitre or higher. ICS efficacy is greatest in this eosinophilic phenotype. (Source: GOLD 2024 Strategy; COPD-X Australian Guidelines)
Theophylline has a narrow therapeutic window and modest bronchodilator effect; it is reserved for refractory cases when inhaled options are exhausted. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)
ICS monotherapy in COPD is inferior to LAMA monotherapy and increases pneumonia risk. Stopping the LAMA is harmful. (Source: GOLD 2024; COPD-X)

explanation.summary: The NHFA/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines recommend oral anticoagulation for non-valvular AF when the CHA2DS2-VA score is 2 or higher. DOACs are preferred over warfarin in non-valvular AF for non-inferior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage, and no INR monitoring. Apixaban is the preferred DOAC in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50). Apixaban dose reduction (2.5 mg twice daily) requires two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. Aspirin is no longer recommended for AF stroke prevention; LAA closure is reserved for those with anticoagulation contraindications.
key_points: CHA2DS2-VA 2 or higher: oral anticoagulation indicated; DOAC preferred over warfarin
Apixaban is preferred in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50)
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or higher
Aspirin is removed from AF stroke prevention; LAA closure if anticoagulation contraindicated
explanation.pearls: AF stroke prevention NHFA/CSANZ: CHA2DS2-VA 2 or higher gets a DOAC, preferably apixaban in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50). Reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 or higher.

sources.label: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.rationale: Dabigatran is highly renally cleared (80%) and is dose-adjusted in CKD. While usable here, apixaban is preferred in moderate CKD due to lower renal dependence and better bleeding profile in elderly patients. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.rationale: Aspirin is no longer recommended for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. It has minimal benefit and similar bleeding risk to anticoagulants. NHFA/CSANZ explicitly removes aspirin from AF stroke prevention. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.rationale: Warfarin is acceptable when DOACs are contraindicated, but DOACs (particularly apixaban) are preferred first-line in this setting given non-inferior efficacy, lower intracranial haemorrhage, and no INR monitoring. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.rationale: Apixaban is the preferred DOAC in moderate CKD (eGFR 30 to 50) under NHFA/CSANZ AF guidance because of its lower renal clearance (about 27%) and a strong real-world safety profile. Standard dose 5 mg twice daily applies; dose reduction to 2.5 mg twice daily requires two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 micromol/L or higher. She meets none. (Source: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

options.rationale: LAA closure is reserved for patients with contraindications to long-term oral anticoagulation. She has no contraindications and tolerates oral therapy. (Source: NHFA/CSANZ AF Guidelines)
source_refs: National Heart Foundation/CSANZ Atrial Fibrillation Guidelines

explanation.summary: Insulin with dextrose is the workhorse shifting therapy in hyperkalaemia, and hypoglycaemia is its predictable complication. Capillary glucose is checked hourly for at least six hours, and a dextrose infusion is considered in renal impairment.
key_points: Hypoglycaemia occurs in up to 15% of patients given insulin for hyperkalaemia.
Renal impairment prolongs insulin action and raises the risk further.
The nadir typically falls after the dextrose bolus has been metabolised, one to six hours later.
explanation.context: Insulin drives potassium into cells by activating the sodium-potassium ATPase in skeletal muscle, an effect that is independent of its glucose lowering action but inseparable from it in practice. A 10 unit dose lowers serum potassium by roughly 0.6 to 1.0 mmol/L within an hour and the effect lasts several hours, whereas 25 g of dextrose is cleared much sooner. Insulin is renally cleared, so the patients who most often need it for hyperkalaemia are exactly the ones in whom it lingers. Anticipating that mismatch, rather than reacting to a collapse, is what the monitoring plan is for.

sources.label: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Hypoglycaemia follows insulin given for hyperkalaemia in up to one in six patients, often after the dextrose bolus has been cleared and most often in renal impairment, where insulin clearance is reduced. Hourly testing for about six hours detects it. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

A single pre-meal glucose suits routine inpatient surveillance in a patient with diabetes who has not received a potassium shifting dose of insulin. It is far too infrequent to catch the post-insulin nadir. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
A morning venous glucose tracks glycaemic control over days. Hypoglycaemia after a shifting dose happens within hours and will have come and gone by then. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)

Hourly blood pressure belongs in routine observations, but haemodynamic monitoring does not detect the specific complication that this treatment causes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Renal Dysfunction)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

options.rationale: Stopping glucose checks is safe only where no insulin has been given. The dextrose is cleared well before the insulin effect ends, which is precisely when the glucose falls. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook)
source_refs: Kidney Health Australia CARI - Hyperkalaemia management

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency with mortality strongly correlated with time to debridement. Clinical clues are pain out of proportion to skin findings, dusky or purpura-like skin, crepitations, tenderness beyond erythema, rapid progression, and systemic toxicity (septic shock, AKI). The LRINEC score uses CRP, WCC, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, and glucose; a score of 6 or higher is high risk and 8 or higher is very high risk. Empirical antibiotics in Australia are meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin (clindamycin for exotoxin suppression in group A streptococcal cases). Imaging must not delay theatre.
key_points: Time to surgical debridement is the strongest mortality determinant
Empirical antibiotics: meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin
LRINEC 6 or higher is high risk; 8 or higher is very high risk
Imaging must not delay theatre
explanation.pearls: Necrotising fasciitis: immediate surgical debridement plus IV meropenem + vancomycin + clindamycin (clindamycin for exotoxin suppression). LRINEC 6 or higher is high risk. Do not delay theatre for imaging.

options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, dusky skin, tenderness beyond erythema, septic physiology, and LRINEC of 9 (high risk, more than 6) make necrotising fasciitis the working diagnosis. Survival depends on time to surgical debridement, which is the definitive treatment. Empirical IV antibiotics (meropenem plus vancomycin plus clindamycin under Therapeutic Guidelines) and resuscitation are given concurrently. CT or MRI must not delay theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Outlining cellulitis and watching is appropriate for uncomplicated cellulitis without sepsis or red flags. The features here mandate operative assessment, not observation. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Imaging supports diagnosis but must not delay theatre when clinical suspicion is high. CT or MRI may show gas or fascial fluid but a normal scan does not exclude necrotising fasciitis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Hyperbaric oxygen is an adjunct considered only after surgical debridement. It does not replace operative source control. Piperacillin-tazobactam alone misses the clindamycin role in suppressing exotoxin production. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Monotherapy with flucloxacillin and observation in the setting of suspected necrotising fasciitis delays definitive care and increases mortality. The patient needs immediate broad-spectrum cover and theatre. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism is defined by sustained hypotension (systolic BP under 90 mmHg for at least 15 minutes or needing vasopressors) or shock not from another cause. Mortality without reperfusion is high. ESC and Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular recommend systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg IV over 2 hours, or a weight-based bolus during cardiac arrest) with unfractionated heparin if there are no absolute contraindications (active intracranial pathology, recent ischaemic stroke, active bleeding). Catheter-directed thrombolysis and surgical embolectomy are alternatives. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient.
key_points: Massive PE: shock or sustained hypotension warrants reperfusion therapy
Alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin is the standard regimen
Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an alternative where available
Surgical embolectomy if thrombolysis contraindicated or failed
explanation.pearls: Massive PE with shock: IV alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin if no absolute contraindication. Catheter-directed thrombolysis or surgical embolectomy when contraindications or failure. Anticoagulation alone is insufficient.

sources.label: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Surgical embolectomy is reserved for patients with contraindications to thrombolysis or failed thrombolysis, and where cardiac surgical capability is on-site. Systemic thrombolysis remains first-line where not contraindicated. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Therapeutic enoxaparin alone is appropriate for non-massive PE. With shock and RV failure, the patient needs reperfusion therapy; anticoagulation alone has high mortality. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: DOAC monotherapy is appropriate for intermediate-low or low-risk PE in haemodynamically stable patients suitable for outpatient care. Shock and RV dysfunction exclude this pathway. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: Massive (high-risk) pulmonary embolism with sustained hypotension and right heart dysfunction has high short-term mortality. Australian and ESC guidelines recommend systemic thrombolysis (alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours, or 0.6 mg/kg over 15 minutes in cardiac arrest) when there are no absolute contraindications. Catheter-directed thrombolysis is an alternative in centres where it is available. (Source: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism; Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

options.rationale: IVC filters are considered when anticoagulation is absolutely contraindicated or when recurrent PE occurs despite anticoagulation. They do not address the existing clot burden and provide no haemodynamic benefit. (Source: ESC PE Guidelines)
source_refs: ESC Guidelines for Acute Pulmonary Embolism

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and altered mental status, typically precipitated by a stress event (infection, surgery, trauma) in a patient with adrenal insufficiency. Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology directs immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus followed by 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly), IV crystalloid resuscitation (1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride in the first hour, then guided by haemodynamics), and IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Always treat empirically; diagnostic short Synacthen testing waits for stability. Sick-day rules and emergency hydrocortisone injection kits prevent crises in known patients.
key_points: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly)
IV 0.9% sodium chloride resuscitation; IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Empirical treatment; do not wait for short Synacthen testing in crisis
Sick-day rules and emergency injection kit prevent crisis in known patients
explanation.pearls: Adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg per 24 hours by infusion (or 50 mg six hourly). IV 0.9% saline resuscitation and IV dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Empirical treatment; do not wait for Synacthen testing.

options.rationale: Oral hydrocortisone is inappropriate in a vomiting drowsy patient; absorption is unreliable and the patient cannot keep it down. IV is the route in crisis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dexamethasone is used when diagnostic short Synacthen testing is planned and cortisol assay must not be confounded, in patients without an established diagnosis. In an established Addison's patient with a clear crisis, hydrocortisone is preferred for its mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis is a life-threatening glucocorticoid deficiency state. Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology and the Endocrine Society direct immediate IV hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus, then 200 mg per 24 hours as a continuous infusion (or 50 mg six hourly), plus IV fluid resuscitation and dextrose for hypoglycaemia. Bolus hydrocortisone at this dose has sufficient mineralocorticoid effect; separate fludrocortisone is unnecessary acutely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Endocrine Society Adrenal Insufficiency Guideline)

Fludrocortisone is not available as an IV preparation in Australia. Hydrocortisone at high dose provides mineralocorticoid activity that adequately covers the acute phase. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Adrenal crisis is treated empirically. Withholding glucocorticoid pending diagnostic testing in an established or suspected crisis is associated with mortality. Diagnostic testing is performed later, on stable dose. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Inferior STEMI carries a 30 to 50% risk of right ventricular involvement, especially when the proximal RCA is occluded. V4R lead with ST elevation of 1 mm or more confirms RV involvement. The right ventricle is preload-dependent, so RV infarction creates pseudo-cardiogenic shock that responds to fluid loading. Nitrates, morphine, and diuretics are avoided because they reduce preload. Primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact is the reperfusion strategy of choice; fibrinolysis only if PCI not accessible within 120 minutes. Bradycardia and AV block are common in inferior infarcts and may need atropine or temporary pacing.
key_points: RV infarction is preload-dependent: load fluid, avoid nitrates, morphine, and diuretics
V4R ST elevation 1 mm or more confirms RV involvement
Primary PCI within 90 minutes is preferred over fibrinolysis
Bradycardia and AV block are common; atropine or temporary pacing as needed
explanation.pearls: Inferior STEMI with V4R ST elevation: RV infarct is preload-dependent. Fluid load, AVOID nitrates/morphine/diuretics, refer for primary PCI within 90 minutes. Be ready for bradyarrhythmia.

options.rationale: Inferior STEMI with right-sided V4R elevation indicates right ventricular involvement. RV infarcts are preload-dependent: nitrates and morphine are AVOIDED because they reduce preload and cause hypotension. Fluid loading restores RV output. Primary PCI within 90 minutes is the reperfusion strategy of choice. (Source: CSANZ Acute Coronary Syndrome Guidelines)

Nitrates are contraindicated in RV infarction because they drop preload to the already volume-dependent right ventricle and can precipitate hypotension and cardiogenic shock. The first GTN dose already caused profound hypotension; further GTN would worsen this. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)
Diuresis worsens RV infarct shock by reducing preload further. Furosemide is appropriate for LV failure with pulmonary oedema, which is not present here. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

Beta-blockers are deferred in haemodynamically unstable inferior STEMI, particularly with bradycardia and RV infarction, due to risk of cardiogenic shock and worsening AV block. They are introduced once stable. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)
Primary PCI is preferred over fibrinolysis when available within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Fibrinolysis is reserved for centres without timely access to PCI. (Source: CSANZ ACS Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura is suggested by microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia (schistocytes, raised LDH, low haptoglobin, DAT-negative anaemia), thrombocytopenia, with or without neurology, renal impairment, or fever, in the absence of an alternative explanation. Plasma exchange is the definitive treatment and is initiated urgently. Platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes and is reserved for major bleeding only.
key_points: TTP pentad (now non-mandatory): MAHA, thrombocytopenia, neurology, renal impairment, fever.
PLASMIC score predicts severe ADAMTS13 deficiency.
Plasma exchange is first-line; FFP is a bridge if exchange is delayed.
Avoid platelet transfusion except for major bleeding.
explanation.pearls: TTP demands urgent plasma exchange; platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes because it fuels microvascular thrombosis, so reserve transfusion for life-threatening bleeding.

options.rationale: Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia plus thrombocytopenia in the absence of an alternative explanation is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura until proven otherwise. PLASMIC score is high. Plasma exchange is the definitive treatment because it removes the inhibitor and replaces ADAMTS13. Platelet transfusion is associated with worse outcomes (thrombosis) and is reserved for life-threatening bleeding. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP; BSH guidelines for thrombotic microangiopathies)

Platelet transfusion in suspected TTP can precipitate microvascular thrombosis (stroke, myocardial infarction, mesenteric ischaemia) and is associated with worse outcomes. Reserve for major or life-threatening bleeding. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

There is no clinical evidence of sepsis (no fever beyond mild, no focal source, normal lactate, normal coagulation). Treating as sepsis delays plasma exchange in TTP. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

Corticosteroids are an adjunct to plasma exchange (often combined with caplacizumab and rituximab) but monotherapy delays definitive treatment. Plasma exchange is the upstream intervention. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

FFP infusion is a temporising measure when plasma exchange cannot be initiated immediately, but it does not replace exchange. The question stem indicates haematology is available and the next step is to initiate exchange, not infuse FFP indefinitely. (Source: ISTH guidelines for TTP)

explanation.summary: Prosthetic valve endocarditis (PVE) within 12 months of surgery is dominated by Staphylococcus aureus and coagulase negative staphylococci, often methicillin resistant, with biofilm formation on the prosthesis. Australian empirical therapy is vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin. Late PVE (over 12 months) and native valve endocarditis follow a different empirical regimen (benzylpenicillin plus flucloxacillin plus gentamicin). Surgery is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection, large vegetation greater than 10 mm with embolism, perivalvular abscess, or fungal endocarditis.
key_points: Early PVE (< 12 months): vancomycin + gentamicin + rifampicin
Late PVE and native valve: benzylpenicillin + flucloxacillin + gentamicin
Modified Duke criteria for diagnosis
TOE more sensitive than TTE; mandatory for PVE
Surgical indications: heart failure, uncontrolled infection, abscess, large vegetation with embolism
explanation.pearls: Rifampicin must NEVER be started before two negative blood cultures on vancomycin or daptomycin - introducing rifampicin into a high inoculum staphylococcal bacteraemia rapidly selects rifampicin-resistant mutants and renders the biofilm-active drug useless.

options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin plus gentamicin is appropriate for empirical native valve endocarditis with subacute presentation but does not cover methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus or coagulase negative staphylococci, both of which are common in early prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Flucloxacillin covers methicillin sensitive Staphylococcus aureus but misses MRSA, coagulase negative staphylococci, and lacks biofilm penetration appropriate for prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Prosthetic valve endocarditis under 12 months from surgery is treated empirically as for staphylococci including MRSA, with vancomycin plus gentamicin plus rifampicin to penetrate biofilm. Rifampicin is added once stable on vancomycin/gentamicin for biofilm activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Q fever endocarditis is unusual outside livestock contact and typically presents with culture negative endocarditis; empirical cover for the common pathogens of prosthetic valve endocarditis is the priority while serology is pending. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

Piperacillin-tazobactam is appropriate for nosocomial sepsis but does not cover MRSA or coagulase negative staphylococci which dominate early prosthetic valve endocarditis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) in Australia follows ASHM guidelines. High risk exposures (percutaneous injury with hollow needle and visible blood from a known HIV source, receptive anal intercourse with HIV positive source) warrant three drug PEP for 28 days within 72 hours; tenofovir/emtricitabine plus an integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir) is the preferred backbone. Baseline HIV, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, syphilis, and pregnancy testing where applicable are arranged. Follow up HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months (4th generation antigen-antibody) confirms or excludes seroconversion. Counselling on safer sex and abstinence from blood donation until cleared is essential.
key_points: Start PEP within 72 hours (earlier the better), continue for 28 days
Three drug regimen: tenofovir + emtricitabine + integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir)
Baseline HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis, pregnancy test where applicable
Follow up 4th generation HIV serology at 6 weeks and 3 months
Discontinue PEP if source confirmed HIV negative or genuinely durably undetectable
explanation.pearls: Source virological suppression (durable undetectable on ART for at least 6 months with documented adherence) reduces sexual transmission risk to effectively zero (U=U) but for high risk percutaneous needlestick the residual uncertainty about source adherence usually still warrants PEP unless real-time viral load can be confirmed.

options.rationale: Undetectable viral load on treatment for at least six months strongly reduces transmission risk but the ASHM guideline still recommends offering PEP for high risk percutaneous needlestick exposures unless source recent viral load is documented undetectable AND adherence is verified. Documented adherence requires a more recent check than three months. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

PEP duration is 28 days as a fixed course; truncated regimens have not been shown to prevent infection. The chosen regimen is also not the ASHM first line PEP combination. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

Two drug PEP is no longer standard; three drug regimens are preferred for high risk percutaneous exposures because of improved tolerability and resistance profile. Zidovudine is also no longer first line in Australian PEP regimens. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

Hollow bore percutaneous injury with visible blood from a known HIV positive source meets ASHM high risk criteria. Three drug PEP is recommended: tenofovir/emtricitabine backbone plus an integrase inhibitor (raltegravir or dolutegravir) for 28 days, starting within 72 hours (sooner is better; pharmacokinetic effect drops sharply after 48 to 72 hours). (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

Waiting for results delays PEP initiation past the highly time sensitive window. PEP is started immediately and discontinued if the source is later confirmed HIV negative or genuinely undetectable with documented adherence. (Source: ASHM National PEP Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Necrotising soft tissue infection is a surgical emergency with mortality 25 to 35 percent. The LRINEC score (CRP, white cells, haemoglobin, sodium, creatinine, glucose) stratifies probability but does not replace clinical judgement; pain out of proportion, dusky discoloration, bullae, crepitus, and rapidly spreading erythema are red flags. Treatment is simultaneous urgent surgical debridement with empirical broad spectrum antibiotics (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus clindamycin for toxin suppression). IVIG is considered for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome.
key_points: Pain out of proportion to appearance is the classical early sign
LRINEC 6 or more: > 50 percent probability of necrotising fasciitis
Empirical: meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) + vancomycin + clindamycin
Urgent surgical debridement is the cornerstone
Clindamycin added for toxin suppression in streptococcal disease
explanation.pearls: Clindamycin 600 mg IV every 8 hours suppresses streptococcal exotoxin production and continues for at least 48 hours even after surgical source control - the antitoxin benefit is independent of cell wall activity.

options.rationale: LRINEC score of 9 (high probability necrotising fasciitis), pain out of proportion, dusky skin with blistering, and systemic features mandate urgent surgical exploration and broad spectrum antibiotics. Monitoring and narrow spectrum therapy alone is inadequate. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

IVIG is an adjunct for streptococcal toxic shock syndrome where supported, used after source control and broad spectrum antibiotics, not as the first intervention. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

MRI delays definitive treatment and necrotising fasciitis is a clinical diagnosis supported by surgical exploration. Benzylpenicillin alone is inadequate empirical cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)
Hyperbaric oxygen is adjunctive (where available) after surgical debridement, not a substitute for it. Delay risks rapid progression and mortality. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

LRINEC 6 or more raises the probability of necrotising fasciitis to greater than 50 percent and clinical features here (pain out of proportion, dusky/bullous skin, sodium 132, lactate 4.2, CRP 286) all support the diagnosis. Empirical broad spectrum coverage including a beta lactam (meropenem or piperacillin-tazobactam), vancomycin for MRSA, and clindamycin for toxin suppression is standard, with simultaneous surgical debridement. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Acute aortic dissection is classified by Stanford as type A (ascending aorta or arch, always surgical) or type B (descending aorta, usually medical unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture, or persistent pain). Pre-operative management targets dP/dt: heart rate first to 60 to 80 with esmolol or labetalol, then blood pressure to systolic 100 to 120 with vasodilator if needed. CT aortic angiography is the imaging gold standard; transoesophageal echocardiography is an alternative in unstable patients. Mortality is 1 to 2 percent per hour untreated for type A. Predisposing factors include hypertension, bicuspid aortic valve, Marfan and Loeys-Dietz syndromes, family history, and stimulant use.
key_points: Stanford A (ascending): surgical emergency, 1 to 2 percent mortality per hour untreated
Stanford B (descending): medical unless complicated
Heart rate first (esmolol/labetalol) target 60 to 80, then BP target 100 to 120 systolic
Vasodilators alone are dangerous (reflex tachycardia)
CT aortic angiography is the imaging gold standard
explanation.pearls: Untreated Stanford A aortic dissection mortality rises by 1 to 2 percent per hour for the first 48 hours - the 'time is aorta' window is similar in magnitude to STEMI 'time is muscle' but the intervention is operative repair rather than reperfusion.

options.rationale: Type A aortic dissection (ascending aorta involvement on echo, mediastinal widening, asymmetric pulses, new diastolic murmur) is a surgical emergency. Pre-operative care targets heart rate first with esmolol or labetalol to reduce shear stress (dP/dt), then vasodilator if needed for blood pressure. CT aortic angiography confirms anatomy and guides surgical planning. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

Vasodilators alone increase reflex tachycardia and shear stress on the aorta, which can extend the dissection. Heart rate is controlled with a beta blocker first before adding a vasodilator. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

Anticoagulation is contraindicated and catastrophic in aortic dissection; the elevated D-dimer reflects the dissection itself, not pulmonary embolism. CTA must precede any anticoagulation when dissection is suspected. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in hypertensive emergencies because of unpredictable hypotension. Observation without surgical referral for type A dissection has greater than 50 percent mortality at 48 hours. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

Thrombolysis in aortic dissection causes catastrophic haemorrhage. The ECG here shows no ischaemic changes and the clinical picture is dissection, not infarct. (Source: ESC Aortic Diseases Guidelines)

explanation.summary: Massive transfusion in trauma is guided by the National Blood Authority criteria: anticipated requirement of 4 or more units of packed red cells in one hour, or ongoing major bleeding with haemodynamic instability. Australian protocols use balanced 1:1:1 ratios (packed red cells, FFP, platelets), TXA within 3 hours (CRASH-2), goal-directed fibrinogen replacement (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate, target above 1.5 to 2 g/L), calcium supplementation (ionised calcium > 1.1), prevention of hypothermia, and concurrent surgical or interventional radiology source control. ROTEM or thromboelastography guides component therapy.
key_points: Activate MTP for anticipated 4+ units packed red cells in 1 hour or ongoing major bleeding
1:1:1 ratio (RBC:FFP:platelets) until ROTEM/TEG guidance available
TXA 1 g IV bolus + 1 g over 8 hours, within 3 hours of injury (CRASH-2)
Fibrinogen target > 1.5 to 2 g/L (cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate)
Ionised calcium > 1.1 mmol/L; avoid hypothermia and acidosis
explanation.pearls: Every unit of citrated packed red cells lowers ionised calcium - after 4 units, give 10 mL of 10 percent calcium gluconate (or 10 mL of 10 percent calcium chloride via central access) to keep ionised calcium above 1.1 mmol/L and preserve clotting cascade function.

options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is not first line; it is a rescue agent considered after ratio-balanced transfusion, fibrinogen replacement, surgical control, and correction of acidosis/hypocalcaemia. Routine use has not improved mortality and may increase thrombosis. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

Sequential reassessment under-resuscitates in established trauma induced coagulopathy and risks worsening the acidosis-hypothermia-coagulopathy triad. Activation of the massive transfusion protocol is required when there are signs of ongoing significant bleeding. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

Crystalloid resuscitation in major haemorrhage dilutes clotting factors, worsens acidosis, increases bleeding, and is contraindicated as the primary resuscitation fluid. Damage control resuscitation prioritises blood products. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

Trauma induced coagulopathy with hypothermia, acidosis, ionised hypocalcaemia, and low fibrinogen (Code Crimson criteria) needs simultaneous correction.
