The Australian National Blood Authority massive transfusion protocol uses balanced 1:1:1 ratios, TXA within 3 hours, calcium replacement to maintain ionised calcium > 1.1, and goal-directed fibrinogen replacement to keep fibrinogen above 1.5 to 2 g/L (or FIBTEM A10 > 7 mm). (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

CRASH-2 trial showed tranexamic acid 1 g IV within 3 hours of trauma reduces all-cause mortality (number needed to treat about 67) and death from bleeding (NNT about 121). Delaying TXA beyond 3 hours loses the benefit and may increase thrombosis. (Source: NBA Massive Transfusion Protocol)

explanation.summary: Hypertensive emergency is severe hypertension (typically systolic above 180 or diastolic above 120 mmHg) plus end-organ damage (hypertensive encephalopathy, retinopathy with papilloedema, acute kidney injury, acute pulmonary oedema, aortic dissection, acute coronary syndrome, eclampsia). Australian guidance is to reduce mean arterial pressure by 20 to 25 percent over the first hour, then to about 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours, then gradually to normal over 24 to 48 hours. Specific situations have specific targets (aortic dissection systolic under 120, acute ischaemic stroke under 185/110 if thrombolysis, eclampsia under 160/110). First line agents are intravenous labetalol, nicardipine, or clevidipine; glyceryl trinitrate when pulmonary oedema or ACS dominates.
key_points: Hypertensive emergency = severe HT + end-organ damage
Target 20 to 25 percent MAP reduction in first hour
Avoid sublingual nifedipine and rapid normalisation
Labetalol, nicardipine, clevidipine are first line
Specific targets: aortic dissection systolic < 120; stroke < 185/110 if thrombolysis; eclampsia < 160/110
explanation.pearls: In hypertensive emergency without aortic dissection, lowering mean arterial pressure below 20 to 25 percent of the presenting value in the first hour can cross the autoregulation lower limit (typically 60 to 70 mmHg MAP in normotensives but shifted up by 20 to 30 mmHg in chronic hypertensives) and precipitate watershed ischaemic stroke.

options.rationale: Rapid reduction to under 140/90 within 30 minutes risks cerebral and coronary hypoperfusion in chronically hypertensive patients whose autoregulation has shifted. The target is a controlled 20 to 25 percent fall over the first hour. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Sublingual nifedipine is contraindicated in hypertensive emergency because of unpredictable hypotension, reflex tachycardia, and risk of ischaemic stroke. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hypertensive emergency (severe hypertension plus end-organ damage: papilloedema/retinopathy, acute kidney injury, mild pulmonary venous congestion) requires controlled lowering. Australian and ESC guidance limits initial mean arterial pressure reduction to 20 to 25 percent in the first hour and to around 160/100 over 2 to 6 hours to avoid cerebral hypoperfusion. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Oral therapy alone is too slow for hypertensive emergency with end-organ damage. Intravenous therapy with continuous monitoring is required for at least the first 24 hours. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Hydralazine causes unpredictable hypotension and reflex tachycardia, and the target diastolic of under 70 risks coronary hypoperfusion in left ventricular hypertrophy. Labetalol or a nicardipine/clevidipine infusion are preferred where available. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Adrenal crisis is a medical emergency with mortality 6 to 15 percent in known Addison disease, precipitated by intercurrent illness, surgery, missed doses, or new corticosteroid antagonists. Immediate management is intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion or divided 50 mg six hourly), 1 L 0.9 percent saline in the first hour, glucose correction, identification and treatment of the precipitant, and continuation of stress dose steroids until clinical recovery. Major surgery requires 100 mg pre-induction, then 200 mg over 24 hours; minor surgery requires double the usual dose for 24 hours. Mineralocorticoid replacement (fludrocortisone) resumes only when hydrocortisone falls below 50 mg/day.
key_points: Diagnose adrenal crisis on clinical grounds; do not delay treatment for testing in established disease
Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours (infusion or 50 mg six hourly)
1 L 0.9 percent saline in first hour; correct glucose with dextrose if hypoglycaemic
Major surgery: 100 mg pre-induction, 200 mg/24 h until oral intake
Fludrocortisone unnecessary while hydrocortisone > 50 mg/day
explanation.pearls: Australian Addison Disease emergency cards specify an intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg dose kept by the patient for self administration before transfer to hospital - the time-critical step that prevents death during gastroenteritis when oral steroids cannot be absorbed.

options.rationale: Adrenal crisis precipitated by sepsis and surgical illness needs immediate parenteral hydrocortisone (100 mg IV bolus then 200 mg over 24 hours by infusion or 50 mg six hourly), aggressive fluid resuscitation, glucose correction, treatment of the precipitant (broad spectrum antibiotics, surgical source control), and continuation of stress dose hydrocortisone perioperatively. Mineralocorticoid replacement is unnecessary at hydrocortisone doses above 50 mg/day because of cross-binding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Oral therapy is inadequate during vomiting, sepsis, and impending major surgery; absorption is unreliable and underdosing precipitates further crisis. Parenteral stress dose hydrocortisone is mandatory. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity and is reserved for the diagnostic phase (does not interfere with cortisol assays). Hydrocortisone is preferred for treatment because it provides both glucocorticoid and at high doses sufficient mineralocorticoid activity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Diagnosis is already established (15 year history of Addison disease). Withholding hydrocortisone for repeat testing during a life threatening crisis is dangerous and unnecessary. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Fludrocortisone is only available orally and has no role during acute crisis; hydrocortisone at stress doses provides adequate mineralocorticoid activity. The acute priority is intravenous hydrocortisone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 or more) or any hyperkalaemia with ECG changes is treated in the order: calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10 percent intravenous over 2 minutes for myocardial stabilisation, insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose for intracellular shift, salbutamol 10 to 20 mg nebulised as additional shift, removal of offending drugs (ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID), and definitive removal via diuresis, gut binders, or dialysis.
key_points: Severe hyperkalaemia: K >= 6.5 or any K with ECG changes
Sequence: stabilise myocardium, shift intracellular, then remove
Calcium gluconate 10 mL 10% IV over 2 min (peripheral preferred)
Insulin 10 units + 50 mL 50% dextrose IV; salbutamol 10-20 mg nebulised
Stop ACE inhibitor, ARB, potassium-sparing diuretic, NSAID
explanation.pearls: Calcium gluconate stabilises the myocardium within 2 to 3 minutes of administration and lasts 30 to 60 minutes, but does not lower potassium - the shift and removal steps must still follow.

options.rationale: Calcium chloride is more vesicant than calcium gluconate; gluconate is preferred for peripheral administration. Calcium also protects the myocardium but does not lower potassium, so further intracellular shift agents are required. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate has slow onset (hours) and limited evidence; it is not appropriate as monotherapy in severe hyperkalaemia with ECG changes. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

Insulin-dextrose is essential to shift potassium intracellularly but does not address myocardial protection or remove potassium. Calcium gluconate is given first for myocardial stabilisation. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

Severe hyperkalaemia (potassium 6.5 or more) with ECG changes requires immediate calcium gluconate for myocardial stabilisation, then potassium-shifting therapy (insulin-dextrose and salbutamol nebuliser), and removal of offending drugs (ACE inhibitor and potassium-sparing diuretic). Definitive removal is via diuresis, resin, or dialysis. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

Sodium bicarbonate has modest potassium-lowering effect and is reserved for severe metabolic acidosis. Haemodialysis is definitive but is preceded by myocardial stabilisation and pharmacological potassium shift. (Source: KHA Hyperkalaemia)

explanation.summary: Adult DKA management is fluid first (0.9 percent saline 500 mL to 1 L over 15 to 30 minutes followed by 250 to 500 mL per hour) then intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour. Add potassium chloride when serum potassium falls below 5.5 mmol/L because total body potassium is depleted despite normal or high initial serum levels. Switch to 5 percent dextrose with saline once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin while resolving ketoacidosis. Identify and treat the precipitant.
key_points: Fluid bolus 500 mL to 1 L 0.9 percent saline over 15-30 min
Ongoing replacement 250-500 mL/hour for total deficit 5-8 L
Insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour after fluids running
Add potassium when serum K < 5.5 mmol/L
Switch to dextrose when glucose < 14 mmol/L
explanation.pearls: Continue the long-acting basal insulin alongside the insulin infusion to avoid rebound DKA when the infusion is stopped, and overlap subcutaneous rapid-acting insulin with the infusion by 1 to 2 hours during transition.

sources.label: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.rationale: Maintenance-only fluids after a single bolus undertreat the typical 5 to 8 litre deficit of adult DKA. Aggressive replacement is required, although tailored to age and comorbidity. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.rationale: Insulin should follow fluid resuscitation by 15 to 30 minutes; insulin without volume expansion risks worsening hypotension and cerebral oedema. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.rationale: Intramuscular insulin is unreliable in DKA because of poor peripheral perfusion; a continuous intravenous insulin infusion is required after fluid resuscitation. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.rationale: Dextrose is added only once blood glucose falls below 14 mmol/L to allow ongoing insulin infusion without hypoglycaemia; it is not first-line fluid in early DKA. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

options.rationale: Adult DKA initial management: rapid crystalloid bolus to restore intravascular volume, then ongoing replacement at 250 to 500 mL/hour, with intravenous insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour commenced after fluids are running and potassium has been measured. Add potassium when serum K is below 5.5 mmol/L. (Source: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines)
source_refs: APEG and ADS Adult DKA Guidelines

explanation.summary: Severe and life-threatening asthma exacerbation is treated with oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95 percent, repeated nebulised salbutamol (with ipratropium for severe exacerbations), systemic corticosteroid (oral prednisolone 50 mg or intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg), and intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes when peak flow remains below 50 percent. Refractory cases escalate to aminophylline, salbutamol infusion, heliox, non-invasive ventilation, or intubation under senior care.
key_points: Severe: PEF < 50 percent, talking words, accessory muscles, HR > 110
Life-threatening: silent chest, SpO2 < 92, exhaustion, normal-rising CO2
Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 20 min when first-line therapy fails
Systemic corticosteroid: prednisolone 50 mg oral or hydrocortisone 200 mg IV
Watch CO2 - rising indicates exhaustion and need for ventilatory support
explanation.pearls: A normal or rising carbon dioxide in a severe asthma exacerbation is a red flag indicating exhaustion and imminent respiratory failure - escalate to senior care and consider intubation rather than continuing the medical ladder.

options.rationale: Severe asthma exacerbation with peak flow under 50 percent, SpO2 under 92 percent on air, and inadequate response to back-to-back beta-agonist gets intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes plus systemic corticosteroid (intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg or oral prednisolone 50 mg) and continuous nebulised salbutamol, with senior review. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Intramuscular adrenaline is reserved for anaphylaxis or peri-arrest asthma where conventional therapy has failed; antibiotics are not routine for asthma exacerbation without a bacterial trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Aminophylline has narrow therapeutic index and is reserved for severe exacerbations refractory to standard therapy; it is not the next step after first-line salbutamol and ipratropium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Intubation is reserved for impending or actual respiratory arrest with falling conscious state, rising carbon dioxide despite maximum therapy, or exhaustion; this patient still has trial of medical therapy remaining. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

Heliox is an adjunct in selected centres for refractory cases; the evidence base is limited and it is not the next step in standard escalation in Australia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Respiratory)

explanation.summary: The two-tier Wells score for PE stratifies pretest probability as PE likely (over 4 points) or unlikely (4 or fewer). PE likely proceeds directly to CT pulmonary angiogram; PE unlikely has D-dimer with age-adjusted threshold (age multiplied by 10 ng/mL above 50 years, i.e. 0.72 mg/L FEU at 72) and only requires CTPA if D-dimer is above threshold. CTPA is first-line imaging in Australia; V/Q scan is reserved for contrast allergy or significant renal impairment with normal chest radiograph.
key_points: Wells > 4: PE likely, proceed direct to CTPA
Wells <= 4: D-dimer first with age-adjusted threshold over 50 years
Age-adjusted D-dimer threshold: age x 10 ng/mL (or x 0.01 if mg/L FEU)
CTPA is first-line imaging; V/Q for contrast allergy or significant CKD
Lower limb Doppler can confirm DVT and avoid CTPA in high probability cases
explanation.pearls: Age-adjusted D-dimer uses the formula (age in years multiplied by 10 ng/mL FEU) above age 50 - this raises the threshold from a fixed 500 to around 720 at age 72 and avoids unnecessary CTPA in older patients with PE unlikely Wells.

options.rationale: Age-adjusted D-dimer is for ruling out PE in low or moderate clinical probability patients. With a Wells score above 4 the pretest probability is too high for D-dimer to safely rule out PE. (Source: BMJ Best Practice: PE)

Wells > 4 (PE likely) skips D-dimer because of inadequate negative predictive value at high pretest probability. CTPA is the first-line imaging in Australia and is required to rule in or out PE. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

V/Q scan is reserved for renal impairment with low risk of indeterminate scan (clear chest radiograph, young patient) or for contrast allergy; CTPA is first-line in adults without contraindication. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Empirical therapeutic anticoagulation can bridge a delay to imaging but does not replace definitive imaging. Outpatient management of suspected PE in a postoperative patient without confirmation is unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

Lower limb Doppler is a reasonable adjunct (positive Doppler with high pretest probability can avoid CTPA) but is not the primary test in a high probability patient who can have CTPA. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Cardiovascular)

explanation.summary: Hyponatraemia after subarachnoid haemorrhage is most commonly SIADH (euvolaemic, normal urine output) or cerebral salt wasting (hypovolaemic, high urine output, weight loss). Volume status is the key discriminator since urinary sodium and osmolality overlap. Cerebral salt wasting is treated with isotonic saline replacement plus salt loading; SIADH is treated with fluid restriction and tolvaptan if severe. Correction rate is limited to 8 to 10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid central pontine myelinolysis.
key_points: SIADH: euvolaemic, normal weight, treat with fluid restriction
CSW: hypovolaemic, weight loss, polyuria, treat with isotonic saline + salt
Both can have urine sodium > 40 and urine osmolality > 100
Maximum correction 8-10 mmol/L per 24 hours to avoid CPM
Hypertonic saline only for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia
explanation.pearls: Weight loss and polyuria differentiate cerebral salt wasting from SIADH after subarachnoid haemorrhage; the management diverges sharply (fluid replacement vs restriction) so getting the diagnosis right matters more than any single laboratory value.

options.rationale: The picture is volume-contracted (weight loss, dry mucous membranes, polyuria) rather than euvolaemic, making cerebral salt wasting more likely than SIADH. Fluid restriction would worsen cerebral perfusion. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

Hypertonic saline is reserved for severe symptomatic hyponatraemia (seizures, coma). Rapid correction risks central pontine myelinolysis. The current sodium is amenable to careful isotonic replacement. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

Cerebral salt wasting after subarachnoid haemorrhage is treated with isotonic saline replacement and salt loading, with the goal of restoring intravascular volume and sodium without exceeding 8 to 10 mmol/L rise per 24 hours (central pontine myelinolysis risk). Fluid restriction is contraindicated in cerebral salt wasting because it worsens cerebral perfusion. (Source: Australian Stroke Foundation Guidelines)

Demeclocycline blocks vasopressin action and would worsen polyuria and hypovolaemia in cerebral salt wasting. It is also slow to act and rarely used in acute care. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

Tolvaptan is used in euvolaemic or hypervolaemic hyponatraemia (SIADH, heart failure) and is dangerous in hypovolaemic hyponatraemia such as cerebral salt wasting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Stanford type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and is a surgical emergency with mortality rising at 1 to 2 percent per hour without operation. Initial medical therapy targets heart rate under 60 (beta-blocker first to reduce dP/dt and wall stress) and systolic blood pressure under 120, plus opioid analgesia. Beta-blocker must precede any vasodilator (nitroprusside) because vasodilator-induced reflex tachycardia would worsen dissection. Antiplatelets and anticoagulants are contraindicated. Type B is medical first line unless complicated.
key_points: Type A: ascending aorta, surgical emergency, mortality 1-2 percent per hour
Type B: descending aorta beyond left subclavian, medical first line
Pre-op: HR < 60, SBP < 120, beta-blocker before vasodilator
Antiplatelets and anticoagulants contraindicated
Blood pressure differential > 20 mmHg and widened mediastinum are classical signs
explanation.pearls: Beta-blocker before vasodilator in aortic dissection: nitroprusside alone causes reflex tachycardia that increases the shear stress (dP/dt) on the dissection flap and propagates the tear.

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis carries 25 to 35 percent mortality even with prompt surgery and approaches 100 percent without it. Skin signs lag behind subcutaneous disease, so pain out of proportion to appearance and systemic toxicity should prompt operative exploration regardless of how the skin looks. LRINEC 8 or more is high risk (PPV around 65 percent) but a lower score does not rule out the diagnosis. Empirical antibiotics are broad spectrum: meropenem (or piperacillin-tazobactam) plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect plus vancomycin for MRSA, then narrowed on culture.

explanation.summary: This is life-threatening hyperkalaemia (potassium 7.4 mmol/L with PR prolongation and QRS widening beyond peaked T waves) in CKD stage 4. The AU pathway is concurrent: stabilise myocardium (calcium), shift potassium intracellularly (salbutamol then insulin-dextrose), and definitively remove potassium (haemodialysis when eGFR cannot excrete the load). Calcium and salbutamol are bridges only, not definitive potassium removal. QRS widening from 90 to 110 ms indicates progression beyond first-degree changes and the need for both ongoing shifting and definitive removal. Competing guideline cutoffs (KDIGO international vs KHA-CARI Australian) on dialysis indications are similar but the AU framing emphasises early renal team activation in CKD stage 4 with acute hyperkalaemia rather than waiting for a fixed potassium threshold. In context, every acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes in CKD requires concurrent action on three fronts (stabilise, shift, remove) and an immediate dialysis decision rather than a sequential pathway.
key_points: Calcium stabilises myocardium; does NOT lower potassium.
Salbutamol and insulin-dextrose are temporising shifting agents (0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L drop, 2 to 6 hour effect).
Definitive removal requires kidneys, gut binders (slow, chronic), or dialysis (acute, fast).
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow and carries intestinal necrosis risk; not for emergency use.
QRS widening beyond peaked T waves is a sign of progression and an indication for emergency dialysis activation.
explanation.pearls: In acute hyperkalaemia with ECG changes in CKD stage 4 or 5, call the renal team for emergency dialysis concurrently with insulin-dextrose - do not wait for medical management to fail.

options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia of 7.4 mmol/L with ECG changes beyond peaked T waves (PR prolongation, QRS widening from 90 to 110 ms) is life-threatening and requires both ongoing shifting therapy AND definitive removal of potassium. Insulin-dextrose is the second-line shifting agent after calcium and salbutamol; calcium stabilises the myocardium but does NOT lower potassium. Salbutamol shifts potassium intracellularly by approximately 0.5 to 1.0 mmol/L for 2 to 6 hours. The CKD stage 4 (eGFR 18) means the kidney cannot excrete the potassium load and the patient will rebound; emergency haemodialysis is the definitive removal therapy and should be arranged concurrently, not after the medical management has failed. (Source: KHA-CARI: Acute Kidney Injury and Hyperkalaemia; Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology; Australian Resuscitation Council guideline 11.5.1)

Sodium bicarbonate has a small and variable effect on potassium shift and is not recommended as routine first-line shifting therapy in AU guidelines; its role is limited to severe metabolic acidosis with concurrent hyperkalaemia where the acidosis is the dominant contributor. The pH of 7.28 is mild-moderate and the dominant issue is the potassium of 7.4 with ECG changes. Insulin-dextrose plus emergency dialysis is the AU pathway. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)

Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is slow-acting (4 to 6 hours), has limited evidence for emergency hyperkalaemia, and carries a risk of intestinal necrosis (particularly with sorbitol). The Therapeutic Goods Administration has issued warnings; AU practice now favours patiromer or zirconium cyclosilicate for chronic management. In acute life-threatening hyperkalaemia with ECG changes, Resonium is NOT the next step. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia; Australian Medicines Handbook)

Stopping the offending medications is appropriate as part of the management but is not sufficient when potassium is 7.4 with ECG changes; the patient needs ongoing shifting therapy and emergency dialysis or other definitive removal. Outpatient review in 1 week does not address acute hyperkalaemia. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)

Repeating calcium is appropriate if ECG changes persist (every 30 to 60 minutes), but calcium does NOT lower potassium - it only stabilises the myocardium. Repeating salbutamol can add a further 0.3 to 0.5 mmol/L drop. Neither addresses the underlying need to remove potassium from the body in a patient with eGFR 18. Insulin-dextrose plus dialysis activation is the next step. (Source: KHA-CARI: Hyperkalaemia)
